# Machinic Reality Inspire — catalog

A catalog of the most salient artworks, robot art, performances, speculative design and research that reflect on AI and machines, read through machine phenomenology: machine perception, machine bodies, machine interiority, intimacy and care, memory and afterlives, labour and infrastructure, classification and power. Works that merely use AI to generate images are left out. Compiled by Reality Design Lab as idea material for artists, designers and researchers. Each work lists its core idea, how it works, and links to its paper, video and images.

https://machinic.reality.design · 2026-10-18 · 722 creators · 966 works

## Machine Perception

How machines see, hear and sort the world, and what it is like to be seen, heard and labelled by them.

### Seeing Machines & Operational Images

Computer vision, images made by and for machines, the world as a machine sees it.

#### How to See Like a Machine: Images After AI — Trevor Paglen (2026)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Computer vision, Generative model & latent space, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: After AI, images are less pictures for people than operations performed on them: to see like a machine is to ask what an image does and who it is for.
- What it is: Paglen's book on how computer vision and generative AI have changed what images are, moving through psyops, UFO imagery, magicians, PR professionals, adtech and recommendation algorithms to ask what images now do and where they come from rather than what they show.
- How it works: Essays drawing on the artist's two decades of work on machine vision, surveillance and training data, combining visual analysis with cases from military psychological operations to platform advertising (Verso, 192 pages).
- Lens: Machine seeing, Opacity & latent space
- Paper: https://www.versobooks.com/products/3477-how-to-see-like-a-machine (Verso, 2026)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iG4Li4aEwwk
- Images: https://www.versobooks.com/cdn/shop/files/getimage_1f5737da-3f72-437c-86ed-435640d94e53.jpg?v=1791779288
- Project page: https://www.versobooks.com/products/3477-how-to-see-like-a-machine

#### Sixty-seven Milliseconds — fleuryfontaine (2025)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: At 15 frames per second, a surveillance camera can contradict a police account and still miss what happens between its frames: evidence lives in the machine's intervals.
- What it is: A 15-minute animated documentary that reconstructs in CGI a night in 2020 when a French police officer shot a 19-year-old in the head with a 40-mm riot-control launcher; a CCTV camera recording at 15 frames per second caught the projectile in mid-air on a single frame, a 67-millisecond interval.
- How it works: A CGI reconstruction modelled on chronophotography, combining the CCTV footage, eyewitness accounts and wiretaps of the officers involved.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Failure, glitch & error
- Shown at: Visions du Réel, Nyon, 2025; Prix Ars Electronica 2025, Honorary Mention (New Animation Art)
- Video: https://vimeo.com/1064236455
- Images: https://squareeyesfilm.com/content/uploads/2025/03/67MS_Vimeo-1120x630.jpg
- Project page: https://squareeyesfilm.com/films/sixty-seven-milliseconds/

#### The Innocence of Unknowing — Ryat Yezbick, Milo Talwani (2025)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Computer vision, Chatbot & language model
- Idea: Teaching a machine to read news images critically exposes its rash certainty as much as the media's framing; what it cannot learn is to admit not knowing.
- What it is: A feature-length animated documentary in which the artists question 'Aurora', an AI agent they trained in critical theory, about news footage of US mass shootings; its computer-vision readings of police formations, weapons and fleeing bodies become shimmering Gaussian-splat scenes, and the AI never manages to say 'I don't know'.
- How it works: A custom AI agent with computer vision tags archival broadcast footage (police weapons, uniforms, formations, victims' raised arms); the clips are converted into volumetric Gaussian-splat animation and framed by a live dialogue with the agent.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: Tribeca Festival 2025 (Immersive); Prix Ars Electronica 2026, Honorary Mention (New Animation Art); Lumen Prize 2026, Legacy Future finalist
- Video: https://vimeo.com/1160008874
- Images: https://archive.aec.at/asset/3887150/preview/ https://archive.aec.at/asset/3887151/preview/
- Project page: https://ryatyezbick.com

#### Anatomy of Non-Fact. Chapter 1: AI Hyperrealism — Martyna Marciniak (2024)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Generative model & latent space
- Idea: Once photographs become training data, a synthetic image forces us to ask what visual evidence still is.
- What it is: An 18-minute video in which an actor playing the viral AI-generated 'Balenciaga Pope' delivers a monologue on fact and fakery, while the mechanics of image generation, news imagery and digital cloning are taken apart.
- How it works: Forensic and historical research on hoaxes is staged with slapstick, costume, hands-on props and AI-generated material in a single-channel film.
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Machine seeing
- Shown at: Ars Electronica Festival 2024; Prix Ars Electronica 2025, Award of Distinction (Artificial Life & Intelligence)
- Images: https://archive.aec.at/asset/3844471/preview/ https://archive.aec.at/asset/3844472/preview/ https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/63f9efede196cc0cf7cd41e6/66faa9495e2b8520ac801f38_IMG_7524.JPEG
- Project page: https://www.martyna.digital/projects/anatomy-of-non-fact-chapter-1

#### Body Oracle — Ke Huang, Botao Amber Hu (2024)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Generative model & latent space
- Idea: A machine that writes bodies as glyphs makes you notice how you hold yourself toward others.
- What it is: A camera reads a participant's pose, alone or in a group, and turns it into a new pictogram in the style of Chinese oracle-bone script, so a posture becomes a character that can be revisited, imitated and discussed.
- How it works: MoveNet detects body keypoints; a pix2pix model trained on volunteers re-enacting oracle characters maps skeletons to glyphs, then neural style transfer renders them (with Danlin Huang and Cun Lin).
- Lens: Machine seeing, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Shown at: China National Art Exhibition 2024, Chongqing; CVPR 2025 AI Art Gallery, Nashville; IJCAI 2025 Art Gallery, Montréal; SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 XR, Hong Kong
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/3689050.3707688 (TEI 2025)
- Video: https://vimeo.com/1020163664
- Images: https://reality.design/media/_resources/Body%20Oracle/project-body-oracle-figure-01.jpg
- Project page: https://reality.design/project/body-oracle

#### Seeing Forest — Robert Zhao Renhui (2024)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision
- Idea: The forest appears only when something moves: the camera trap is a machine witness to a world no person was there to see.
- What it is: Singapore's pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale: a two-channel video that mixes years of footage from motion-triggered camera traps in Singapore's secondary forests, where wild animals and the occasional human pass by, with scenes of an imagined forest.
- How it works: Camera traps triggered by motion and heat, set by the artist in secondary forests over about eight years, combined with staged and thermal-camera footage in a two-channel video installation.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Machine umwelt
- Shown at: Singapore Pavilion, 60th Venice Biennale 2024; Singapore Art Museum 2025
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LV2X8KQVRgE
- Images: https://images-eflux.b-cdn.net/assets/d615a60a-1b95-4341-9472-fa1bbe306fe1.jpg?&modified=2025-01-24T12:18:09.000Z
- Project page: https://www.e-flux.com/announcements/569538/robert-zhao-renhuiseeing-forest

#### Paragraphica — Bjørn Karmann (2023)
- Type: Speculative design · Machines: Generative model & latent space, Computer vision
- Idea: A camera can perceive without light; its picture shows how a machine imagines a place from data rather than what is there.
- What it is: A camera without a lens: it reads the place you stand in through data (address, weather, time, nearby places), writes it as a paragraph, and turns the paragraph into a 'photograph' with a text-to-image model.
- How it works: Raspberry Pi with a touchscreen queries open location and weather APIs, composes a text prompt and sends it to Stable Diffusion; three dials set data radius, noise seed and guidance scale, and the viewfinder form is modelled on the star-nosed mole.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Machine umwelt, Opacity & latent space
- Video: https://bjoernkarmann.dk/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/paragraphica_30s.mp4
- Images: https://bjoernkarmann.dk/wp-content/uploads/2023/05/camera_below.png
- Project page: https://bjoernkarmann.dk/paragraphica

#### The Follower — Dries Depoorter (2022)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Every staged photo has a second, unposed image taken by a machine, and AI can link the two.
- What it is: Depoorter recorded open webcams in public squares for weeks, scraped Instagram photos tagged at those places, and used AI to find the exact moment each photo was taken: side-by-side clips show the posing influencer and the unseen camera watching.
- How it works: Weeks of footage from publicly accessible webcams were matched against scraped, location-tagged Instagram posts with image-similarity and person-detection software.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mkqT32CEIk8
- Images: https://driesdepoorter.be/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/The-Follower-Dries-Depoorter-small.jpg
- Project page: https://driesdepoorter.be/thefollower/

#### Wind Verification — Guo Cheng (2021)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: A machine that can only see wind through images tries to rebuild it physically: digital reality becomes the reference for the real.
- What it is: A computer-vision model watches short videos of flags from Chinese social media and drives an air pump so that a real flag in the gallery flutters the same way, recreating the wind in the footage.
- How it works: A deep-learning vision algorithm analyses flag motion in collected Douyin/Kuaishou clips and sends control data to an air compressor behind a flag.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Machine umwelt
- Images: https://cdn.guo-cheng.net/files/projectImg/WindVerification/WV_ocat_7.jpg https://cdn.guo-cheng.net/files/projectImg/WindVerification/WV_ocat_1.jpg
- Project page: https://guo-cheng.net/index.php/projects/wind-verification/

#### What the Robot Saw — Amy Alexander (2020)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Platform & recommender algorithm, Computer vision
- Idea: The platform's forgotten videos become visible only through the machine's demographic gaze.
- What it is: A never-ending live-streamed film edited by a robot from the least-viewed YouTube videos of the last hours, titled and grouped using a commercial face-analysis service's labels of age, gender and mood.
- How it works: Software searches YouTube for low-view uploads, analyses them with Amazon Rekognition and other vision models, and edits a continuous film streamed on Twitch.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Images: https://what-the-robot-saw.com/dir/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Screen-Shot-2020-02-07-at-10.40.07-PM-1.png
- Project page: https://what-the-robot-saw.com

#### Membrane — Ursula Damm (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Generative model & latent space
- Idea: A seeing machine does not record the street; it remembers features and reassembles them into a street of its own.
- What it is: A fixed camera watches a Berlin street while a neural network learns its patterns and generates new image sequences from them. Visitors use an interface to steer which learned features the network recombines, watching analysis turn into invention.
- How it works: Live video from a street camera trains a Temporal GAN (TGAN, extended with wavelets) that generates new sequences; an interface lets visitors choose image features.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Opacity & latent space, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Shown at: Kunstverein Tiergarten, Berlin, 2019; Entangled Realities, HEK Basel, 2019
- Video: https://vimeo.com/393106068
- Images: https://ursuladamm.de/api/media/file/Bild06-scaled.jpg https://ursuladamm.de/api/media/file/dunkel3-1536x1116.jpg
- Project page: https://ursuladamm.de/membrane-2019

#### Recoding Art — Bruno Moreschi, Gabriel Pereira (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Machine misreadings of art expose both the machine's categories and the museum's authority.
- What it is: Commercial computer-vision services are asked to read the Van Abbemuseum's collection; their literal, banal labels ('furniture', 'person', 'art') are shown next to the works and set against the museum's expert descriptions.
- How it works: Images of museum works processed by commercial vision APIs; outputs displayed as an alternative catalogue.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Failure, glitch & error
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-020-01059-y (AI & Society 2021)
- Project page: https://brunomoreschi.com/Recoding-Art-Van-Abbemuseum-collection

#### Outra 33ª Bienal de São Paulo — Bruno Moreschi, Gabriel Pereira (2018)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Letting machines and unseen workers describe an art biennial shows how official and automated ways of seeing both decide what counts as the work.
- What it is: Commissioned by the 33rd São Paulo Biennial, an alternative archive of the show: computer-vision systems describe photos and footage of its installation and old archive images, and audio-guide tracks carry the comments of guards, installers and cleaners.
- How it works: Several commercial image-recognition and captioning services label photos and footage of the biennial and its archive; results, unconventional footage of the set-up and interviews are published on a website with the Fundação Bienal. With Bernardo Fontes, Nina Bamberg and Guilherme Falcão.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction
- Shown at: 33ª Bienal de São Paulo, 2018 (commission)
- Video: https://vimeo.com/304188271
- Images: https://freight.cargo.site/t/original/i/0b2c27c426059f35eb9209ca83cc73fd1e01ed3ff7343c62032f1d71ccd3061d/bienal5.jpg https://freight.cargo.site/t/original/i/a94c354d81725099357ce4f666ee06df0089cf207fb041d3bec7cee6dd23636b/bienal3.jpg
- Project page: https://brunomoreschi.com/Outra-33-Bienal

#### TransVision — Jiabao Li, Honghao Deng (2018)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Prosthesis & cyborg
- Idea: Push a media filter to an extreme and wear it, and you feel how much of your seeing is already mediated.
- What it is: Three wearable 'perceptual machines' exaggerate how digital media filter sight: a helmet gives the wearer an allergy to the colour red that grows or shrinks, a breathing silicone mask replaces vision with touch, and a headset lets you earn money by watching ads or pay to see an ad-free world.
- How it works: Head-mounted cameras and displays process the live view in real time (colour masking, light-to-breathing translation, ad overlays); developed with Honghao Deng and Panagiotis Michalatos at Harvard GSD.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Shown at: SIGGRAPH 2019 Art Gallery, Los Angeles; CHI 2019, Glasgow; S+T+ARTS Prize Honorary Mention; ISWC 2018 Design Award
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/3267242.3267293 (ISWC 2018)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xHWTLGjHsyc
- Images: https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/58688c8a6a496327e937e35b/05a54608-e457-4d43-a7ca-82ff78294298/Jiabao+Li+TransVision.jpg
- Project page: https://www.jiabaoli.org/transvision

#### Behold These Glorious Times! — Trevor Paglen (2017)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: We rarely see what a network sees; here the images that teach machines and the machine's own decomposition of them share one screen.
- What it is: A 10-minute video that alternates training images used to teach AI to recognise objects, faces and emotions with the grids of features a deep neural network extracts from them, set to music by Holly Herndon.
- How it works: Training-library images are fed through a convolutional network and its intermediate activations are visualised; the score was made partly with neural voice synthesis and speech-recognition training data.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Opacity & latent space
- Images: https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Paglen-Behold_2017.jpg https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Paglen-Behold_detail.jpg
- Project page: https://paglen.studio/2020/04/09/behold-these-glorious-times/

#### Blink: Humanising Autonomy — Humanising Autonomy (Maya Pindeus, Leslie Nooteboom, Raunaq Bose, Adam Bernstein) (2017)
- Type: Speculative design · Machines: Autonomous vehicle & drone, Computer vision
- Idea: A self-driving car could show what it sees and ask, instead of silently deciding who is in its way.
- What it is: Light panels on the four corners of an autonomous car show the silhouettes of pedestrians it has detected; if a pedestrian's intent is unclear, their silhouette flashes and a tone asks them, and a hand gesture answers, turning the silhouette red or green.
- How it works: Pedestrian detection feeds silhouette displays on the car body; a supervised machine-learning model trained on culture-specific gestures reads pedestrians' replies.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Shown at: S+T+ARTS Prize 2017, Honorary Mention
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B7J8aOFQo70
- Images: https://ars.electronica.art/starts-prize/files/2017/05/humanisingautonomy.jpg
- Project page: https://ars.electronica.art/starts-prize/en/blink-humanising-autonomy/

#### Computed Curation — Philipp Schmitt (2017)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision
- Idea: Letting a machine edit a photobook teaches readers to see through the eyes of an algorithm, including its blind spots.
- What it is: A 29-metre leporello photobook sequenced entirely by a computer: vision algorithms tag, caption and arrange the artist's photographs by content and composition. The odd captions and links invite readers to guess the machine's logic.
- How it works: Image-recognition services generate tags and captions while a layout algorithm links photos by visual and semantic similarity; printed as a leporello and web version.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Failure, glitch & error, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Shown at: DAAD Art Show, German Consulate New York, 2018
- Video: https://vimeo.com/225081193
- Images: https://cdn.philippschmitt.com/media/pages/work/computed-curation/2cadd14424-1586887798/philipp-schmitt_computed-curation-2-1200x630-crop.jpg
- Project page: https://philippschmitt.com/work/computed-curation

#### Dragonfly Eyes — Xu Bing (2017)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: When everyday life is already filmed by machines, a narrative can be assembled from their gaze, and the people in it never consented to be characters.
- What it is: An 81-minute feature film with no camera crew and no actors: a love story edited entirely from over ten thousand hours of Chinese surveillance and livestream footage found online.
- How it works: The team collected public surveillance and livestream clips over several years, then wrote and re-wrote a script to fit the footage and dubbed the voices.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: Locarno Film Festival 2017; Toronto International Film Festival 2017
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-ccfz77ifeU
- Images: https://www.xubing.com/Uploads/Source/Image/20221025/20221025164745_4227.jpg https://www.xubing.com/Uploads/Source/Image/20221025/20221025164831_2975.jpg

#### Learning to See — Memo Akten (2017)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Generative model & latent space
- Idea: A network can only see through what it already knows, and so can we.
- What it is: A camera looks at everyday objects on a table (cables, keys, cloth) and neural networks trained only on waves, fire, clouds or flowers redraw them in real time as seascapes and skies.
- How it works: Custom image-to-image networks (pix2pix-style) trained on single-theme datasets reconstruct a live camera feed of the table as an interactive installation and a series of videos.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Opacity & latent space
- Shown at: AI: More than Human, Barbican, London, 2019; Understanding AI, Ars Electronica Center, Linz
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DE3402nH1wA
- Images: https://media.superradiance.net/cdn-cgi/image/width=1200,fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect/memotv/projects/2017/learning-to-see/images/learning-to-see.jpg
- Project page: https://www.memo.tv/works/learning-to-see/

#### Sight Machine — Trevor Paglen (2017)
- Type: Performance, dance & music · Machines: Computer vision
- Idea: A concert watched by machines shows how little of music, gesture and feeling survives in a machine's description of people.
- What it is: The Kronos Quartet plays live while cameras feed a suite of computer-vision algorithms; what the machines 'see' in the musicians is projected on a screen behind them.
- How it works: Live camera feeds pass through face detection, object recognition, pose and other vision algorithms whose outputs are rendered and projected in real time during the performance.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Failure, glitch & error
- Shown at: Pier 70, San Francisco, 2017; Holland Festival, Amsterdam, 2018; Smithsonian American Art Museum, 2018; Barbican, London, 2019
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5mg3MXETfj4
- Images: https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Paglen-Site_Machine-2017.jpg
- Project page: https://paglen.studio/2019/07/01/sight-machine/

#### VFRAME — Adam Harvey (2017)
- Type: Research prototype · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Machine vision can be turned from the watcher's tool into a witness's tool, if someone builds the dataset for it.
- What it is: A computer-vision toolkit for human-rights researchers that scans huge conflict-zone video archives for specific munitions, such as the 9N235 cluster submunition.
- How it works: Object detectors are trained on synthetic images of munitions made with photogrammetry, 3D rendering and 3D-printed replicas, then run over archives such as the Syrian Archive.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dZgDMvaLLPQ
- Images: https://adam.harvey.studio/vframe/9n235_t4t_02_0306.jpg https://adam.harvey.studio/vframe/vframe_9n235_benchmark_montage.jpg
- Project page: https://vframe.io
- Code: https://github.com/vframeio

#### Objectifier — Bjørn Karmann (2016)
- Type: Research prototype · Machines: Computer vision
- Idea: Teaching a machine to see through examples makes its perception, and its misunderstandings, part of everyday domestic play.
- What it is: A camera-and-socket device you train by example: show it a gesture or situation a few times and it learns when to switch a lamp or radio on, turning the user from consumer into the trainer of a small AI.
- How it works: A camera feeds a neural-network classifier on an embedded computer that controls a power socket; a companion app lets users record positive and negative examples.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Shown at: Copenhagen Institute of Interaction Design (CIID) final project, 2016
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3a825NJMLjk
- Images: https://bjoernkarmann.dk/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/objectifier_apprentice_bjorn_karmann_2016.jpg https://bjoernkarmann.dk/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Objectifier.jpg
- Project page: https://bjoernkarmann.dk/objectifier

#### Words That Remake the World «The Seeker» — Nye Thompson (2016)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: When machines describe the world through surveillance cameras, they begin to write a vocabulary of the world made for and by machines.
- What it is: The Seeker, an AI entity, watched the world through millions of insecure security cameras and named what it saw; its descriptions became a huge drawing and whispering robot avatars (CKRBT, 2019).
- How it works: Custom software harvested frames from unsecured internet cameras and sent them to cloud image-recognition services; labels and confidence scores were logged, mapped and spoken by synthesised voices.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Machine umwelt, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: Victoria and Albert Museum, London
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xv_kITdeCMQ
- Images: https://nyethompson.net/images/WTRTW-2025-thumb.png
- Project page: https://nyethompson.net/works/the-seeker.html

#### Exhausting a Crowd — Kyle McDonald (2015)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Surveillance footage becomes a dataset the moment people start labelling it; the crowd does the machine's watching.
- What it is: Twelve hours of Piccadilly Circus filmed from above become a website where anyone can pause, zoom and attach notes to any person in the crowd. After Georges Perec's 'An Attempt at Exhausting a Place in Paris', it shows what crowd-sourced, annotating surveillance looks like.
- How it works: A 4K camera recorded 3 pm to 3 am from a building on Piccadilly Circus; a custom web player stores time-coded, spatial annotations from online visitors. Made with Jonas Jongejan.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction
- Shown at: All of This Belongs to You, V&A London 2015; IDFA DocLab 2015
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XCEX-B59Sx8
- Images: https://exhaustingacrowd.com/og_image.jpg
- Project page: https://www.exhaustingacrowd.com/
- Code: https://github.com/kylemcdonald/ExhaustingACrowd

#### False Positives — Esther Hovers (2015)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Behavioural detection makes ordinary gestures suspicious; to be 'normal' is to move the way the algorithm expects.
- What it is: Photographs of Brussels' business district, composed from a CCTV vantage point, each staging one of eight 'anomalies' that intelligent surveillance systems are trained to flag, such as standing still or looking back repeatedly.
- How it works: Digital composites of several photographs per scene, based on eight anomalies identified with surveillance experts (standing still, fast movements, lonely objects, corner placement, clusters breaking apart, synchronised movements, repeatedly looking back, deviant directions).
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Shown at: Scotiabank CONTACT Photography Festival, Toronto, 2019; Resistant Faces, Pinakothek der Moderne, Munich, 2021
- Images: https://freight.cargo.site/w/1000/i/O2310842155385471171937562539865/EstherHovers-FalsePositives-08.jpg
- Project page: https://www.estherhovers.com/false-positives-1

#### Jaywalking — Dries Depoorter (2015)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Automated detection makes reporting effortless, and hands the visitor the moral weight of the machine's judgement.
- What it is: Visitors watch live traffic webcams from around the world in which software flags pedestrians crossing on red; with one button they can send a screenshot of the offence to the nearest police station.
- How it works: Live feeds from publicly accessible traffic cameras are analysed for pedestrians in the crossing during a red light; a button emails the captured frame to the local police.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: Mirage Festival, Lyon 2019
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Lxei5Svo0Pg
- Images: https://driesdepoorter.be/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/Mirage-2019-Marion_Bornaz.116.jpg
- Project page: https://driesdepoorter.be/jaywalking/

#### Patterns of Life — Julien Prévieux (2015)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Machine-readable movement has a history: every tracking system first taught bodies how to be measured.
- What it is: Five dancers of the Paris Opera perform choreographies derived from scientific protocols that turned human movement into data, from Marey's chronophotography and Gilbreth's time-motion studies to point-light displays and today's tracking software. The title is the military term for analysing a target's habits from surveillance data.
- How it works: A film shot in six settings in which the dancers re-enact historical and contemporary motion-capture and tracking experiments; co-produced by the Paris Opera's 3e Scène for Prévieux's Centre Pompidou show.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Shown at: Prix Marcel Duchamp 2014 exhibition, Centre Pompidou, Paris 2015–16
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c45IfGRkJ_w
- Project page: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c45IfGRkJ_w

#### Computers Watching Movies — Benjamin Grosser (2013)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Computer vision
- Idea: A machine without our narrative habits looks at different things than we do, which exposes how culturally trained our own looking is.
- What it is: A computer vision system watches six famous film scenes (2001, American Beauty, Inception, Taxi Driver, The Matrix, Annie Hall) and its gaze is drawn as moving sketch lines over black, synced to the original audio.
- How it works: Custom software using computer-vision and AI routines decides where to look in each frame; the traces are rendered as temporal sketches (computationally produced HD video).
- Lens: Machine seeing, Machine umwelt
- Shown at: VIDA 16.0, first prize, 2014
- Video: https://vimeo.com/78711521
- Images: http://bengrosser.com/wp-content/themes/grosser/images/cwm-fb-og-1200x674.png https://bengrosser.com/wp-content/resources/cwm-ludwig-museum-530x345.jpg
- Project page: https://bengrosser.com/projects/computers-watching-movies/

#### Cloud Face — Shinseungback Kimyonghun (2012)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision
- Idea: A detection error reveals that machines, like people, find faces where there are none, but without imagining them.
- What it is: A camera pointed at the sky and a face-detection algorithm collect clouds that the machine identifies as human faces. The prints set machine pareidolia next to our own habit of seeing faces in clouds.
- How it works: Camera, face-detection algorithm and custom software select cloud images; shown as pigment prints and video.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Failure, glitch & error
- Shown at: Ars Electronica Center, Linz 2014–2021
- Video: https://vimeo.com/68958093
- Images: https://djhznh41oxwef.cloudfront.net/works/cloud_face/resized/ssbkyh_detail1.png
- Project page: https://ssbkyh.com/works/cloud_face/

#### AZ: Move and Get Shot — Joana Moll (2011)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Delegating the watch to a motion sensor empties the surveillance of its intent: the machine sees everything that moves and understands none of it.
- What it is: Six films assembled by a bot from motion-triggered surveillance cameras that Arizona landowners set up on the US–Mexico border to publish images of migrants. The cameras fired at any movement, so the archive fills with animals, wind and light as much as people.
- How it works: From 2011 to 2014 a bot checked the landowners' website every 24 hours, saved newly uploaded captures from six cameras to a local server and appended them algorithmically to six continuous films.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine umwelt
- Images: http://www.janavirgin.com/img/works/AZ_MOVE.jpg http://www.janavirgin.com/img/works/az_move_22.jpg
- Project page: http://www.janavirgin.com/azmove.html

#### Desire of Codes — Seiko Mikami (2010)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Industrial robot arm, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Being watched by machines that seem to want something turns surveillance into an encounter with another species.
- What it is: A wall of 90 small sensor units that turn towards visitors like insects, six ceiling-hung robotic arms with cameras and projectors that follow them, and a compound-eye screen mixing their images with other surveillance footage.
- How it works: Infrared and camera tracking steer motorised wall units and robotic search arms; captured footage is stored as a database and replayed with past visitors' images.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: YCAM, Yamaguchi 2010; NTT ICC, Tokyo 2011
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5PKT44tU658
- Images: https://www.ycam.jp/asset/image/_resize/large/archive/works_desire-of-codes_1__MG_9047@2x.jpg?s=1725165
- Project page: https://www.ycam.jp/en/archive/works/desire-of-codes/

#### Postcards from Google Earth — Clement Valla (2010)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Infrastructure, energy & supply chain
- Idea: These are not glitches but the system working as designed: Google Earth is a database disguised as a photograph.
- What it is: Screenshots from Google Earth of bridges melting into rivers and highways draped over hills, sold as postcards on postcard racks.
- How it works: Unmanipulated screenshots where aerial photographs are texture-mapped onto a 3D terrain model that knows nothing about bridges; printed as inkjet postcards and shown on a website.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Failure, glitch & error
- Images: https://www.clementvalla.com/img/wp/2013/09/deception_pass.jpg https://www.clementvalla.com/img/wp/2013/09/MG_9679.jpg
- Project page: https://www.clementvalla.com/work/postcards-from-google-earth.html

#### Sniff — Karolina Sobecka (2009)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Give computer vision a dog's body and its judgements about us become something we feel.
- What it is: A projected virtual dog on a street-facing shop window follows passers-by, sniffs at them, and becomes friendly or hostile depending on how each person moves and how they treated it before.
- How it works: Made with James George: a camera and machine-vision software track and distinguish people, read posture and gestures, and drive a game-engine dog whose behaviour accumulates memory of each person.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Alterity & the uncanny
- Shown at: VIDA 12.0, Special Mention
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HEsOktyLeGs

#### The Nine Eyes of Google Street View — Jon Rafman (2008)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Infrastructure, energy & supply chain
- Idea: An indifferent automated camera produces a new kind of photograph: nobody chose the moment, yet it still says something about the world.
- What it is: An ongoing collection of screenshots from Google Street View, where the nine-lens camera cars have recorded arrests, accidents, animals and odd moments without anyone looking.
- How it works: Screen captures selected by the artist from Street View imagery, shown online, as prints and in books.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Machine umwelt
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E-yH0GpfDK8
- Images: https://64.media.tumblr.com/4dda5b7bf161a81c01f98014b6e6b674/8395f54aeb8544ee-a7/s500x750/166454b46f54ac8f8f130f901369b9a39c37c600.png
- Project page: https://9-eyes.com

#### Deep Play — Harun Farocki (2007)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: The same match becomes many different images once machines watch it: a spectacle for fans, a dataset for coaches, a crowd for the police.
- What it is: A 12-channel installation that replays the 2006 World Cup final through TV feeds, surveillance cameras, player-tracking software and animated data graphics, all running in sync.
- How it works: Twelve synchronised video tracks of 2 h 15 min combine the broadcast clean feed, security-camera footage and computer-generated tracking and statistics of every player.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: documenta 12, Kassel, 2007; AV Festival, Newcastle, 2008
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mIjrKxzFvpY

- Project page: https://www.harunfarocki.de/installations/2000s/2007/deep-play.html

#### Sorting Daemon — David Rokeby (2003)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Automated profiling does not see people, only features it can sort; the painterly composite is a portrait of that reduction.
- What it is: A robotic camera scans the street outside the gallery for people, cuts each passer-by out of the background and breaks them into colour patches, which are sorted by hue into a large projected composite.
- How it works: Pan-tilt-zoom camera with motion detection and background subtraction; extracted figures are segmented by colour and placed by hue, saturation and size (flesh tones sorted separately).
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Shown at: Goethe-Institut Toronto, 'Surveillance Terrorism Democracy', 2003
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vhjoupz_e1s
- Images: http://www.davidrokeby.com/SortingDaemonComposite_web.jpg http://www.davidrokeby.com/SD_Install_web.jpg
- Project page: http://www.davidrokeby.com/sorting.html

#### Eye/Machine I–III — Harun Farocki (2001)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Computer vision, Autonomous vehicle & drone, Industrial robot arm
- Idea: Once images become part of an operation rather than a picture of it, seeing turns into targeting, sorting and control.
- What it is: A three-part video installation (2001–03) that assembles footage from missile-head cameras, industrial robots and computer-vision research, images that no human was meant to watch.
- How it works: Double-projection montage of found military, industrial and laboratory footage (smart bombs, welding robots, object recognition), with guidance lines and overlays drawn by the machines themselves.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Hidden labour & extraction
- Shown at: ICA London (Eye/Machine III co-production), 2003
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r4sDXhHqndk
- Images: https://www.harunfarocki.de/fileadmin/_processed_/4/2/csm_harun-farocki-eye-machine-III-wien_9e5e84595f.jpg
- Project page: https://www.harunfarocki.de/installations/2000s/2003/eye-machine-iii.html

#### Molecular Informatics — Seiko Mikami (1996)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Eye tracking turns an unconscious act of looking into data the viewer can see.
- What it is: A VR installation in which a headset tracks the visitor's eye movements and turns every glance into growing molecular structures, so looking itself becomes something visible and shared with a second viewer.
- How it works: Head-mounted display with an eye tracker; gaze coordinates generate 3D molecule-like forms in real time; first shown at Canon ARTLAB, Tokyo.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Shown at: Canon ARTLAB, Tokyo 1996; DEAF96, V2_ Rotterdam; NTT ICC 2011 (Eye-Tracking Informatics)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vasyoHyklL8

- Project page: https://www.ntticc.or.jp/en/archive/participants/mikami-seiko/

#### Liquid Views — Monika Fleischmann, Wolfgang Strauss (1992)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: A computer mirror is never just a mirror: it captures, stores and redistributes your image, so self-reflection becomes being watched.
- What it is: Visitors lean over a horizontal touchscreen of simulated water and see their own face reflected in it; touching the surface sends ripples that dissolve the reflection, while a large projection behind shows the enlarged face to everyone else in the room.
- How it works: A hidden video camera captures the viewer's face, which real-time graphics software maps onto a simulated water surface that reacts to touch; the stored images are also shown on a wall projection.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Alterity & the uncanny
- Shown at: Electric Dreams, Tate Modern 2024–25
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bjq13wyjhA8

- Project page: http://www.eculturefactory.de/liquid-views

#### Surface Tension — Rafael Lozano-Hemmer (1992)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Machine tracking has a gaze: once it is given an eye, being followed by it feels like being watched by someone.
- What it is: A giant human eye on a screen follows each visitor around the room with 'Orwellian precision'. Made during the first Gulf War, the first war of camera-guided 'intelligent' bombs, it gives the tracking machine an eye that looks back.
- How it works: A computerised tracking system detects the viewer's position and selects frames from over 500 stop-motion photographs of an eye so that it appears to follow them.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Alterity & the uncanny
- Shown at: Venice Biennale 2007; Whitechapel Gallery, London 2016; West Kowloon Cultural District, Hong Kong 2023
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JXLoLPkzdto
- Images: https://www.lozano-hemmer.com/image_sets/surface_tension/hong_kong_2023/surface_tension_hong_kong_2023_rlh_001.jpg
- Project page: https://www.lozano-hemmer.com/surface_tension.php

#### The Giver of Names — David Rokeby (1991)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Voice & listening machine
- Idea: Machine naming works by association, not understanding; its misreadings show perception as a chain of guesses.
- What it is: Visitors place any object on an empty pedestal; a camera captures it, the computer analyses its outline, colour and texture, and then speaks aloud a poetic, often odd, sentence naming it.
- How it works: Video camera and image processing (outline, segmentation, colour and texture analysis) feed an associative database of words and ideas that generates a grammatical sentence, voiced by speech synthesis.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Failure, glitch & error, Machine umwelt
- Shown at: Kiasma Museum of Contemporary Art, Helsinki (commission); Art Gallery of Windsor, 2008
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sO9RggYz24Q

- Project page: http://www.davidrokeby.com/gon.html

#### Machine Vision — Steina Vasulka (1978)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Industrial robot arm
- Idea: A camera that moves by itself shows space as a machine would sense it, without a body.
- What it is: An installation in which video cameras on slowly rotating motorised mounts, one pair aimed at a mirrored sphere, scan the room and show it on monitors from viewpoints no human eye occupies.
- How it works: Turntables and motorised arms carry cameras around a mirrored sphere; the live feeds play on monitors in the room.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Machine umwelt
- Shown at: Albright-Knox Art Gallery, Buffalo 1978
- Images: http://www.vasulka.org/Steina/Steina_MachineVision/img/MachineVision01.jpg http://www.vasulka.org/Steina/Steina_MachineVision/img/MachineVision02.jpg

#### Videoplace — Myron Krueger (1975)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision
- Idea: Long before webcams, the computer perceived the whole body, and the body learned to act for the machine's eye.
- What it is: Participants' live video silhouettes appear on a large screen where the computer recognises their outlines and lets them touch, draw with and play with graphic creatures and remote participants.
- How it works: Video cameras, custom hardware for real-time silhouette extraction and contour analysis, and projected computer graphics; shown in a two-way version at the Milwaukee Art Museum in 1975.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Machine seeing, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Shown at: Milwaukee Art Museum, 1975; SIGGRAPH Art Show, 1985 and 1990
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/317456.317463 (CHI 1985)
