#### TV Buddha — Nam June Paik (1974)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: A closed-circuit camera turns meditation into self-surveillance: the machine eye becomes a mirror with no outside.
- What it is: A Buddha statue sits facing a monitor that shows its own live image, filmed by a closed-circuit camera behind the screen. The Buddha contemplates itself through the machine in an endless loop.
- How it works: An antique Buddha sculpture, a video camera on a tripod and a CRT monitor in a live closed-circuit loop; many versions exist.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Alterity & the uncanny
- Shown at: Galeria Bonino, New York 1974; Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam (collection)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MVwR1n0IZAs
- Images: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/53/TV_Buddha.jpg
- Project page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_Buddha

#### La Région Centrale — Michael Snow (1971)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Industrial robot arm, Computer vision
- Idea: A camera released from the human body sees the landscape as no person could.
- What it is: A three-hour film shot on a remote mountaintop in Quebec by a camera mounted on a programmable robotic arm that swings, spins and loops through every direction, with no human operator behind the lens.
- How it works: Snow commissioned engineer Pierre Abbeloos to build a motorised camera arm controlled by pre-recorded sound signals.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Machine umwelt
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KWyv7mSaXHM
- Project page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_R%C3%A9gion_Centrale

### Listening Machines & Voice

Speech recognition, voice assistants, accent analysis and synthetic voices.

#### After Words — Machine Listening (Sean Dockray, James Parker, Joel Stern) (2022)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Dataset & training data, Chatbot & language model
- Idea: Data is never mined, it is made: audio datasets are performances, often by actors, and every 'Hey Alexa' is a performance for the machine.
- What it is: An 8-channel sound installation of speculative scenes built from readymade audio in machine-learning datasets, from acted emotional speech to Google AudioSet, woven through a script written with and against a language model.
- How it works: Samples from the Toronto Emotional Speech Set, DCASE sound-event datasets and Google AudioSet, voiced additions by critical-data researchers, and an autoregressive language model's text, spatialised over eight channels (18 min loop).
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Hidden labour & extraction
- Shown at: Data Relations, Australian Centre for Contemporary Art (ACCA), Melbourne (2022–23)
- Images: https://machinelistening-web.somethingilearned.today/works/after-words/af2.jpg https://machinelistening-web.somethingilearned.today/works/after-words/1500-1001-max.jpg
- Project page: https://machinelistening.exposed/works/after-words/

#### Dark Matters — Johann Diedrick (2021)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Dataset & training data
- Idea: A voice assistant can only hear the voices its datasets contain; the missing speech is a dark matter that shapes who is understood.
- What it is: An interactive web experience and video installation about the absence of Black speech in the datasets used to train voice interfaces such as Alexa and Siri, told through 3D space, sound and storytelling.
- How it works: Browser-based 3D environment built from speech-dataset analysis and recorded voices, shown publicly as a beta web piece and a 24/7 window-gallery video.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: Squeaky Wheel Film & Media Art Center, Buffalo (2021); Mozilla Creative Media Awards 2021
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1XDpu2gabc
- Images: https://squeaky.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/IMG_4224-scaled.jpg
- Project page: https://squeaky.org/event/johann-diedrick-dark-matters/

#### Machine Listening, a Curriculum — Machine Listening (Sean Dockray, James Parker, Joel Stern) (2020)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Surveillance & biometrics, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Our devices now analyse and respond to sound, not just record it; machine listening is a field of knowledge-power that needs collective study and counter-strategies.
- What it is: An open, evolving curriculum of reading lists, a library, prompts, interviews, commissioned texts, music and recorded online events on the politics and aesthetics of listening machines, launched with broadcasts for Liquid Architecture and Unsound in 2020.
- How it works: Open-source pedagogy platform (built on Pirate Care's curriculum tool) combining syllabi, archives and Zoom-era radio broadcasts.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction
- Shown at: Unsound Festival 2020 (online); Liquid Architecture 2020
- Paper: http://archive.machinelistening.exposed/curriculum/ (Liquid Architecture & Unsound, 2020)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iUbglqQLdrI
- Images: https://machinelistening.exposed/images/home/hero.png
- Project page: https://machinelistening.exposed/curriculum/

#### Racial Disparities in Automated Speech Recognition — Allison Koenecke (2020)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Voice & listening machine
- Idea: Listening machines hear some voices worse than others; the gap comes from what their acoustic models were trained on, not from how people speak.
- What it is: An audit of five commercial speech-recognition systems (Amazon, Apple, Google, IBM, Microsoft) on interviews with Black and white Americans, finding an average word error rate of 0.35 for Black speakers against 0.19 for white speakers.
- How it works: Transcribed matched audio snippets from the CORAAL and VOC corpora with each vendor's ASR API and compared word error rates, isolating acoustic-model effects.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1915768117 (PNAS 117(14), 2020)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1fQ7q4_x00I
- Project page: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1915768117

#### On the Apparently Meaningless Texture of Noise — Pedro Oliveira (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Dataset & training data, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: What a listening machine is trained to discard as noise is exactly where a migrant voice keeps its history.
- What it is: A binaural sound essay on the 'dialect recognition software' used in German asylum procedures: it listens to the breaths, pauses and other paraverbal 'noise' that the software's training data tells it to ignore, and builds a counter-archive of voices and leaked training documents.
- How it works: Sound essay recorded at EMS Stockholm (2019), composed from annotated paraverbal features, voices and documents from German Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF) field offices; published online for the Akademie Schloss Solitude and ZKM web residencies.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: HASH Award 2020, 2nd prize (ZKM / Akademie Schloss Solitude)
- Images: https://oliveira.work/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/schulung-mod-1.jpg https://oliveira.work/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/echoes-m.jpg
- Project page: https://oliveira.work/meaningless-texture/

#### Project Alias — Bjørn Karmann, Tore Knudsen (2018)
- Type: Speculative design · Machines: Voice & listening machine
- Idea: You can negotiate with an always-listening machine by giving it a machine of your own that controls what it hears.
- What it is: A fungus-like 'parasite' that sits on top of a Google Home or Amazon Echo and keeps it deaf with a constant murmur; only when it hears the user's own chosen wake word does it go quiet and whisper the real one.
- How it works: A Raspberry Pi with microphones and two small speakers runs a locally trained wake-word classifier; it feeds noise into the assistant's microphones until triggered.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Shown at: S+T+ARTS Prize 2019, Grand Prize – Artistic Exploration; Ars Electronica Festival 2019
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qZFytvJ6ano
- Images: https://bjoernkarmann.dk/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Alias-2.jpg https://bjoernkarmann.dk/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/Alias-3.jpg
- Project page: https://bjoernkarmann.dk/project_alias
- Code: https://github.com/bjoernkarmann/project_alias

#### DolphinAttack: Inaudible Voice Commands — USSLAB, Zhejiang University (2017)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Voice & listening machine
- Idea: The machine hears a different world from ours: the non-linearity of its own ear becomes a channel for voices only machines receive.
- What it is: Voice commands modulated onto ultrasound above 20 kHz are inaudible to people, but the microphones of phones, smart speakers and cars demodulate them, so Siri, Google Now, Alexa and an Audi navigation system obey voices no one in the room can hear.
- How it works: Amplitude-modulated ultrasonic carriers played from a speaker; the non-linear response of MEMS microphones recovers the baseband voice command, which speech recognition then accepts.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Failure, glitch & error
- Shown at: ACM CCS 2017, Dallas
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/3133956.3134052 (ACM CCS 2017)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=21HjF4A3WE4
- Project page: https://doi.org/10.1145/3133956.3134052

#### The Dark Age of Connectionism — Wesley Goatley (2017)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine
- Idea: An always-listening device reshapes behaviour: to escape its ear you must change how you exist in the room.
- What it is: An Amazon Echo surrounded by microphones: every sound visitors make triggers Siri to ask the Echo a question about its politics and function, and to hear the answers visitors must learn to stay quiet around it.
- How it works: Surrounding microphones detect nearby sound events and trigger scripted questions spoken by an Apple Siri voice to an Amazon Echo, which interrupts itself with each new sound.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Opacity & latent space
- Shown at: Haunted Random Forests Festival, UK (2017); IMPAKT Festival, Utrecht (2018); Sonic Arts Seoul (2018)
- Video: https://vimeo.com/241915190
- Images: https://wesleygoatley.com/images/da-detail.webp
- Project page: https://wesleygoatley.com/dark-age.html

#### Rubber Coated Steel — Lawrence Abu Hamdan (2016)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Voice & listening machine
- Idea: Machine audio analysis can hear what human witnesses cannot, but the film asks whose silences a court is still unable to hear.
- What it is: A 21-minute video staged as a tribunal for gunshots: it re-enacts the acoustic evidence from the 2014 killing of two Palestinian teenagers, where Abu Hamdan's spectral analysis showed that live rounds had been disguised to sound like rubber bullets.
- How it works: Audio-ballistic analysis made with Forensic Architecture for Defence for Children International, visualising sound frequencies of recorded gunshots, re-staged as an empty courtroom with subtitles and silences.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Opacity & latent space
- Shown at: Earshot, Portikus, Frankfurt (2016); International Film Festival Rotterdam (IFFR)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NsZHAliJihk
- Images: https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5209b9c5e4b0bc18c96df1ec/1633429204074-1Q6FTZP2L0W47AWT341C/earshot+2.jpg https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5209b9c5e4b0bc18c96df1ec/1633525130412-322L2ZAC9UXE628Q3X6I/Lawrence-Abu-Hamdan_31-b.jpg
- Project page: http://lawrenceabuhamdan.com/earshot

#### Conversnitch — Brian House, Kyle McDonald (2014)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: The 'listening machine' is partly people: automated eavesdropping runs on hidden human transcribers and ends in public broadcast.
- What it is: A small device disguised as a light bulb that eavesdrops on conversations nearby; snippets are transcribed by anonymous Mechanical Turk workers and posted to Twitter.
- How it works: A microphone and Raspberry Pi hidden in a lamp-socket housing stream audio to Amazon Mechanical Turk for transcription; the text is tweeted automatically.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Hidden labour & extraction, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ueeQ7T0thwc
- Images: https://brianhouse.net/works/conversnitch/conversnitch.jpg https://brianhouse.net/works/conversnitch/conversnitch_1.jpg
- Project page: https://brianhouse.net/works/conversnitch/

#### Conflicted Phonemes — Lawrence Abu Hamdan (2012)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: When a state listens to accents to decide nationality, the voice is treated like a passport; mapping a voice's mixed history refuses that reduction.
- What it is: Wall-sized diagrams, made with designer Janna Ulrich, map the voices of twelve Somali asylum seekers whose claims the Dutch authorities rejected after a language-and-accent analysis. The maps trace lives of migration and camps that a single 'correct' accent cannot hold.
- How it works: Research meeting in Utrecht (2012) with the rejected applicants, linguists and activists, turned into vinyl wall timelines and take-away A4 sheets; the maps were later submitted to a Dutch immigration judge and a UK asylum court.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: Casco Office for Art, Design and Theory, Utrecht (commission, 2012)
- Images: https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5209b9c5e4b0bc18c96df1ec/1487689651283-1IJLGTCD230AZQVHJSYS/LH001-ConfictedPhonemes-det-web.jpg https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5209b9c5e4b0bc18c96df1ec/1487689643617-IWQ7CJM52SRIJXJL6XDR/_MG_9667.JPG
- Project page: http://lawrenceabuhamdan.com/conflicted-phonemes

#### The Freedom of Speech Itself — Lawrence Abu Hamdan (2012)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Voice analysis turns the way you speak into a territory; the state's ear, not your words, decides where you belong.
- What it is: A 34-minute audio documentary on the UK's use of forensic speech analysis and 'voiceprints' to test the origin of asylum seekers' accents, heard among acoustic-foam sculptures shaped like the voiceprint of the word 'you'.
- How it works: Interviews with lawyers, phoneticians, asylum seekers and Home Office officials edited with radiophonic techniques; foam sculptures are contour maps of the frequency and amplitude of two voices.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: The Showroom, London (commission, 2012)
- Images: https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5209b9c5e4b0bc18c96df1ec/1487690498833-HX5J9ER5A4EN8SHONRBC/foam%2Bvoice%2Bprint.jpg https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5209b9c5e4b0bc18c96df1ec/1487690496112-HWUTKCQALIUYA2L3TI4D/Extra%2Bcity%2Bfoam%2B2%2Bcopy.jpg
- Project page: http://lawrenceabuhamdan.com/the-freedom-of-speech-itself

#### The Whole Truth — Lawrence Abu Hamdan (2012)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Voice-stress analysis claims to hear beneath speech into the body; turning it on its own makers shows how arbitrary its verdicts are.
- What it is: An installation and audio documentary about voice-analysis lie detectors piloted by European, Russian and Israeli governments and used by border agencies and insurers. While visitors listen to interviews with the software's developers and sellers, a reverse-engineered lie detector judges those same voices in real time.
- How it works: Reverse-engineered voice lie-detection software runs on the documentary's audio; three-channel video, stereo sound, a desk, chairs and artificial plants stage an interview room.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Classification, bias & surveillance, Failure, glitch & error
- Shown at: Casco Office for Art, Design and Theory, Utrecht (commission, 2012)
- Images: https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5209b9c5e4b0bc18c96df1ec/1568880234051-G7XRKWGT7ZVT1IMO6KIW/LA_EThe+Whole+Truth_2012_Reverse+engineered+lie+detector%2C+3+channel+video%2C+stereo+sound%2C+desk%2C+3+chairs%2C+3+artificial+plants_24+minutes_612x435x190cm_1.jpg https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5209b9c5e4b0bc18c96df1ec/1568880459670-25NI8IPE3QWLMOWXG69F/LA_EThe+Whole+Truth_2012_Reverse+engineered+lie+detector%2C+3+channel+video%2C+stereo+sound%2C+desk%2C+3+chairs%2C+3+artificial+plants_24+minutes_612x435x190cm_5.jpg
- Project page: http://lawrenceabuhamdan.com/the-whole-truth

#### Blendie — Kelly Dobson (2004)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine
- Idea: Instead of the machine learning our language, we must learn its voice; control becomes mimicry and a strange empathy with an appliance.
- What it is: A 1950s Osterizer blender that only responds to a person's voice: you have to growl, whirr and hum like a blender, and it spins at the speed and power of your imitation.
- How it works: Custom hardware and software for real-time sound analysis map the pitch and loudness of the user's blender-like sounds onto the motor's speed.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Alterity & the uncanny, Intimacy, care & companionship
- Shown at: HOME\SICK, Science Gallery Dublin
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tph40hgcLpU
- Images: http://www.kellydobson.com/blendie.png
- Project page: https://www.media.mit.edu/projects/blendie/overview/

#### Text Tones — Stephan von Huene (1983)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine
- Idea: A listening machine hears everything and keeps only what fits its own body; speech comes back as the resonance of a tube.
- What it is: Six white plinths carry aluminium tubes struck by small hammers. A microphone takes in the sounds of the gallery, voices, footsteps, closing doors, and the sculpture plays them back through the tubes, so whatever is said in the room returns as a monotone reflection at the tubes' own pitches.
- How it works: Microphone input is stored and split into an analog and a digital signal: the digital signal drives pairs of hammers striking each tube while the analog signal plays through a loudspeaker into the tube; tube lengths divide two octaves into five intervals. Originally tape-based, later reworked with sensors and a computer.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice
- Shown at: Baden-Baden, 1983; Hamburger Kunsthalle, Galerie der Gegenwart (collection)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4-quIUsCgEI
- Images: https://www.stephanvonhuene.de/en/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2019/06/text-tones-hamburg6-1.jpg https://www.stephanvonhuene.de/en/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2019/06/text-tones-kestner6-1.jpg
- Project page: https://www.stephanvonhuene.de/en/portfolio_page/text-tones/

### Datasets & Labels

Training sets, labels and the worldviews built into them.

#### The Dark Side of Dataset Scaling: Evaluating Racial Classification in Multimodal Models — Abeba Birhane (2024)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: Scale is not a cure: more web data can make a machine's gaze more prejudiced, not less.
- What it is: An audit of 14 CLIP-style vision-language models trained on LAION-400M and LAION-2B: when the training set grew fivefold, the larger models became 65% and 69% more likely to label photos of Black and Latino men as 'criminal'.
- How it works: Zero-shot classification of the Chicago Face Dataset against human and non-human labels across model sizes and dataset scales, with a qualitative and historical reading of the results.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/3630106.3658968 (FAccT 2024)
- Images: https://arxiv.org/html/2405.04623v1/heatmap-summary.png
- Project page: https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04623

#### Tinder_gun_boys_@Brussels_ — Loïs Soleil (2022)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Turning a dating app's sorting logic back on its users shows how easily a machine can build a dataset of people, and what that dataset is for.
- What it is: A robot swipes through Tinder on its own while a weapon-detecting AI screenshots men posing with guns; the images are printed on tatami mats used for feminist self-defence classes held in the installation.
- How it works: A physical swiping robot operates a phone running Tinder; an object-detection model flags profile photos with weapons and saves hundreds of screenshots a day; legal advice was compiled into the video How not to get sued as an artist.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Shown at: Prix Ars Electronica 2025, Honorary Mention (Artificial Life & Intelligence)
- Video: https://vimeo.com/1084594874
- Images: http://loissoleil.com/pages/tinder/Robot.jpg https://archive.aec.at/asset/3845109/preview/
- Project page: http://loissoleil.com/tinder

#### Sorting Song — Simone C. Niquille (2021)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: Object categories that seem trivial to people are negotiations the machine cannot have; the boundary between bowl and vase is a political choice.
- What it is: Domestic objects from the SceneNet RGB-D training dataset morph endlessly between vase and bowl, bench and couch, chair and toilet. When shape is all a dataset records, a wheelchair, a toilet and an electric chair can end up in the same category.
- How it works: 3D meshes from Imperial College London's SceneNet RGB-D indoor dataset are animated morphing between category labels.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Failure, glitch & error
- Video: https://vimeo.com/555060893
- Images: https://technofle.sh/static/media/SOS_SortingSong_001.jpg https://technofle.sh/static/media/SOS_CowSharkFalling.png
- Project page: https://technofle.sh/sorting-song.html

#### Lacework — Everest Pipkin (2020)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: A training set is made of other people's lives, reduced to one word each; watching it all restores their weight.
- What it is: A slow, dreamlike video river made from MIT's Moments in Time dataset: one million three-second clips scraped from the web and each tagged with a single verb such as 'praying' or 'flying'. Pipkin watched the whole dataset and stretched its clips into hallucinatory slow motion.
- How it works: Clips from the Moments in Time action-recognition dataset were processed with neural frame interpolation and super-resolution to slow and enlarge them into a continuous video.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction, Machine seeing
- Shown at: The Photographers' Gallery, London (Data / Set / Match), 2020
- Video: https://everest-pipkin.com/projects/lacework/flickr-5-6-5-8-9-7-1-8-4756589718_2.slowed_x2.00_x2.00_x2.00_x2.00_x1.00-20.webformat.mp4
- Images: https://thephotographersgallery.org.uk/sites/default/files/styles/banner_image/public/ep2.png.webp?itok=wVNy-Lyc
- Project page: https://everest-pipkin.com/projects/lacework.html

#### Large Image Datasets: A Pyrrhic Win for Computer Vision? — Abeba Birhane (2020)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: What a vision model can see depends on images collected without consent and labels no one checked.
- What it is: Abeba Birhane and Vinay Uday Prabhu audited large image datasets, including ImageNet and MIT's 80 Million Tiny Images, and found slurs among the labels and non-consensual, pornographic and harmful images. The paper led MIT to withdraw Tiny Images.
- How it works: A quantitative and qualitative audit of labels and image content in large-scale vision datasets, with proposed remedies.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1109/WACV48630.2021.00158 (WACV 2021)
- Project page: https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16923

#### Model Zoo — Forensic Architecture (2020)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Where real images of violence are scarce, synthetic training sets let machines learn to see what investigators need to find.
- What it is: A growing catalogue of 3D models of munitions and weapons, together with the machine-learning classifiers trained on synthetic renderings of them to recognise these objects in images from conflicts.
- How it works: Photorealistic renderings of 3D weapon models form synthetic datasets; classifiers trained on them are tested on open-source footage.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Images: https://i.vimeocdn.com/video/864290475-35c09a4a9d98e29cb953c40599ec67ec2e384f73e62ec820ed4e0e80c17c162a-d_1280x720.jpg
- Project page: https://forensic-architecture.org/investigation/model-zoo

#### Pique Nique pour les Inconnues — Rosa Menkman (2020)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: The standards by which machines see images were calibrated on women whose faces survive endless copying while their names disappear.
- What it is: The anonymous women on colour test cards (Lena, Shirley and others), along with bots and stock-photo placeholders, gather on a desktop and try to sing together using only computer system sounds.
- How it works: Desktop video 'tele-chorale' animating historical test images and virtual assistants, voiced with operating-system sounds performing Paul McCartney's 'We All Stand Together'.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Alterity & the uncanny
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6n7t3A3UF3o
- Images: https://freight.cargo.site/i/2bf5877371a4095252b3a01af61a332deb9cc1a034752cce60fd6b0afa06d8c3/iRD.png
- Project page: https://beyondresolution.info/COLOR-TEST-CARDS

#### Salaf (Ancestors) — Nouf Aljowaysir (2020)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Machine vision inherits the colonial archive: to refuse its gaze, the artist trains on absence.
- What it is: Tracing her family's migrations across Arabia and Mesopotamia, the artist ran archival photographs, many from Gertrude Bell's colonial archive, through computer-vision models. They failed to see veiled women as women and tagged Bedouin as 'soldier' and 'army'; she then erased the figures to make an 'absent dataset' of about 6,000 images.
- How it works: Scraped museum and archival photographs were labelled by commercial computer-vision models; an AI segmentation technique then removed the orientalist figures to create an empty-image dataset.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Failure, glitch & error, Grief, memory & afterlife
- Shown at: ThoughtWorks Arts residency, New York, 2020
- Images: https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/55039003e4b04b9963242639/1763375737992-MHJQB7XNFGLGYDDDY41V/186--Woman%2Bseated%2Bcross-legged%2Bwith%2Bshoes%2Boff-209.jpg https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/55039003e4b04b9963242639/1763375946970-N2HOYYFEJ9ZTJ56QK06N/188--Paysannes%2Begyptiense%2Ballant%2Ba%2Bl%25E2%2580%2599eua-1133.jpg
- Project page: https://www.noufaljowaysir.com/work/salaf

#### Declassifier (Humans of AI) — Philipp Schmitt (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Every act of machine recognition is a recollection of someone else's photographs.
- What it is: A computer-vision program looks at photographs, but instead of drawing boxes around the objects it detects, it overlays the actual COCO training images that taught it to see each object. Part of Humans of AI, which also credits the thousands of Flickr photographers whose pictures built the dataset.
- How it works: An object detector trained on Microsoft's COCO dataset processes images; for each detection the software retrieves and collages the COCO training photos of that class, with photographer credits.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction
- Shown at: The Photographers' Gallery, London, 2020
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOZe5wEcXxY
- Images: https://cdn.philippschmitt.com/media/pages/work/humans-of-ai/58fb56c131-1586885726/philipp-schmitt_humans-of-ai-1-1200x630-crop.jpg
- Project page: https://philippschmitt.com/work/humans-of-ai

#### Excavating AI: The Politics of Images in Machine Learning Training Sets — Kate Crawford, Trevor Paglen (2019)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: Every training set encodes a politics: deciding what an image means is an act of power, never neutral description.
- What it is: An essay that digs through ImageNet, JAFFE, UTKFace and other training sets layer by layer, from their taxonomies and categories down to individual labelled images.
- How it works: Archaeological reading of dataset structure (WordNet hierarchy, label choices, sourcing) with image examples; published online by the authors with the AI Now Institute.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Opacity & latent space
- Paper: https://excavating.ai (excavating.ai (AI Now Institute), 2019)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZiHHsKALwBc
- Images: https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Paglen-Excavating_AI-1024x385.jpg
- Project page: https://excavating.ai

#### From ‘Apple’ to ‘Anomaly’ (Pictures and Labels) — Trevor Paglen (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: A training set is a worldview: walking along its labels shows how quickly naming things slides into judging people.
- What it is: About 30,000 printed photographs from the ImageNet dataset line the Barbican's curved gallery, grouped under their labels, moving from harmless nouns like 'apple' to judgments about people.
- How it works: Selection of ImageNet categories and images printed individually and pinned in label clusters along the 90-metre Curve wall; a homage to Magritte's The Treachery of Images.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Shown at: Barbican Centre, The Curve, London, 2019–20
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=juSXaQWNXgU
- Images: https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Paglen-From_Apple_to_Anomaly-2019-03-1024x683.jpg https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Paglen-From_Apple_to_Anomaly_2019-01-1024x683.jpg
- Project page: https://paglen.studio/2020/04/09/from-apple-to-anomaly-pictures-and-labels-selections-from-the-imagenet-dataset-for-object-recognition/

#### HOMESCHOOL — Simone C. Niquille (2019)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data, Robot creature & mobile robot
- Idea: Before a robot can live in your home, the home must be rebuilt as a dataset, and whatever does not fit a category disappears.
- What it is: A 13-minute 3D-animated film set inside the synthetic model homes used to train the computer vision of household robots. It asks how thousands of homes, people's most private spaces, are turned into categories a robot can navigate: is this a vase, a bowl or a cup?
- How it works: 3D animation built from assets and floor plans of synthetic indoor training datasets for domestic robot vision, with a four-channel soundtrack.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine umwelt
- Shown at: Commissioned by Housing the Human, with Swissnex San Francisco and Fotomuseum Winterthur, 2019
- Video: https://vimeo.com/362563329
- Images: https://technofle.sh/static/media/SCN_Homeschool_Still02_SimoneNiquille-Technoflesh.jpg https://technofle.sh/static/media/HS_Homeschool_depth_SimoneNiquille-Technoflesh.png
- Project page: https://technofle.sh/homeschool.html

#### ImageNet Roulette — Trevor Paglen, Kate Crawford (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Letting the training set 'speak for itself' showed that classifying people by appearance is harmful by design, not by accident.
- What it is: A web app and installation that labelled anyone's selfie using a model trained on ImageNet's 'person' categories, returning terms that were often absurd, racist or cruel; millions of people tried it in September 2019.
- How it works: A classifier trained on ImageNet's roughly 2,800 person sub-categories detected faces and returned the nearest label; the online version was withdrawn and continues as the installation Faces of ImageNet (2022).
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Failure, glitch & error
- Shown at: Training Humans, Fondazione Prada, Milan, 2019; Poetics of Encryption, Kunsthal Charlottenborg, 2024 (as Faces of ImageNet); The World Through AI, Jeu de Paume, Paris, 2025 (as Faces of ImageNet)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K_lN4JD1sBY
- Images: https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Crawford_Paglen.jpg https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/failure.jpg
- Project page: https://paglen.studio/2020/04/29/imagenet-roulette/

#### MegaPixels / Exposing.ai — Adam Harvey, Jules LaPlace (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Face recognition is built from ordinary photos taken for other reasons; the dataset is where the surveillance begins.
- What it is: A research project and search engine that traces where face and biometric training datasets came from and lets anyone check whether their Flickr photos were used in them.
- How it works: Photo IDs and metadata from dozens of public face datasets scraped from Flickr (2004–2020) are indexed so users can search them; MegaPixels ran 2017–2020 and was relaunched as Exposing.ai in 2021.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction
- Shown at: Ars Electronica Center, Understanding AI 2019; Ludwig Forum Aachen, Training the Archive 2020
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ey9lPMknV2E
- Images: https://adam.harvey.studio/exposing-ai/exposing-ai.webp https://exposing.ai/assets/img/og-share.png
- Project page: https://exposing.ai

#### Training Humans — Kate Crawford, Trevor Paglen (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Training images are a vernacular photography nobody looks at, yet they decide how machines will see everyone.
- What it is: An exhibition of the photographs used to train computer vision to recognise people, from early government-funded face databases such as FERET to images scraped from the web and sets built for emotion recognition.
- How it works: Curated display of historical and current training datasets (faces, gestures, emotions, gait) as prints and wall grids, with ImageNet Roulette as an interactive piece.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Shown at: Osservatorio Fondazione Prada, Milan, 2019–20
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P4JpD1PWBDI

- Project page: https://paglen.studio/2020/04/09/kate-crawford-trevor-paglen-training-humans/

#### Triple-Chaser — Forensic Architecture (2019)
- Type: Film & video · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Computer vision can be turned against power: a machine taught with synthetic images becomes a witness to state violence.
- What it is: Made for the 2019 Whitney Biennial, the film traces Triple-Chaser tear-gas grenades fired at civilians back to Safariland, a company owned by Whitney vice-chair Warren B. Kanders. Because few real photographs existed, the team trained classifiers on photorealistic synthetic images to search for the grenades online.
- How it works: 3D models of the grenade were rendered into thousands of synthetic training images with varied lighting and backgrounds, used to train machine-learning classifiers that scan online imagery; film made with Praxis Films.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: Whitney Biennial, New York, 2019
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=93rjwQMww9M

- Project page: https://forensic-architecture.org/investigation/triple-chaser

#### Zizi – Queering the Dataset — Jake Elwes (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Generative model & latent space, Dataset & training data, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Adding the faces a dataset left out shifts what the machine can imagine, and shows what it had not learned.
- What it is: A multi-channel video of faces in constant transition, generated after a face model trained on 70,000 photographs was retrained with 1,000 images of drag and gender-fluid faces. The network's weights drift away from the normative faces it learned first.
- How it works: StyleGAN trained on the FFHQ face dataset was fine-tuned with about 1,000 drag and gender-fluid faces found online; the latent space is traversed to make a 135-minute loop.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Opacity & latent space, Alterity & the uncanny
- Shown at: Edinburgh Fringe (Inspace), 2019; You and AI, Onassis Foundation, Athens, 2021; Among the Machines, Zabludowicz Collection, London, 2022
- Video: https://vimeo.com/388245510
- Images: https://www.jakeelwes.com/images/project-zizi19.jpg https://www.jakeelwes.com/images/project-zizi19/Zabludowicz.jpg
- Project page: https://www.jakeelwes.com/project-zizi-2019.html

#### Myriad (Tulips) — Anna Ridler (2018)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Generative model & latent space
- Idea: Showing the dataset instead of the model reveals the slow human labour and judgement on which machine learning rests.
- What it is: An installation of thousands of photographs of tulips that Ridler bought, photographed and labelled by hand over one tulip season; the images became the training set for her GAN work Mosaic Virus. Each print carries her handwritten label.
- How it works: About 10,000 tulip photographs taken and hand-annotated by the artist, displayed as prints with handwritten labels; the set was later used to train a GAN.
- Lens: Hidden labour & extraction, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: AI: More than Human, Barbican, London, 2019
- Video: https://vimeo.com/428168704
- Images: https://annaridler.com/content/works/myriad-tulips/block_1/DSC01064.webp https://annaridler.com/content/works/myriad-tulips/block_3/group_3/0IMG_1672.jpeg
- Project page: https://annaridler.com/myriad-tulips

#### This is the Problem, the Solution, the Past and the Future — Sebastian Schmieg (2017)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: Any category can be taught to a machine once enough people click; the absurd labels expose how arbitrary all labels are.
- What it is: A conceptual training dataset of 2,931 photographs from The Photographers' Gallery website, sorted by almost 30,000 visitor clicks into four categories: Problem, Solution, Past and Future. The clicks were collected in Schmieg's intervention Decision Space (2016), which overlaid the gallery's site with these four buttons.
- How it works: A web intervention collected crowd classifications of gallery images; the resulting labelled dataset was published online and as wallpaper, and used to train an image classifier (Decisive Camera).
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction
- Shown at: Commissioned by The Photographers' Gallery, London, 2016–17
- Images: https://sebastianschmieg.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/titptstpatf-dc-q21-1-1024x1024.jpg https://sebastianschmieg.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/decision-space-1-1024x683.png
- Project page: https://sebastianschmieg.com/this-is-the-problem-the-solution-the-past-and-the-future/

#### Animal Classifier — Shinseungback Kimyonghun (2016)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: Every machine classification rests on an arbitrary taxonomy; this one simply makes the arbitrariness visible.
- What it is: A neural network is trained to sort animals into the 14 absurd categories of the 'Chinese encyclopedia' in Borges's essay, such as 'belonging to the emperor', 'fabulous' and 'that from a long way off look like flies'.
- How it works: TensorFlow convolutional neural network trained on online images, running on 14 Raspberry Pis under glass domes with monitors.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Video: https://vimeo.com/198948703
- Images: https://djhznh41oxwef.cloudfront.net/works/animal_classifier/ssbkyh_animal_classifier_01.png
- Project page: https://ssbkyh.com/works/animal_classifier/

#### Segmentation.Network — Sebastian Schmieg (2016)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: Machine vision is drawn by hand: someone decided where each object ends and what stays unrecognised.
- What it is: A website that plays back more than 600,000 outlines drawn by crowd-workers around objects in Flickr photos for Microsoft's COCO dataset. Line by line, it shows the hand work that decides what machines can see.
- How it works: Custom software animates the polygon segmentation annotations of the COCO dataset in sequence; also shown as a projection (2018).
- Lens: Hidden labour & extraction, Machine seeing
- Images: https://sebastianschmieg.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/segmentation-network-ani-01.gif https://sebastianschmieg.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/segmentation-network-01-1024x683.png
- Project page: https://sebastianschmieg.com/segmentation-network/

#### ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database — Jia Deng (2009)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: A machine's way of seeing is inherited from a dictionary's hierarchy of nouns and from thousands of anonymous clicks.
- What it is: The CVPR 2009 paper by Jia Deng, Wei Dong, Richard Socher, Li-Jia Li, Kai Li and Li Fei-Fei introducing ImageNet: millions of web images sorted into the noun hierarchy of WordNet and verified by crowd-workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk. It became the benchmark that launched deep-learning computer vision.
- How it works: Images were collected by querying search engines with WordNet synonym sets, then cleaned and verified by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction, Machine seeing
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR.2009.5206848 (CVPR 2009)
- Project page: https://www.image-net.org/

### Faces, Emotion & Biometrics

Face recognition, emotion detection and bodies turned into data.

#### The Flemish Scrollers — Dries Depoorter (2021)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Automated face recognition, usually aimed at citizens, is turned on the people who make the rules for it.
- What it is: Software watches the Flemish Parliament's daily livestreams, detects when a politician is looking at their phone, identifies them by face and posts the clip on social media, tagging them by name.
- How it works: Keras object-detection and face-recognition models analyse the parliament's YouTube livestreams; FFmpeg cuts clips that are posted automatically to Twitter and Instagram. Running since 5 July 2021.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5YHfK6DBvGE
- Images: https://driesdepoorter.be/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/TheFlemishScollers-photo-by-Dries-Depoorter-01-1612x845.jpg https://driesdepoorter.be/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/The-Flemish-Scrollers-Software-Dries-Depoorter-1024x522.png
- Project page: https://driesdepoorter.be/theflemishscrollers/

#### Capture — Paolo Cirio (2020)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Face recognition feels different when it is pointed at the police: the outrage exposes the asymmetry of who may be identified.
- What it is: Cirio ran 1,000 press photos of protests in France through face recognition, built a database of 4,000 police officers' faces and invited the public to identify them by name, and pasted the headshots as posters across Paris. France's interior minister demanded the work be censored.
- How it works: Public photographs were processed with face-detection and recognition software to extract and cluster officers' faces, published on the platform Capture-Police.com and printed as street posters; linked to a campaign to ban facial recognition in Europe.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Shown at: Le Fresnoy, Tourcoing 2020 (co-production)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JPybxTM-daE
- Images: https://paolocirio.net/work/capture/slideshow/NIK_2255.jpg
- Project page: https://paolocirio.net/work/capture/

#### Facework — Kyle McDonald (2020)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Playing to a face classifier builds an intuition for seeing like a machine, and for how arbitrary its categories are.
- What it is: A browser game set in a gig economy where face analysis is the job: as a 'Faceworker', the player takes gigs that require the webcam to judge them as, say, wearing glasses or looking happy, and learns in real time how the classifier sees and where it fails.
- How it works: In-browser face-attribute classifiers run on the player's webcam; gig tasks are scored live against their outputs. Supported by the Mozilla Foundation.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction, Failure, glitch & error
- Images: https://facework.app/assets/images/social-card.jpg
- Project page: https://facework.app
- Code: https://github.com/kylemcdonald/facework

#### Vibe Check — Lauren Lee McCarthy, Kyle McDonald (2020)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Emotion recognition turns every encounter into a score, and the gallery becomes a small social-credit system.
- What it is: Cameras in the exhibition use face recognition and expression analysis to log what emotions each visitor provokes in others. A screen at the entrance names the people who cause the most happiness, disgust, sadness, surprise or boredom, and visitors may find themselves listed on the way out.
- How it works: Off-the-shelf face recognition and expression classifiers track visitors across cameras, attribute the expressions of nearby people to whoever they are looking at, and publish the rankings on screens.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Shown at: Real Feelings, HEK Basel 2020 (commissioned by HEK and MU)
- Video: https://vimeo.com/488636450
- Images: https://freight.cargo.site/w/1200/i/9d8ca3ebcda018fd8d992785901291c8e601d1a17ded09962faa0a6789609ae2/_DSC4566_1_crop.jpg
- Project page: https://get-lauren.net/Vibe-Check

#### Emotional Expressions Reconsidered: Challenges to Inferring Emotion From Human Facial Movements — Lisa Feldman Barrett (2019)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Emotion-recognition AI detects facial movements, not feelings; the inference from one to the other is the weak link.
- What it is: Barrett, Adolphs, Marsella, Martinez and Pollak review more than 1,000 studies and conclude that people do not reliably make the same facial movements for the same emotions across situations and cultures, so a scowl cannot be read as anger.
- How it works: A systematic review of evidence on the reliability and specificity of facial configurations for anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and surprise in adults, infants, children and remote cultures.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Failure, glitch & error
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100619832930 (Psychological Science in the Public Interest 20(1))
- Project page: https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100619832930

#### How do you see me? — Heather Dewey-Hagborg (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Generative model & latent space
- Idea: What counts as a face to a machine can be almost unrecognisable to us.
- What it is: Dewey-Hagborg uses adversarial image generation to build pictures that a face detector accepts as her face, although to a human eye they look like abstract smudges.
- How it works: An image generator is optimised against a face-detection and recognition model until its outputs are classified as the artist.
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Machine seeing
- Video: https://vimeo.com/361593768
- Images: https://www.deweyhagborg.com/media/pages/projects/how-do-you-see-me/9b1078df08-1643025907/heatherdeweyhagborg_kateelliott_01.jpg
- Project page: https://www.deweyhagborg.com/projects/how-do-you-see-me

#### Mind — Shinseungback Kimyonghun (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Emotion AI is turned into weather: a collective 'mind' that exists only as the machine measures it.
- What it is: An emotion-recognition system reads the faces of people in the room, and mechanical ocean drums turn the average emotion of the last 100 faces into the sound of waves. The sea changes with the crowd's detected mood.
- How it works: Network camera with FER+ emotion recognition (ONNX Runtime), microcontroller-driven mechanical ocean drums and a sea simulation.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine umwelt
- Shown at: National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea (commission) 2019
- Video: https://vimeo.com/364570360
- Images: https://djhznh41oxwef.cloudfront.net/works/mind/ssbkyh_Mind_01.png
- Project page: https://ssbkyh.com/works/mind/

#### Perception iO — Karen Palmer (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: The installation reads the viewer the way a biased system reads a suspect, making them feel whose perception becomes consequence.
- What it is: The viewer takes the point of view of a police officer's body camera in a tense encounter with a Black and a white protagonist; eye tracking and facial emotion analysis read the viewer's reactions, and the story branches according to their implicit bias.
- How it works: Tobii eye tracking and AI facial-expression analysis (developed with ThoughtWorks Arts) feed a branching narrative film engine.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Shown at: Face Values, Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York 2019–20; BIAS: Built This Way, Science Gallery Dublin 2021
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bfgmo05XdXM
- Images: https://i0.wp.com/karenpalmer.uk/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/IMG_7016.jpg?fit=1200%2C750&ssl=1
- Project page: https://karenpalmer.uk/portfolio/perceptionio/

#### RASA-BOX — Iris Long (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Chatbot & language model
- Idea: Emotion inference turns the body into a text a machine claims to read.
- What it is: A 'mirror' that reads visitors' body posture with a camera, infers their emotional state and writes a sentence in the same emotional category, testing how private our feelings remain.
- How it works: Pose estimation from camera skeleton data feeds an emotion classifier and a text generator; made with Hanbin Deng and Wu Tiancheng.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Shown at: Ars Electronica Festival 2019
- Images: https://ars.electronica.art/outofthebox/files/2019/08/RASABOX_Iris-Long.jpg
- Project page: https://ars.electronica.art/outofthebox/en/rasa-box/

#### They Took the Faces from the Accused and the Dead… (SD18) — Trevor Paglen (2019)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Face recognition was benchmarked on people who could not consent: the accused, the imprisoned and the dead.
- What it is: A grid of thousands of mugshots from NIST Special Database 18, a set of arrest photographs, many of people now dead, supplied to researchers to develop and test face recognition.
- How it works: Images drawn from the NIST mugshot database used as a research benchmark, printed as pigment prints and as a large wall installation.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Grief, memory & afterlife
- Shown at: Pace Gallery, Geneva, 2019; Uncanny Valley, de Young Museum, San Francisco, 2020
- Images: https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Paglen-They_took_the_faces-2019_exhibition_view.jpg https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Paglen-They_Took_the_Faces_2019-03.jpg
- Project page: https://paglen.studio/2020/04/09/they-took-the-faces-from-the-accused-and-the-dead/

#### Expression Mirror — Zach Lieberman (2018)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Emotion recognition turns a face into matching parts; the mirror shows you as the system's composite of other people's 'same' feeling.
- What it is: A screen tracks the visitor's face and reads its emotion, then mixes it with the eyes, noses and mouths of earlier visitors who showed the same expression, drawn over with white lines.
- How it works: Face detection tracks 68 landmarks, an emotion classifier labels the expression, and the software pulls matching facial parts from a growing database of visitors; built with openFrameworks, Python and Keras.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Shown at: London Design Biennale, 2018 (Face Values, US pavilion by Cooper Hewitt; Biennale medal); Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum, New York, 2019–23
- Images: https://www.cooperhewitt.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/08/CH-LDB-Photo-David-Levene-3-1.jpg https://www.cooperhewitt.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/unspecified-1.jpg
- Project page: https://www.cooperhewitt.org/channel/face-values/

#### Random String of Emotions — Coralie Vogelaar (2018)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Reversing emotion AI's decoding exposes how thin its vocabulary of six basic emotions is.
- What it is: An actress performs 200 facial expressions assembled from random combinations of Action Units, the muscle movements that emotion-recognition software uses, and commercial software then tries to name the emotion of each strange, sometimes impossible face.
- How it works: A computer generates random strings of FACS Action Units that the actress learns to perform; the filmed fragments are analysed live by Noldus FaceReader and shown on a second screen.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Failure, glitch & error
- Video: https://vimeo.com/331861983
- Images: https://freight.cargo.site/w/1200/i/5a0df0b0e55f08e1ed9a2a99f301542141b7e8051d9ef693c50faf2b9b11c743/RANDOM_16-9-26-43.jpg
- Project page: https://www.coralievogelaar.com/Random-String-of-Emotions

#### Surveillance Paparazzi — Dries Depoorter (2018)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Paparazzi work can now be done by any open camera plus a classifier; everyone is filmed, only some are recognised.
- What it is: A machine that watches unsecured surveillance cameras around the world and uses face recognition to 'snap' celebrities who happen to pass, like an automated paparazzo.
- How it works: Scrapes live feeds from publicly accessible, unencrypted CCTV cameras and runs a celebrity face-recognition model on them.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: Entangled Realities, HEK Basel 2019
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mS2tx3G7930
- Project page: https://driesdepoorter.be/

#### The Normalizing Machine — Mushon Zer-Aviv (2018)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Dataset & training data, Computer vision
- Idea: Algorithmic prejudice is built from our own small judgements, collected and hidden inside a black box.
- What it is: Visitors are recorded and then asked to point at the person who looks 'most normal' in a line-up of earlier participants. The machine aggregates these choices into an algorithmic image of normality, echoing Alphonse Bertillon's 19th-century 'speaking portrait'.
- How it works: A camera records each participant; their pointing choices label previous faces, and a machine-learning model aggregates the votes into a map of facial 'normality' (software by Dan Stavy and Eran Weissenstern, openFrameworks).
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: Ars Electronica ERROR exhibition, Berlin, 2018; BIAS: Built This Way, Science Gallery Dublin, 2021
- Video: https://vimeo.com/323711041
- Images: https://mushon.com/tnm/img/tnm_space.jpg https://mushon.com/tnm/img/tnm_cards.jpg
- Project page: https://mushon.com/tnm/

#### Faces in the Mist — Nicolas Gourault (2017)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Misused on clouds, face recognition becomes a machine of pareidolia, an augur reading the sky for signs.
- What it is: An installation in which a face-recognition bot watches a stream of clouds, searching it for the faces of historical figures involved in weather and climate manipulation, and builds an obsessive 'hall of fame' of its finds.
- How it works: Made with Antoine Chapon: a TensorFlow-based face recogniser, its memory filled with portraits of geoengineering figures, runs on Raspberry Pis over cloud footage; matches appear on screens set into framed black-and-white photographs.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Failure, glitch & error
- Images: https://www.nicolasgourault.fr/thumbs/fitm_zkm_1-204e4739d20385fbe9052b336f88df3b.jpg https://www.nicolasgourault.fr/thumbs/a1-6e7cfc3d19933ee7b5f0559991f67648.jpg
- Project page: https://www.nicolasgourault.fr/films/faces-in-the-mist

#### It Began as a Military Experiment — Trevor Paglen (2017)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Face recognition was built on the faces of particular people, the 'Adam and Eves' of a technology they never chose to found.
- What it is: Ten portraits chosen from FERET, the DARPA-funded face database of the 1990s built largely from staff at a military base in Maryland, printed with the keypoints a face-recognition algorithm finds.
- How it works: Months of curating the FERET database, retouching and colour-correcting selected images, then running them through a facial-landmark algorithm; set of 10 pigment prints.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Images: https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Paglen-It_Began-2017.jpg https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/Paglen-It_Began_2017-01-784x1024.jpg
- Project page: https://paglen.studio/2020/04/09/it-began-as-a-military-experiment/

#### Machine Readable Hito — Trevor Paglen (2017)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Facial analysis turns a known person into columns of confident guesses that contradict each other from one image to the next.
- What it is: A wall of hundreds of portraits of the artist Hito Steyerl, each captioned with what facial-analysis algorithms guess about her age, gender, emotion, glasses or beard.
- How it works: Hundreds of photographs run through several commercial and open-source facial-analysis classifiers; outputs printed under each image on adhesive wall material.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Shown at: Metro Pictures, New York, 2017
- Images: https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Paglen-Machine_readable_Hito-Metro.jpg https://paglen.studio/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/Paglen-Machine_Readable_Hito_detail-2-1-935x1024.jpg
- Project page: https://paglen.studio/2020/04/09/machine-readable-hito-and-holly/

#### Physiognomy's New Clothes — Blaise Agüera y Arcas (2017)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: A classifier trained on biased photographs learns the bias and returns it as objective 'science'.
- What it is: An essay by Blaise Agüera y Arcas, Margaret Mitchell and Alexander Todorov dissecting a 2016 paper that claimed deep learning could detect 'criminality' from ID photos, and tracing the idea back to Lombroso and nineteenth-century physiognomy.
- How it works: A long-form critical essay combining machine-learning analysis of the claimed results (dataset differences such as expression and clothing) with the history of physiognomy and scientific racism.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Paper: https://medium.com/@blaisea/physiognomys-new-clothes-f2d4b59fdd6a (Medium, May 2017)
- Images: https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:907/1*nhh283c26V1tYWjqH3UjXg.jpeg
- Project page: https://medium.com/@blaisea/physiognomys-new-clothes-f2d4b59fdd6a

#### Probably Chelsea — Heather Dewey-Hagborg (2017)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Dataset & training data
- Idea: One genome yields thirty plausible faces: DNA does not determine a face, and identity cannot be read off the body.
- What it is: Thirty different 3D-printed faces hang in a crowd, all generated by algorithms from the same DNA: cheek swabs and hair that Chelsea Manning mailed from prison. Made with Manning to mark her release in 2017.
- How it works: Manning's DNA was analysed with forensic phenotyping methods; varying the algorithm's interpretations of the same genetic data produced 30 face models, 3D-printed in colour.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Alterity & the uncanny
- Shown at: Fridman Gallery, New York 2017
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A-EhRw11JiQ
- Images: https://deweyhagborg.com/media/pages/projects/probably-chelsea/9769243e4c-1643025328/heatherdeweyhagborgchelseamanning_pap5596.jpg
- Project page: https://deweyhagborg.com/projects/probably-chelsea

#### Emotion Hero — Ruben van de Ven (2016)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Emotion recognition does not read feelings; it trains people to perform its categories.
- What it is: A mobile game in the style of Guitar Hero in which players score points by making facial expressions on cue, then receive feedback on how to express emotions better for the machine.
- How it works: Smartphone game built on a commercial emotion-recognition SDK (likely Affectiva) that scores expressions against its categories.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Images: https://emotionhero.com/emotionhero.png
- Project page: https://rubenvandeven.com/emotionhero

#### Level of Confidence — Rafael Lozano-Hemmer (2015)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: A surveillance algorithm built to find suspects is turned into a tool of mourning that searches for victims.
- What it is: A face-recognition camera compares each visitor's face with the portraits of the 43 students abducted in Iguala, Mexico, in 2014, and shows which student they most resemble with a percentage of confidence. The match is never positive; the search does not stop.
- How it works: Eigenface, Fisherface and LBPH face-recognition algorithms trained on the students' photographs run on a camera-and-screen unit; proceeds from sales go to the students' community.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Grief, memory & afterlife
- Shown at: FOFA Gallery, Concordia University, Montreal 2015; Collection MUAC, Mexico City
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sOCZLLgc1lQ
- Images: https://www.lozano-hemmer.com/image_sets/level_of_confidence/montreal_2018/level_of_confidence_montreal_2018_glh_001.jpg
- Project page: https://www.lozano-hemmer.com/level_of_confidence.php

#### Zoom Pavilion — Rafael Lozano-Hemmer, Krzysztof Wodiczko (2015)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Being picked out and enlarged by a face detector makes the ordinary experience of public surveillance suddenly personal.
- What it is: In a room surrounded by projections, twelve computerised surveillance systems detect visitors' faces and robotic cameras zoom in on them up to 35 times, cutting from crowd views to abstract close-ups and recording the spatial relationships between strangers.
- How it works: Face detection software steers independent robotic PTZ cameras with up to 35x optical zoom, whose feeds are projected across the walls.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: MUAC, Mexico City 2015; Art Basel Unlimited 2016
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ENWBRsvn7qA
- Images: https://www.lozano-hemmer.com/image_sets/zoom_pavilion/monterrey_2019/zoom_pavilion_monterrey_2019_my_505A7260.jpg
- Project page: https://www.lozano-hemmer.com/zoom_pavilion.php

#### Face Cages — Zach Blas (2014)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Biometric diagrams look abstract and neutral; made in steel and worn, they become a cage.
- What it is: Four queer artists each wear a metal cage built from the biometric diagram of their own face, enduring it on camera until the pain shows. The four-channel video sets the clean geometry of face recognition against the discomfort of the body it measures.
- How it works: Facial-recognition landmark diagrams of each performer were generated and 3D-printed in stainless steel, then worn in endurance performances filmed as a four-channel HD video (12 min).
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Shown at: MUAC, Mexico City 2015; Sonic Acts, Amsterdam 2017; ICA Singapore 2017
- Video: https://vimeo.com/161973235
- Images: https://zachblas.info/wp-content/uploads/2013/08/FACECAGES-1-1024x576.jpg
- Project page: https://zachblas.info/works/face-cages/

#### Selfiecity — Lev Manovich, Moritz Stefaner (2014)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Dataset & training data, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Reading culture through face analysis mixes machine estimates with hidden human judgement.
- What it is: An interactive analysis of 3,200 Instagram selfies from five cities, sortable by estimated age, gender, head tilt, smile and mood, produced by a mix of face-analysis software and Mechanical Turk workers.
- How it works: Instagram images filtered and tagged by Mechanical Turk workers, measured with face-analysis software, and shown in interactive visualisations.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction
- Images: http://selfiecity.net/assets/img/selfiecity-600.jpg
- Project page: http://selfiecity.net

#### Smile — Tomás Laurenzo (2014)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Autonomous vehicle & drone
- Idea: Making the sight of destruction depend on a performed smile turns emotion recognition into a test of how we consume war as spectacle.
- What it is: A black screen in a black box plays slowed-down drone footage of the ruins of Gaza only while the viewer smiles broadly at it; when the smile stops, the video stops.
- How it works: Face detection and smile recognition on a camera feed gate the playback of drone footage of Gaza after the 2014 war, slowed down by the artist.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Machine seeing
- Shown at: SIGGRAPH Asia, Brisbane, 2019; NeurIPS, Vancouver, 2019; Ars Electronica Garden Hong Kong, 2020
- Video: https://vimeo.com/338535511
- Images: https://laurenzo.net/media/projects/smile/cover.webp https://laurenzo.net/media/projects/smile/smilea.webp
- Project page: https://laurenzo.net/projects/smile/

#### Data-masks — Sterling Crispin (2013)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: What a surveillance algorithm calls a face is a ghostly average that no person has.
- What it is: 3D-printed nylon masks evolved until face detection and recognition software accepts them as faces: portraits of a human as the machine imagines one.
- How it works: Face detection and recognition algorithms were reverse-engineered and genetic algorithms evolved forms that satisfy them, which were then 3D-printed (2013–2015).
- Lens: Machine seeing, Alterity & the uncanny, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Shown at: GLOBALE: Infosphere, ZKM Karlsruhe 2015; Noorderlicht Photofestival 2015; The Face, Deutsches Hygiene-Museum Dresden 2017

#### Digital Pareidolia: A Personal Index of Facebook's Erroneous Portraits — Emilio Vavarella (2013)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Machines also see faces in clouds; their pareidolia shows what a face is to them.
- What it is: A collection of photos from the artist's Facebook in which the platform's face detector framed a face that is not there: a knot of wood, a shadow, a pattern on a wall.
- How it works: Screenshots of Facebook's automatic face-tagging boxes on objects, compiled as an index.
- Lens: Failure, glitch & error, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Images: https://emiliovavarella.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/DIGITAL-PAREIDOLIA-1.jpg
- Project page: http://emiliovavarella.com/digital-pareidolia/

#### Stranger Visions — Heather Dewey-Hagborg (2013)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Dataset & training data
- Idea: A face predicted from data is a statistical guess presented as a likeness, and the guess is already a form of surveillance.
- What it is: Dewey-Hagborg collected hairs, chewed gum and cigarette butts from New York streets, extracted DNA and computed life-size, full-colour 3D-printed portraits of what the strangers might look like. The masks hang beside the sample and where it was found.
- How it works: DNA was extracted and sequenced at a community biolab; SNPs linked to ancestry, sex, eye and hair colour fed custom software that set parameters of a 3D face model, printed in full colour.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Opacity & latent space
- Shown at: Ars Electronica Honorary Mention 2015; VIDA 15.0 special mention; Fotomuseum Winterthur; Science Gallery Dublin
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kYhSYLXN-KA
- Images: https://deweyhagborg.com/media/pages/projects/stranger-visions/d8bb0edf45-1643025614/wall_of_faces.jpg https://deweyhagborg.com/media/pages/projects/stranger-visions/83ebebdc4a-1643025584/sample4_face_web.jpg
- Project page: https://deweyhagborg.com/projects/stranger-visions

#### us+ — Lauren Lee McCarthy, Kyle McDonald (2013)
- Type: Research prototype · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Voice & listening machine, Computer vision
- Idea: When software reads our faces and words to improve a conversation, it also decides what a good conversation is.
- What it is: A Google Hangout app that listens to and watches a video call, scoring each speaker's words and facial expressions and popping up advice such as 'stop talking about yourself'; if the conversation gets out of balance, it mutes someone automatically.
- How it works: Audio, facial-expression and linguistic analysis based on the LIWC word database and Linguistic Style Matching drive live visualisations, notifications and auto-muting inside Google Hangouts.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Intimacy, care & companionship
- Video: https://vimeo.com/81903116
- Images: https://freight.cargo.site/i/ad160b0c7b6e9061fcbc3bbda3fb065202d10e85f700d065098d874b49761367/_01-copy.jpg
- Project page: https://get-lauren.net/us

#### Saving Face — Lancel & Maat (2011)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Touch turns face recognition from identification into a gesture of shared intimacy.
- What it is: Visitors caress their own face in front of a camera; face recognition tracks the touch and blends their portrait, stroke by stroke, with the faces of earlier visitors into a shared, merged face on a large screen.
- How it works: Camera and face-tracking software map touched regions of the visitor's face onto a composite of stored portraits.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Intimacy, care & companionship
- Video: https://vimeo.com/28499178
- Project page: https://lancelmaat.nl/work/saving-face/

#### Cheese — Christian Moeller (2003)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: A machine that grades sincerity turns a smile into exhausting labour.
- What it is: Six actresses each hold a smile on camera for as long as they can, up to an hour and a half, while emotion-recognition software scores it; when the measured happiness drops, an alarm tells them to smile more sincerely.
- How it works: Multi-screen video installation; an emotion-recognition system (likely a research prototype of the time) analysed each face live and triggered an alarm below a happiness threshold.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Video: https://vimeo.com/42719594
- Images: https://payload.cargocollective.com/1/7/229866/4243042/67-1.jpeg https://payload.cargocollective.com/1/7/229866/4243042/40-1.jpeg
- Project page: https://christianmoeller.com/Cheese

### Adversarial Seeing & Evasion

Camouflage, adversarial patterns and tactics to hide from or confuse machine perception.

#### Trompe l'œil — Esther Hovers, Raphaël Dallaporta (2026)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Computer vision
- Idea: Cardboard can talk back to 'smart' surveillance: a low-tech decoy turns the street into a stage built for the camera.
- What it is: Cardboard silhouettes of people, screen-printed from photographs, are staged on Paris streets in view of the city's AI-assisted surveillance cameras: a trick any person sees through at once but an algorithm finds hard to recognise; in the gallery they stand as small cut-outs on cardboard boxes.
- How it works: Photographs of people are screen-printed and mounted on cardboard; the cut-outs are staged before Paris street cameras (likely the algorithmic video surveillance France authorised for the 2024 Olympics) and shown as maquettes about 28 cm high on cardboard boxes.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Failure, glitch & error
- Shown at: Quickscan #3 – Photography Now, Nederlands Fotomuseum, Rotterdam, 2026
- Images: https://freight.cargo.site/t/original/i/B2310869672983901734834413778777/RaphaelDallaporta-EstherHovers-TrompelOeil-01.jpg https://freight.cargo.site/t/original/i/V3037089665492288790133837150041/Quickscan-05-H-LR.jpg
- Project page: https://www.estherhovers.com

#### How (not) to get hit by a self-driving car — Tomo Kihara, Daniel Coppen (2023)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Autonomous vehicle & drone, Computer vision
- Idea: Every successful trick is an edge case the car would miss, showing whom its training data does not see.
- What it is: A game installation in which players try to cross a virtual street without being detected by a self-driving car's pedestrian detector, disguising themselves to lower their detection score.
- How it works: A camera feeds a pedestrian-detection model that scores each player live; winners can donate their edge-case data to improve the model or delete it.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance, Failure, glitch & error
- Shown at: Playable City Sandbox, Watershed Bristol 2023; S+T+ARTS Prize 2024, Honorary Mention
- Video: https://vimeo.com/883161343
- Images: https://www.tomokihara.com/images/how-not-to-main2.jpg https://www.tomokihara.com/images/how-not-to_01-low-res.jpg
- Project page: https://www.tomokihara.com/en/how-not-to-get-hit-by-a-self-driving-car.html

#### Manifesto Collection — Cap_able (2022)
- Type: Product & platform · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: An adversarial example can be knitted: the machine's weakness becomes a garment you choose to wear.
- What it is: Knitted jumpers, trousers and dresses whose woven patterns make AI detectors label the wearer as an animal or object instead of a person.
- How it works: Adversarial patterns, likely optimised against YOLO-type real-time object detectors, are woven into knitwear with a computerised knitting machine; made in Italy.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance, Failure, glitch & error
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZGp9bZpD6Rg

- Project page: https://www.capable.design/pages/technology

#### Unlearning Language — Lauren Lee McCarthy, Kyle McDonald (2022)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Evading machine perception becomes a way of rediscovering what is most human in how we communicate.
- What it is: Up to eight people are guided by an AI that 'wants to train humans to be less machine-like': whenever it detects their speech, gestures or expressions it intervenes with light, sound and vibration, so the group has to invent ways of communicating it cannot detect, such as humming, clapping or shifting pitch.
- How it works: Speech detection, gesture recognition and expression detection run on cameras and microphones in the room and trigger light, sound and haptic feedback; made with the Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Classification, bias & surveillance, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Shown at: Yamaguchi Center for Arts and Media (YCAM) 2022

- Project page: https://get-lauren.net/Unlearning-Language

#### A Technique of Evading Face Detection — Guo Cheng (2020)
- Type: Artwork & installation · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Escaping machine vision can be a bodily skill: a small, absurd choreography of the face.
- What it is: A deadpan tutorial in which the artist twists and turns his head at the exact angles that make a face detector lose track of him.
- How it works: The artist tested head poses against a standard face-detection algorithm and recorded the moments when detection fails.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Images: https://cdn.guo-cheng.net/files/projectImg/ATechniqueOfEvadingFaceDetection/ATechniqueOfEvadingFaceDetection_1.jpg

#### Google Maps Hacks — Simon Weckert (2020)
- Type: Performance, dance & music · Machines: Platform & recommender algorithm, Infrastructure, energy & supply chain
- Idea: A platform perceives the city through proxies; fool the proxy and the map, and then the traffic, follows.
- What it is: The artist pulls a handcart of 99 second-hand smartphones through Berlin streets, and Google Maps turns the empty streets red with a virtual traffic jam.
- How it works: Each phone runs Google Maps navigation, so the location data of 99 slow-moving devices is read as congested traffic.
- Lens: Failure, glitch & error, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Shown at: Japan Media Arts Festival 2021, Social Impact Award
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k5eL_al_m7Q
