- Project page: https://doi.org/10.7208/chicago/9780226486840.001.0001

#### Vehicles: Experiments in Synthetic Psychology — Valentino Braitenberg (1984)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Robot creature & mobile robot, Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Behaviour that is easy to build is hard to analyse from outside, so observers read minds into simple machines.
- What it is: A series of fourteen imaginary vehicles, each a little more complex, whose sensors wired straight or crossed to their motors make them look afraid, aggressive, in love or curious.
- How it works: Thought experiments in "synthetic psychology": build first, then interpret; widely rebuilt as robots and simulations.
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny, Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262521123/ (MIT Press, 1984)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A-fxij3zM7g
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780262521123-L.jpg

#### Computer Power and Human Reason: From Judgment to Calculation — Joseph Weizenbaum (1976)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Chatbot & language model
- Idea: The question is not what machines can do but what we ought not to let them do.
- What it is: Shaken by how people and psychiatrists embraced ELIZA, Weizenbaum argues that some tasks, such as therapy, judging and caring, should never be delegated to computers even if they could perform them.
- How it works: Book-length ethical argument drawing on his own programming experience and the history of instrumental reason.
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_Power_and_Human_Reason (W. H. Freeman, 1976)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/15228817-L.jpg https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fd/Weizenbaum_1982.jpg

#### Man-Computer Symbiosis — J. C. R. Licklider (1960)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Prosthesis & cyborg, Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: The machine is imagined as a partner in thinking rather than a replacement for the thinker.
- What it is: Licklider proposes that people and computers be coupled in real time so that the machine handles routine work while the human sets goals and judges, like a fig tree and its pollinating wasp.
- How it works: Position paper based on a time-and-motion study of his own working day, with requirements for time-sharing, memory and interfaces.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1109/THFE2.1960.4503259 (IRE Transactions on Human Factors in Electronics HFE-1, 1960)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncCPTgWX6a8
- Images: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e6/Portrait_of_J._C._R._Licklider.jpg

#### A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence — John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, Claude Shannon (1955)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system, Chatbot & language model
- Idea: AI began as a bet that "every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence" could be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate.
- What it is: The funding proposal for a two-month 1956 workshop at Dartmouth College, where the term "artificial intelligence" first appears, listing language use, neuron nets, abstraction, self-improvement and creativity as problems to solve.
- How it works: A short research proposal to the Rockefeller Foundation, reprinted in AI Magazine in 2006.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://ojs.aaai.org/aimagazine/index.php/aimagazine/article/view/1904 (Dartmouth College, 1955; reprinted in AI Magazine 27(4), 2006)
- Images: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/36/John_McCarthy_%28computer_scientist%29_Stanford_2006_%28272020300%29.jpg/1280px-John_McCarthy_%28computer_scientist%29_Stanford_2006_%28272020300%29.jpg
- Project page: https://ojs.aaai.org/aimagazine/index.php/aimagazine/article/view/1904

#### Design for a Brain — W. Ross Ashby (1952)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Learning may be nothing more mysterious than a system searching its own settings until it can survive its environment.
- What it is: Ashby explains adaptive behaviour in animals and machines with one mechanism: a system whose 'essential variables' must stay within limits changes its own parameters, step by step, until they do. The Homeostat serves as the worked example.
- How it works: A mathematical theory of state-determined systems, stability and ultrastability, illustrated with experiments on the Homeostat; a revised second edition followed in 1960.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-015-1320-3 (Chapman & Hall, 1952; 2nd rev. ed. 1960)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/5952056-L.jpg
- Project page: https://archive.org/details/designforbrain00ashb

#### An Imitation of Life — W. Grey Walter (1950)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Robot creature & mobile robot, Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Lifelike behaviour can come from a few connections interacting with an environment, not from complexity inside.
- What it is: Grey Walter's Scientific American report on his robot tortoises Elmer and Elsie, which wander, seek moderate light, avoid obstacles, return to their hutch to recharge and "dance" in front of a mirror.
- How it works: Two vacuum-tube "neurons", a light sensor and a bump contact drive steering and wheel motors in a feedback loop.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Embodiment & kinesthesia, Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/scientificamerican0550-42 (Scientific American 182(5), 1950)
- Images: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e5/Cybernetic_Tortoise_by_William_Grey_Walter_c_1950_%28Ank_Kumar%29.jpg/1280px-Cybernetic_Tortoise_by_William_Grey_Walter_c_1950_%28Ank_Kumar%29.jpg

#### Computing Machinery and Intelligence — Alan Turing (1950)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Chatbot & language model, Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Machine intelligence was defined from the start as a performance judged by humans, not as an inner state.
- What it is: Turing replaces the question "Can machines think?" with the imitation game, in which a judge converses by teletype with a hidden human and a hidden machine, and then answers nine objections to machine thought.
- How it works: Thought experiment and philosophical argument; it also sketches a "child machine" that would learn rather than be fully programmed.
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1093/mind/LIX.236.433 (Mind 59(236), 1950)
- Images: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f8/Alan_Turing_%281951%29.jpg
- Project page: https://www.turing.org.uk

#### The Human Use of Human Beings: Cybernetics and Society — Norbert Wiener (1950)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Cybernetics was born with a labour politics: Wiener saw that automatic machines would set the price of human work and that how we use them is a social choice.
- What it is: Wiener's book for a general audience treats society as a network of messages between people and machines, and warns that the automatic factory is 'the precise economic equivalent of slave labor', so any human work that competes with it must accept the same conditions unless society decides otherwise.
- How it works: Essayistic book extending the theory of feedback and information from Cybernetics (1948) to language, law, education and labour; revised edition 1954.
- Lens: Hidden labour & extraction, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://archive.org/details/humanuseofhumanb00wien (Houghton Mifflin, 1950; rev. ed. 1954)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/164463-L.jpg
- Project page: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Human_Use_of_Human_Beings

#### Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine — Norbert Wiener (1948)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system, Prosthesis & cyborg
- Idea: Once organisms and machines share one logic of feedback, a machine can behave as if it had purpose.
- What it is: The book that named cybernetics: Wiener describes feedback, information and control as principles shared by nervous systems, servomechanisms and computing machines.
- How it works: Mathematical theory drawn from wartime anti-aircraft prediction, neurophysiology and statistical mechanics.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/11810.001.0001 (Technology Press / John Wiley, 1948; MIT Press reissue 2019)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJWDJvbea0M
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/152654-L.jpg
- Project page: https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262537841/

### Philosophy & Machine Phenomenology

Postphenomenology, philosophy of technology and what it is like to be a machine.

#### The AI Mirror: How to Reclaim Our Humanity in an Age of Machine Thinking — Shannon Vallor (2024)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Chatbot & language model, Generative model & latent space
- Idea: Ask what the mirror is made of: an AI built from yesterday's data can only show us the past, so treating it as an oracle freezes moral and political imagination.
- What it is: Vallor argues that today's AI is not a new mind but a mirror: systems trained on our recorded past reflect it back, flattened and amplified, and the danger is that we mistake the reflection for intelligence and stop shaping who we could become.
- How it works: Philosophy of technology and virtue ethics, using the mirror as a working metaphor for large language and image models; published by Oxford University Press.
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny, Opacity & latent space
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780197759066.001.0001 (Oxford University Press, 2024)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IKAx1wLBWUE
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780197759066-L.jpg
- Project page: https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-ai-mirror-9780197759066

#### Communing with the Dead Online: Chatbots, Grief, and Continuing Bonds — Joel Krueger, Lucy Osler (2022)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Chatbot & language model
- Idea: A griefbot may matter less as a copy of the dead than as a way to keep practising a relationship.
- What it is: Krueger and Osler analyse chatbots trained on the texts of the dead, and argue that they can support "continuing bonds" by sustaining the habits of intimacy a mourner shared with the person who died.
- How it works: Phenomenology of grief combined with continuing-bonds theory and cases of chatbots built from the texts of people who died.
- Lens: Grief, memory & afterlife, Intimacy, care & companionship
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.53765/20512201.29.9.222 (Journal of Consciousness Studies 29(9–10), 2022)

#### Non-Human Words: On GPT-3 as a Philosophical Laboratory — Tobias Rees (2022)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Chatbot & language model
- Idea: If words can be made without a speaker, the human/machine divide needs rethinking, not defending.
- What it is: Rees argues that large language models break the modern idea that only humans have language, and treats GPT-3 as a laboratory in which a structural, non-human concept of language becomes visible.
- How it works: Philosophical essay in the Daedalus issue on AI and society.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1162/daed_a_01908 (Daedalus 151(2), 2022)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DUCIdgCLlf0

#### Non-things: Upheaval in the Lifeworld — Byung-Chul Han (2021)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Platform & recommender algorithm, Chatbot & language model
- Idea: A phenomenology of the infosphere: when things become information, we lose the resistance and weight of the world.
- What it is: Essays on how information displaces things: the smartphone, smart objects and data replace durable objects we could hold, and a chapter argues that artificial intelligence cannot think because it has no body and no mood.
- How it works: Philosophical essay collection (German original Undinge, Ullstein 2021; English trans. Daniel Steuer, Polity 2022).
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Paper: https://www.ullstein.de/werke/undinge/hardcover/9783550201257 (Ullstein (German original))
- Project page: https://www.ullstein.de/werke/undinge/hardcover/9783550201257

#### Recursivity and Contingency — Yuk Hui (2019)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system, Generative model & latent space
- Idea: Machines that learn are recursive, organism-like systems that absorb contingency, which changes what a machine is.
- What it is: A book tracing 'recursivity', the logic of loops that turn contingency into organisation, from Kant and German Idealism through cybernetics to today's machine learning.
- How it works: History and philosophy of the organic and the mechanical, from Kant's Critique of Judgment to Wiener and contemporary AI.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.5771/9781786600547 (Rowman & Littlefield International, 2019)
- Project page: https://doi.org/10.5771/9781786600547

#### The Alien Subject of AI — Luciana Parisi (2019)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Platform & recommender algorithm, Generative model & latent space
- Idea: AI can be read as a different logic of thought rather than an imitation of ours.
- What it is: Parisi argues that automated decision systems do not simply copy human reasoning; they form an alien kind of subjectivity that unsettles the humanist image of the rational subject.
- How it works: Theoretical essay drawing on philosophy of computation and critiques of instrumental reason.
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1057/s41286-018-00064-3 (Subjectivity 12(1), 2019)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9oGx0ejmdgg

#### Contingent Computation: Abstraction, Experience, and Indeterminacy in Computational Aesthetics — M. Beatrice Fazi (2018)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Computers are not failed copies of human thought; their aesthetics lie in their own contingency.
- What it is: Fazi argues that computation is not a closed, predictable procedure: through Turing's incomputability and Whitehead's philosophy she shows that formal systems have their own indeterminacy and mode of experience.
- How it works: Philosophical argument combining Whitehead, Deleuze, Gödel and Turing.
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.5040/9798881812027 (Rowman & Littlefield International, 2018)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NIJnjAs7ysI
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/9200964-L.jpg

#### Robot Rights — David J. Gunkel (2018)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Social & companion robot, Humanoid & android
- Idea: Moral consideration may be something we extend in encounter, which makes the robot a test of our own ethics.
- What it is: Gunkel works through the four logical answers to whether robots can and should have rights, and argues for a relational, Levinas-inspired approach that starts from how we encounter the other.
- How it works: Philosophical analysis of the is/ought positions in the robot-rights debate.
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/11444.001.0001 (MIT Press, 2018)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YKdBHMDlulw
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/8835491-L.jpg

#### Unthought: The Power of the Cognitive Nonconscious — N. Katherine Hayles (2017)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system, Autonomous vehicle & drone
- Idea: Machines already think, nonconsciously, alongside us; the question is how agency is shared in the assemblage.
- What it is: Hayles defines cognition broadly enough to include nonconscious processes in humans, animals and computers, and describes "cognitive assemblages" such as high-frequency trading and drone swarms in which humans and machines decide together.
- How it works: Theory built from neuroscience, media studies and case studies; the assemblage argument first appeared in "Cognitive Assemblages" (Critical Inquiry, 2016).
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7208/chicago/9780226447919.001.0001 (University of Chicago Press, 2017)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yUsTa01vJpA
- Images: https://tmm.chicagodistributioncenter.com/IsbnImages/9780226447889.jpg

#### On the Existence of Digital Objects — Yuk Hui (2016)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Infrastructure, energy & supply chain, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Data objects are a new kind of thing, with their own relations and existence beyond natural and technical objects.
- What it is: A philosophy of the 'digital object' (YouTube videos, Facebook profiles, metadata) that asks what kind of being these data structures have and how they form new milieus.
- How it works: Philosophical study drawing on Heidegger, Husserl, Simondon and the history of markup languages and ontologies.
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.5749/minnesota/9780816698905.001.0001 (University of Minnesota Press, 2016)
- Images: https://minnesota-us.imgix.net/covers/9780816698912.jpg?w=400
- Project page: https://www.upress.umn.edu/9780816698912/on-the-existence-of-digital-objects/

#### The Question Concerning Technology in China: An Essay in Cosmotechnics — Yuk Hui (2016)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Infrastructure, energy & supply chain
- Idea: There is no single universal technology; AI and machines could be imagined from other cosmologies.
- What it is: A book that reopens Heidegger's question of technology from Chinese philosophy (the relation of qi and dao, tool and way) and proposes 'cosmotechnics': every technology is tied to a particular cosmology.
- How it works: Comparative philosophy reading Heidegger, Stiegler and Simondon with Confucian, Daoist and New Confucian thought.
- Lens: Machine umwelt, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://www.urbanomic.com/book/question-concerning-technology-china/ (Urbanomic, 2016)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=66ivnhe8YF4
- Project page: https://www.urbanomic.com/book/question-concerning-technology-china/

#### The Stack: On Software and Sovereignty — Benjamin Bratton (2016)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Infrastructure, energy & supply chain, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Computation is no longer a tool inside the world; it is a layered world we live inside.
- What it is: Bratton describes planetary computation as an accidental megastructure of six layers (Earth, Cloud, City, Address, Interface, User) that now competes with states as a form of sovereignty.
- How it works: Design-theoretical model built from geopolitics, platform studies and architecture.
- Lens: Hidden labour & extraction, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/9780262029575.001.0001 (MIT Press, 2016)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cUhhHw_xS4w
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/14832820-L.jpg

#### Alien Phenomenology, or What It's Like to Be a Thing — Ian Bogost (2012)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: We can only grasp a machine's experience by metaphor, and building things is a legitimate way to do that philosophy.
- What it is: Bogost applies object-oriented ontology to computers and other things, and proposes methods for speculating on their experience: ontography (lists of things), metaphorism and carpentry, making artefacts that do philosophy.
- How it works: Philosophical essay using the Atari 2600 and his own small programs such as I Am TIA as cases.
- Lens: Machine umwelt, Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.5749/9780816681426 (University of Minnesota Press, 2012)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z1V2z3wjtqo
- Images: https://minnesota-us.imgix.net/covers/9780816678983.jpg?w=400

#### Humans, Animals, and Robots: A Phenomenological Approach to Human-Robot Relations — Mark Coeckelbergh (2011)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Social & companion robot, Humanoid & android
- Idea: A robot's moral standing grows out of the relations we have with it, not out of a checklist of inner properties.
- What it is: Coeckelbergh argues that what counts in human–robot relations is how robots appear to us in experience, and compares our relations to robots with our relations to animals.
- How it works: Phenomenological and relational analysis; developed further in his book Growing Moral Relations (2012).
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny, Intimacy, care & companionship
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12369-010-0075-6 (International Journal of Social Robotics 3(2), 2011)

#### Cyborg Intentionality: Rethinking the Phenomenology of Human–Technology Relations — Peter-Paul Verbeek (2008)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Prosthesis & cyborg, Computer vision
- Idea: Machines do not only extend our senses; they bring their own perception, and artworks can make us experience it.
- What it is: Verbeek adds two relations beyond Ihde: hybrid intentionality, where technology merges with the body, and composite intentionality, where a device's own way of sensing (an infrared camera, for example) is added to ours.
- How it works: Philosophical article extending postphenomenology with examples from implants, imaging and art.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Machine seeing, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11097-008-9099-x (Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences 7(3), 2008)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FVhrLwBNbvU

#### A stroll through the worlds of robots and animals: Applying Jakob von Uexküll's theory of meaning to adaptive robots and artificial life — Tom Ziemke (2001)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Robot creature & mobile robot, Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: A robot's world is what its sensors and actions make meaningful to it; the question is whether that world is its own or one we built for it.
- What it is: Ziemke and Noel Sharkey ask whether Jakob von Uexküll's umwelt theory, in which every animal lives in a world of its own meanings, can apply to robots. Comparing classic AI, behaviour-based robots and evolved artificial-life agents, they find that learning and evolving robots begin to build their own sensorimotor worlds, but that without a living body their meanings remain largely derived from their designers.
- How it works: Theoretical paper revisiting Uexküll's 'A stroll through the worlds of animals and men' (1934) in the light of behaviour-based robotics, evolutionary robotics and artificial life; published in a Semiotica special issue on Uexküll.
- Lens: Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1515/semi.2001.050 (Semiotica 134, 2001)
- Project page: https://doi.org/10.1515/semi.2001.050

#### Does a Robot Have an Umwelt? Reflections on the Qualitative Biosemiotics of Jakob von Uexküll — Claus Emmeche (2001)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Robot creature & mobile robot, Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Sensorimotor coupling may give a robot a world, but whether that world is lived is still open.
- What it is: Emmeche asks whether a situated robot, coupled to its surroundings through sensors and motors, can have an Umwelt, the meaningful perceptual world that Uexküll attributed to animals.
- How it works: Biosemiotic analysis of behaviour-based robotics, in the Semiotica special issue on Uexküll.
- Lens: Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1515/semi.2001.048 (Semiotica 134, 2001)

#### How We Became Posthuman: Virtual Bodies in Cybernetics, Literature, and Informatics — N. Katherine Hayles (1999)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system, Prosthesis & cyborg
- Idea: Treating mind as disembodied information is a historical choice, and embodiment is what it leaves out.
- What it is: Hayles tells how information "lost its body" through the Macy cybernetics conferences and post-war science and fiction, and argues for an embodied posthuman that does not dream of uploading the mind.
- How it works: Intellectual history of cybernetics read alongside novels by Philip K. Dick, Bernard Wolfe and others.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7208/chicago/9780226321394.001.0001 (University of Chicago Press, 1999)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rryjPdKMxO4
- Images: https://tmm.chicagodistributioncenter.com/IsbnImages/9780226321462.jpg

#### The Extended Mind — Andy Clark, David Chalmers (1998)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Prosthesis & cyborg
- Idea: The boundary of the mind is set by function, not by skin, so our devices may already be part of us.
- What it is: Clark and Chalmers argue that when a device such as a notebook reliably plays the role of memory, it is part of the mind; Otto's notebook counts as much as Inga's biological memory.
- How it works: Short philosophical argument built on the parity principle and thought experiments.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1093/analys/58.1.7 (Analysis 58(1), 1998)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kc-TdMjuJRU

#### Technology and the Lifeworld: From Garden to Earth — Don Ihde (1990)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Prosthesis & cyborg, Computer vision
- Idea: Every machine artwork puts us in one of these relations, and the interesting ones switch between them.
- What it is: Ihde sorts human–technology relations into four kinds: embodiment (seeing through glasses), hermeneutic (reading a thermometer), alterity (facing a device as a quasi-other) and background (an unnoticed milieu).
- How it works: Postphenomenological analysis of concrete instruments, extending Husserl and Heidegger through case studies.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Alterity & the uncanny, Machine seeing
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.2979/3108.0 (Indiana University Press, 1990)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UiRkzZEMDxU
- Images: https://ingram-indiana.imgix.net/covers/9780253205605.jpg?w=400
- Project page: https://iupress.org/9780253205605/technology-and-the-lifeworld/

#### Gramophone, Film, Typewriter — Friedrich Kittler (1986)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Computer vision
- Idea: Recording machines do not extend the human senses so much as replace them with technical inscription; noise and nonsense are stored as faithfully as speech.
- What it is: Kittler argues that around 1900 the gramophone, film and typewriter split what writing once held together into three separate data streams, sound, image and text, recorded by machines without passing through human sense or meaning. 'Media determine our situation': what we can perceive and say depends on the technical systems that store it.
- How it works: Media-archaeological readings of literature, psychoanalysis and engineering texts, arranged around the three devices; German edition Brinkmann & Bose, 1986; English translation by Geoffrey Winthrop-Young and Michael Wutz, Stanford University Press, 1999.
- Lens: Machine listening & voice, Machine seeing
- Paper: https://archive.org/details/gramophonefilmty0000kitt (Brinkmann & Bose, 1986; English: Stanford University Press, 1999)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/577633-L.jpg https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f6/Kittler_Synthesizer.jpg
- Project page: https://archive.org/details/gramophonefilmty0000kitt

#### A Manifesto for Cyborgs: Science, Technology, and Socialist Feminism in the 1980s — Donna Haraway (1985)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Prosthesis & cyborg
- Idea: The cyborg refuses origins and purity, which makes human–machine hybridity a political opening rather than a loss.
- What it is: Haraway's essay takes the cyborg, a hybrid of machine and organism, as an ironic political myth for feminism, after the boundaries between human and animal, organism and machine, and physical and non-physical have broken down.
- How it works: Political essay mixing socialist feminism, science studies and science fiction; reprinted in Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (1991).
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.4324/9780203873106 (Socialist Review 80, 1985; in Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (Routledge, 1991))
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/902702-L.jpg

#### Towards a Philosophy of Photography — Vilém Flusser (1983)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Computer vision, Generative model & latent space
- Idea: Whoever uses an apparatus is also used by its program; this applies directly to generative models.
- What it is: Flusser describes the camera as an apparatus, a black box whose program the photographer only plays inside, producing "technical images" that realise possibilities already written into the device.
- How it works: Short philosophical essay; German original Für eine Philosophie der Fotografie (European Photography, 1983).
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Machine seeing
- Paper: https://www.reaktionbooks.co.uk/work/towards-a-philosophy-of-photography (European Photography, 1983; English: Reaktion Books, 2000)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/917481-L.jpg

#### The Buddha in the Robot — Masahiro Mori (1981)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Humanoid & android, Robot creature & mobile robot
- Idea: A non-Western frame in which machines are not opposed to spirit but part of the same continuum.
- What it is: A book in which Mori argues, from Zen Buddhism, that robots have the Buddha-nature and that building them is a way to understand the self.
- How it works: A collection of essays and talks by a robotics engineer, translated from Japanese and published by Kosei Publishing (Tokyo).
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://openlibrary.org/works/OL5531608W (Kosei Publishing, Tokyo, 1981)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/6620832-L.jpg
- Project page: https://openlibrary.org/works/OL5531608W

#### Minds, Brains, and Programs — John Searle (1980)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Chatbot & language model
- Idea: Fluent output does not prove a mind behind it, which is exactly the question chatbots now raise.
- What it is: Searle's Chinese Room: a person who knows no Chinese follows a rulebook to return fluent Chinese answers, which shows, he argues, that running a program is not the same as understanding.
- How it works: Thought experiment published with open peer commentaries and Searle's replies.
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny, Opacity & latent space
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0140525X00005756 (Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3(3), 1980)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6tzjcnPsZ_w

#### What Computers Can't Do: A Critique of Artificial Reason — Hubert Dreyfus (1972)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Intelligence needs a body and a world; a machine without them breaks down exactly where everyday skill begins.
- What it is: Drawing on Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty, Dreyfus argues that symbolic AI fails because human intelligence rests on an embodied, situated background of know-how that cannot be written down as rules.
- How it works: Phenomenological critique of the assumptions of 1960s AI research; revised as What Computers Still Can't Do (MIT Press, 1992).
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Failure, glitch & error
- Paper: https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262540674/ (Harper & Row, 1972; rev. MIT Press, 1992)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=474A0MAS-Dk
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/151382-L.jpg

#### On the Mode of Existence of Technical Objects — Gilbert Simondon (1958)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system, Infrastructure, energy & supply chain
- Idea: Machines have their own genesis and milieu; understanding them is a form of culture, not a threat to it.
- What it is: Simondon traces how technical objects become more concrete and self-consistent over time, how they form an "associated milieu" with their surroundings, and why a culture that ignores machines alienates itself.
- How it works: Philosophical history of technical lineages such as engines and vacuum tubes; English translation by Cécile Malaspina and John Rogove (Univocal, 2017).
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://www.upress.umn.edu/9781517904876/on-the-mode-of-existence-of-technical-objects/ (Aubier, 1958; English: Univocal / University of Minnesota Press, 2017)
- Images: https://minnesota-us.imgix.net/covers/9781517904876.jpg?w=400

### Critical AI Studies

Books and papers on AI's politics, labour, bias and power.

#### The Eye of the Master: A Social History of Artificial Intelligence — Matteo Pasquinelli (2023)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Infrastructure, energy & supply chain, Dataset & training data
- Idea: AI automates the organisation of labour; its "intelligence" is collective human skill captured as data.
- What it is: Pasquinelli traces AI from Babbage's factory computation to the perceptron and neural networks, arguing that AI imitates the division of labour and the collective knowledge of workers, not the brain.
- How it works: Social history drawing on Marx, the history of statistics and the history of cybernetics; won the 2024 Deutscher Memorial Prize.
- Lens: Hidden labour & extraction, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://www.versobooks.com/products/735-the-eye-of-the-master (Verso, 2023)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U0wECTKNmlY
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/14569589-L.jpg

#### How to Read an AI Image — Eryk Salvaggio (2022)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Generative model & latent space, Dataset & training data
- Idea: A generated image is evidence about the archive behind it, which is how to include generative work critically.
- What it is: Salvaggio proposes reading each generated image as "an infographic about the dataset": its repetitions, clichés and absences show what the training data over- and under-represents.
- How it works: Media-studies close reading of batches of diffusion-model outputs, like a semiotic analysis of photographs.
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Machine seeing
- Paper: https://cyberneticforests.substack.com/p/how-to-read-an-ai-image (Cybernetic Forests, 2022)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FZB3o5WTVm8
- Images: https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tOVn!,w_1200,h_675,c_fill,f_jpg,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep,g_auto/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F941fd849-5808-4de6-97d5-b405ea6c4573_1024x1024.png

#### Atlas of AI: Power, Politics, and the Planetary Costs of Artificial Intelligence — Kate Crawford (2021)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Infrastructure, energy & supply chain, Dataset & training data, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: To see AI clearly, map what it extracts: earth, labour, data and people's categories.
- What it is: Crawford follows AI from lithium mines and Amazon warehouses through training data and classification to affect recognition and state power, arguing that AI is neither artificial nor intelligent but a material industry.
- How it works: Field research at mines, warehouses and archives, combined with the history of classification.
- Lens: Hidden labour & extraction, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.12987/9780300252392 (Yale University Press, 2021)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0PqrZ2lqT70
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/14420723-L.jpg

#### Discriminating Data — Wendy Hui Kyong Chun (2021)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Dataset & training data, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Predictive systems do not only reflect bias; their assumption that similar people cluster produces segregation.
- What it is: A book showing how machine learning and network science inherit eugenics and segregation: correlation and 'homophily' sort people into neighbourhoods of the similar.
- How it works: Critical history of statistics, eugenics and network analysis, with close readings of recommendation and ML methods.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/14050.001.0001 (MIT Press, 2021)
- Project page: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/14050.001.0001

#### On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big? — Emily M. Bender, Timnit Gebru (2021)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Chatbot & language model, Dataset & training data, Infrastructure, energy & supply chain
- Idea: A language model stitches together forms without meaning; the coherence is in the reader's eye.
- What it is: Bender, Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major and Margaret Mitchell set out the environmental costs, undocumented training data, encoded bias and illusion of meaning in ever larger language models; the paper's review led to Gebru's exit from Google.
- How it works: Critical survey of the NLP literature on scale, energy, data documentation and bias.
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/3442188.3445922 (FAccT 2021)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N5c2X8vhfBE

#### Data Feminism — Catherine D'Ignazio, Lauren F. Klein (2020)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Dataset & training data
- Idea: Data is never raw; who collects it, counts whom and leaves whom out are feminist questions.
- What it is: D'Ignazio and Klein set out seven principles, from examining power to making labour visible, for doing data science in a way that challenges rather than reinforces inequality.
- How it works: Intersectional feminist theory applied to case studies of data projects; open access online.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/11805.001.0001 (MIT Press, 2020)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pmNEe6FvduM
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/isbn/9780262044004-L.jpg

#### The Nooscope Manifested: AI as Instrument of Knowledge Extractivism — Matteo Pasquinelli, Vladan Joler (2020)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Dataset & training data, Infrastructure, energy & supply chain
- Idea: AI is not an intelligent subject but an instrument, a telescope for knowledge, that magnifies some patterns, distorts others and extracts value from collective labour.
- What it is: An essay and a large diagram that map machine learning as an instrument of knowledge, from the world and the labour that become training data, through the learning algorithm, to the statistical model with its biases, errors and uses.
- How it works: Joler drew the machine-learning pipeline as a cartography and the two authors wrote the accompanying text, first published at nooscope.ai in May 2020 and then in AI & Society.
- Lens: Hidden labour & extraction, Classification, bias & surveillance, Opacity & latent space
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-020-01097-6 (AI & Society, 2021)
- Project page: https://web.archive.org/web/2020/https://nooscope.ai/

#### Ghost Work: How to Stop Silicon Valley from Building a New Global Underclass — Mary L. Gray, Siddharth Suri (2019)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Dataset & training data, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Behind the promise of automation there is always a "last mile" of hidden human work.
- What it is: Gray and Suri describe the on-demand workers who label data, moderate content and check outputs behind apps and "AI", on platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk and UHRS in the US and India.
- How it works: Five years of ethnography, surveys and experiments with crowdworkers.
- Lens: Hidden labour & extraction
- Paper: https://ghostwork.info (Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2019)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D5fkupjVEp8
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/10131831-L.jpg
- Project page: https://ghostwork.info

#### Race After Technology: Abolitionist Tools for the New Jim Code — Ruha Benjamin (2019)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Discrimination can be engineered into systems that look neutral: the "New Jim Code".
- What it is: Benjamin shows how automated systems in hiring, health, policing and design reproduce racial hierarchy while appearing objective, and collects abolitionist tools to counter them.
- How it works: Sociological analysis of case studies from technology, law and design.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://www.politybooks.com/bookdetail?book_slug=race-after-technology-abolitionist-tools-for-the-new-jim-code--9781509526390 (Polity, 2019)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rY8RkET3KC0
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/10088781-L.jpg

#### Algorithms of Oppression: How Search Engines Reinforce Racism — Safiya Umoja Noble (2018)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: A ranking algorithm is an editor with commercial interests, not a neutral window onto the world.
- What it is: Noble documents how commercial search results, such as Google's for "black girls", reproduced racist and sexist stereotypes, and argues that ranking is shaped by advertising and power.
- How it works: Content analysis of search results combined with Black feminist and information-science theory.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.18574/nyu/9781479833641.001.0001 (NYU Press, 2018)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6KLTpoTpkXo
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/12856940-L.jpg

#### Automating Inequality: How High-Tech Tools Profile, Police, and Punish the Poor — Virginia Eubanks (2018)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Dataset & training data, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Automated decision systems are tested first and hardest on the poor, where surveillance is normal and appeal is weak; the machine inherits the poorhouse's moral sorting.
- What it is: Three case studies of automated decisions about poor people in the United States: Indiana's privatised welfare-eligibility system, the coordinated entry system that ranks homeless people for housing in Los Angeles, and a predictive model that scores child-maltreatment risk in Pittsburgh. Eubanks calls the result a 'digital poorhouse'.
- How it works: Field reporting and interviews with caseworkers, system designers and affected families, set against the history of poor relief in the United States.
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250074317/automatinginequality (St. Martin's Press, 2018)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wzssyn0L5I8
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/8354270-L.jpg
- Project page: https://virginia-eubanks.com/automating-inequality/

#### Psychopolitics: Neoliberalism and New Technologies of Power — Byung-Chul Han (2014)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Dataset & training data, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Surveillance today works through seduction and self-disclosure more than through prohibition.
- What it is: A short essay arguing that data-driven 'smart power' no longer disciplines bodies but reads and steers the psyche; Big Data becomes a tool of psychopolitical control.
- How it works: Philosophical essay (German original Psychopolitik, S. Fischer 2014; English trans. Erik Butler, Verso 2017).
- Lens: Classification, bias & surveillance, Hidden labour & extraction
- Paper: https://www.versobooks.com/products/226-psychopolitics (Verso (English ed. 2017))
- Images: https://www.versobooks.com/cdn/shop/files/getimage_05e7fdd2-de74-4073-8bc6-73bfa358d3cb.jpg?v=1790570326&width=600
- Project page: https://www.versobooks.com/products/226-psychopolitics

#### Human-Machine Reconfigurations: Plans and Situated Actions — Lucy Suchman (2007)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Humanoid & android, Social & companion robot
- Idea: A machine seems intelligent because of the work people and settings do around it.
- What it is: Suchman revisits her 1987 study of people failing to use an "intelligent" photocopier and extends it to humanlike robots such as Kismet and Cog, arguing that machine agency is made in situated interaction.
- How it works: Ethnomethodology and feminist science studies applied to interaction analysis and robotics labs; 2nd expanded edition of Plans and Situated Actions.
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511808418 (Cambridge University Press, 2007)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3_4-6gVbk4E
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/9840684-L.jpg

### Robotics, HRI & Embodied Cognition

Embodied robotics, social robotics and research on how people relate to robots.

#### The New Breed: What Our History with Animals Reveals about Our Future with Robots — Kate Darling (2021)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Social & companion robot, Robot creature & mobile robot
- Idea: We already know how to live with non-human others we use, love and mourn; robots can join that history.
- What it is: Darling argues that robots are better understood on the model of animals than of humans, and uses cases such as soldiers holding funerals for bomb-disposal robots and people refusing to hurt a Pleo dinosaur.
- How it works: Popular-science argument combining HRI experiments, legal history of animals and ethics.
- Lens: Intimacy, care & companionship, Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250296115/thenewbreed/ (Henry Holt, 2021)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sTJ7E7TDTrU
- Images: https://mpd-biblio-covers.imgix.net/9781250296115.jpg?fm=jpg
- Project page: https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250296115/thenewbreed/

#### Alone Together: Why We Expect More from Technology and Less from Each Other — Sherry Turkle (2011)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Social & companion robot, Chatbot & language model
- Idea: We are ready to accept a performance of care in place of care, and that says more about us than about the machines.
- What it is: Based on fifteen years of interviews, Turkle describes a "robotic moment" in which children and elderly people accept Furbies, AIBO, My Real Baby and the seal robot Paro as companions that are "alive enough".
- How it works: Clinical interviews and field observation in homes, schools and nursing homes.
- Lens: Intimacy, care & companionship, Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://www.basicbooks.com/titles/sherry-turkle/alone-together/9780465093656/ (Basic Books, 2011)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MtLVCpZIiNs
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/6952623-L.jpg

#### How the Body Shapes the Way We Think: A New View of Intelligence — Rolf Pfeifer, Josh Bongard (2006)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Robot creature & mobile robot, Humanoid & android
- Idea: Some of a robot's intelligence is in its shape and materials, not its controller.
- What it is: Pfeifer and Bongard argue that intelligence depends on the morphology and materials of a body interacting with its environment, using passive-dynamic walkers and compliant robots as examples.
- How it works: Synthesis of embodied AI research with design principles for robots.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/3585.001.0001 (MIT Press, 2006)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mhWwoaoxIyc
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/13662665-L.jpg

#### In the Hands of Machines? The Future of Aged Care — Robert Sparrow (2006)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Social & companion robot
- Idea: A machine that simulates care may be a harm, not a help, when it replaces the people who would have cared.
- What it is: Robert and Linda Sparrow argue that care robots for older people would reduce human contact and rely on deceiving vulnerable people into believing a machine cares for them.
- How it works: Ethical analysis of the tasks of aged care against the capacities of existing and projected robots.
- Lens: Intimacy, care & companionship, Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1007/s11023-006-9030-6 (Minds and Machines 16(2), 2006)

#### Designing Sociable Robots — Cynthia Breazeal (2002)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Social & companion robot, Humanoid & android
- Idea: A robot that shows needs invites people to care for it, and that care is what makes it social.
- What it is: Breazeal's book on Kismet, the expressive robot head she built at MIT, lays out how a robot can use drives, emotions and facial expression to engage people as a caregiver engages an infant.
- How it works: Synthesis of her doctoral work: motivational and emotional models, perception of faces and voice prosody, and an actuated face with eyebrows, ears, eyelids and lips.
- Lens: Intimacy, care & companionship, Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/2376.001.0001 (MIT Press, 2002)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/151207-L.jpg https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Kismet-IMG_6014.JPG/960px-Kismet-IMG_6014.JPG

#### The Cog Project: Building a Humanoid Robot — Rodney Brooks (1999)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Humanoid & android
- Idea: Giving a robot a humanlike body and social development makes people treat it as someone, which in turn shapes what it learns.
- What it is: Brooks, Breazeal, Marjanović, Scassellati and Williamson report on Cog, an upper-torso humanoid at MIT built to develop skills such as eye movements, reaching and joint attention by interacting with people, as an infant would.
- How it works: Upper-torso humanoid platform with active vision and behaviour-based control, developed 1993–2004.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-48834-0_5 (Computation for Metaphors, Analogy, and Agents, LNCS 1562, Springer, 1999)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oWjWzDzfLBo
- Images: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e3/Cog%2C_1993-2004%2C_view_1_-_MIT_Museum_-_DSC03732.JPG/960px-Cog%2C_1993-2004%2C_view_1_-_MIT_Museum_-_DSC03732.JPG

#### The Media Equation: How People Treat Computers, Television, and New Media Like Real People and Places — Byron Reeves, Clifford Nass (1996)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Voice & listening machine, Social & companion robot
- Idea: Media = real life: social responses to machines are automatic, so design always addresses a social animal.
- What it is: Reeves and Nass report dozens of experiments in which people are polite to computers, respond to their flattery, and assign them gender and personality, even while saying they know the machine is not a person.
- How it works: Classic social-psychology studies replicated with computers and television in place of people.
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny, Intimacy, care & companionship
- Paper: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Media_Equation (Cambridge University Press / CSLI Publications, 1996)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/829557-L.jpg

#### Computers Are Social Actors — Clifford Nass (1994)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Voice & listening machine
- Idea: Minimal social cues, a voice and a role, are enough to trigger full social behaviour towards a machine.
- What it is: Nass, Jonathan Steuer and Ellen R. Tauber ran a series of experiments showing that people apply politeness norms and gender stereotypes to computers that speak, for example rating a computer more kindly when that same computer asks.
- How it works: Controlled lab experiments with tutoring and evaluating computers using recorded voices.
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1145/191666.191703 (CHI 1994)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e7PvUUhDrfk

#### Intelligence without Representation — Rodney Brooks (1991)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Robot creature & mobile robot
- Idea: Intelligence can be situated and embodied rather than planned from an internal model, and it looks more alive that way.
- What it is: Brooks argues that robots should be built from layers of simple behaviours coupled directly to sensors and motors, using "the world as its own best model", as in his six-legged robot Genghis walking over rough ground.
- How it works: Subsumption architecture: stacked finite-state machines that suppress or inhibit each other, tested on mobile robots at the MIT AI Lab.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1016/0004-3702(91)90053-M (Artificial Intelligence 47(1–3), 1991)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-6piNZBFdfY

#### The Uncanny Valley (Bukimi no Tani) — Masahiro Mori (1970)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Humanoid & android, Prosthesis & cyborg
- Idea: Near-likeness is more disturbing than obvious difference, so designers may be wiser to stop short of the human.
- What it is: A short essay in the Japanese magazine Energy proposing that our affinity for robots rises with human likeness until it drops sharply into a 'valley' of eeriness; the examples are prosthetic hands, Bunraku puppets and corpses.
- How it works: A hand-drawn graph of affinity against human likeness, with separate curves for still and moving objects; English translation by Karl MacDorman and Norri Kageki (2012).
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1109/MRA.2012.2192811 (Energy 7(4), 1970; English: IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine, 2012)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0g0sH3jTaVc
- Images: https://spectrum.ieee.org/media-library/the-uncanny-valley-by-masahiro-mori-republished-in-robotics-automation-magazine.png?id=25569782&width=980 https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f0/Mori_Uncanny_Valley.svg
- Project page: https://spectrum.ieee.org/the-uncanny-valley

#### An Experimental Study of Apparent Behavior — Fritz Heider, Marianne Simmel (1944)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Robot creature & mobile robot
- Idea: Motion alone is enough for us to see agents with intentions and feelings, which is why simple robots feel alive.
- What it is: Heider and Simmel showed viewers a 2.5-minute film of two triangles and a circle moving around a box; almost everyone described a story of a bully, a chase and a couple escaping.
- How it works: Stop-motion animation of geometric shapes shown to 114 students, who then described or answered questions about it.
- Lens: Alterity & the uncanny, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.2307/1416950 (American Journal of Psychology 57(2), 1944)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n9TWwG4SFWQ

### Art & Media Theory

Writing on robot art, AI art and machine images.

#### Medium Hot: Images in the Age of Heat — Hito Steyerl (2025)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Generative model & latent space, Infrastructure, energy & supply chain
- Idea: Every machine-made image has a temperature: its aesthetics are tied to the heat, labour and war that produce it.
- What it is: Essays on images in the age of machine learning and global heating: Steyerl argues that statistical AI images cannot be separated from the energy they burn, the workers they depend on and the military uses they serve, and asks whether they can still count as art.
- How it works: Collected essays combining media theory, political economy and artistic practice, written amid the rise of generative AI and the climate crisis (Verso, 192 pages).
- Lens: Hidden labour & extraction, Machine seeing, Opacity & latent space
- Paper: https://www.versobooks.com/products/3329-medium-hot (Verso, 2025)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/15102192-L.jpg
- Project page: https://www.versobooks.com/products/3329-medium-hot

#### Artificial Aesthetics: Generative AI, Art and Visual Media — Lev Manovich, Emanuele Arielli (2024)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Generative model & latent space
- Idea: Generative AI is not a tool added to art but a new medium that rewrites who counts as an author and whose taste the machine learns.
- What it is: A free book in nine chapters, released online between 2021 and 2024 and compiled in 2025, on how generative AI changes ideas of authorship, creativity, perception and taste; it is now being translated into Spanish, Italian, Chinese, Japanese and Korean.
- How it works: Alternating single-author chapters: Arielli writes from aesthetics, philosophy and the psychology of art (techno-animism and the Pygmalion effect, the artificial gaze, aesthetic alignment); Manovich from media history and his own practice with image generators.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Alterity & the uncanny, Opacity & latent space
- Paper: https://manovich.net/content/04-projects/189-artificial-aesthetics/manovich_and_arielli.artificial_aesthetics.all_chapters_final.pdf (manovich.net, 2024 (Spanish: Ediciones Akal, 2025; Italian: Luca Sossella Editore, 2026))
- Images: https://manovich.net/content/04-projects/189-artificial-aesthetics/artificial-aesthetics-top-2.jpg
- Project page: https://manovich.net/index.php/projects/artificial-aesthetics

#### Machine Vision: How Algorithms Are Changing the Way We See the World — Jill Walker Rettberg (2023)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Computer vision, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: Machine vision is not one eye but a set of relations that make some things visible and others unseen.
- What it is: Rettberg organises machine vision into five modes (seeing more, seeing differently, seeing everything, being seen and seeing less) and reads artworks such as Zizi – Queering the Dataset and The Normalizing Machine alongside smart doorbells and face filters.
- How it works: Qualitative analysis of the Machine Vision in Art, Games and Narratives database (500 works) built by her ERC team; open access.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://www.politybooks.com/bookdetail?book_slug=machine-vision-how-algorithms-are-changing-the-way-we-see-the-world--9781509545223 (Polity, 2023)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ybva0y9KF8Q
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/14726453-L.jpg
- Project page: https://machine-vision.no

#### Mean Images — Hito Steyerl (2023)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Generative model & latent space, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Generated images are "mean" in both senses: averages that also enforce norms and exclude.
- What it is: Steyerl reads generative-AI images as statistical averages of scraped data, starting from how images of herself appear in the LAION-5B dataset and what models generate from her name.
- How it works: Essay combining close reading of model outputs with the political economy of datasets.
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://newleftreview.org/issues/ii140/articles/hito-steyerl-mean-images (New Left Review 140/141, 2023)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PFwaqpkd61M
- Images: https://newleftreview.org/system/dragonfly/production/2023/04/28/7rn0jeq677_Steyerl_Figure_1.jpg

#### The Perception Machine: Our Photographic Future between the Eye and AI — Joanna Zylinska (2023)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Computer vision, Generative model & latent space
- Idea: Perception is now a joint human–machine process, so critique has to work from inside it.
- What it is: Zylinska argues that photography has become a planetary perception machine of cameras, sensors and algorithms, and asks how humans can still see and act within it.
- How it works: Media-philosophical essay with her own artistic experiments; open access.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/14471.001.0001 (MIT Press, 2023)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jsdZFeTs2VA

#### Art in the Age of Machine Learning — Sofian Audry (2021)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Generative model & latent space, Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: The artist's material is the training process itself, and it has a longer history than the current hype admits.
- What it is: Audry explains how machine-learning systems are trained and places ML art in the lineage of cybernetic, artificial-life and evolutionary art, with case studies of contemporary ML artworks.
- How it works: Technical-conceptual framework (data, training, model) applied to case studies; Leonardo series.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Opacity & latent space
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/12832.001.0001 (MIT Press / Leonardo, 2021)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TwtgaQSmnXc

#### AI Art: Machine Visions and Warped Dreams — Joanna Zylinska (2020)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Generative model & latent space, Computer vision
- Idea: The interesting AI art is the one that shows how the machine works and who works for it.
- What it is: Zylinska rejects the question "can computers be creative?" and instead reads works such as Lauren McCarthy's LAUREN, Pierre Huyghe's UUmwelt and Trevor Paglen's Sight Machine against neural-network imagery she calls kitsch.
- How it works: Critical essay in the Media : Art : Write : Now series, open access; includes her own photo-and-AI project.
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Machine umwelt
- Paper: https://www.openhumanitiespress.org/books/titles/ai-art/ (Open Humanities Press, 2020)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jASV6Hjd2bY
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/14833507-L.jpg
- Project page: https://www.openhumanitiespress.org/books/titles/ai-art/

#### Platform Seeing: Image Ensembles and Their Invisualities — Adrian Mackenzie, Anna Munster (2019)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: Machine vision happens in datasets and pipelines, not in any single image or eye.
- What it is: Mackenzie and Munster argue that on platforms, seeing is done by huge ensembles of images, formats, hardware and models, and that this "platform seeing" produces invisualities rather than views.
- How it works: Media-theoretical analysis of deep-learning datasets such as ImageNet and their hardware.
- Lens: Machine seeing
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1177/0263276419847508 (Theory, Culture & Society 36(5), 2019)

#### AI Aesthetics — Lev Manovich (2018)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Generative model & latent space, Platform & recommender algorithm
- Idea: AI's biggest aesthetic effect is not generating art but quietly sorting and predicting taste.
- What it is: A short book on how AI already shapes everyday aesthetic decisions, from photo filters and recommendations to design, and what it means for culture when machines learn and predict taste.
- How it works: Essay from the Strelka Press series, drawing on his cultural-analytics research.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Opacity & latent space
- Paper: http://manovich.net/index.php/projects/ai-aesthetics (Strelka Press, 2018)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oR1NyrAY_w4
- Images: https://manovich.net/content/04-projects/184-ai-aesthetics/ai_new.jpg
- Project page: http://manovich.net/index.php/projects/ai-aesthetics

#### The Robotic Imaginary: The Human and the Price of Dehumanized Labor — Jennifer Rhee (2018)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Humanoid & android, Autonomous vehicle & drone, Social & companion robot
- Idea: To ask what makes a robot humanlike is to ask whose labour counts as human.
- What it is: Rhee reads robots in AI research, film, literature and art, from ELIZA and Kismet to drone art such as #NotABugSplat, and shows that each definition of the humanlike robot rests on devalued human labour.
- How it works: Cultural analysis across chapters on care labour, emotional labour, drone warfare and the Turing test.
- Lens: Hidden labour & extraction, Intimacy, care & companionship, Alterity & the uncanny
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.5749/j.ctv62hh4x (University of Minnesota Press, 2018)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7APzxormknw
- Images: https://minnesota-us.imgix.net/covers/9781517902988.jpg?w=400

#### Art in the Age of Machine Intelligence — Blaise Agüera y Arcas (2017)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Generative model & latent space, Computer vision
- Idea: Like photography, machine intelligence will change what art is, and artists should shape it rather than just react.
- What it is: Agüera y Arcas compares machine learning to photography's arrival in the 19th century, uses DeepDream as an example, and argues that artists should work with neural networks as a new medium.
- How it works: Essay by the founder of Google's Artists + Machine Intelligence programme, open access.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.3390/arts6040018 (Arts 6(4), 2017)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uSUOdu_5MPc

#### Making Sense: Cognition, Computing, Art, and Embodiment — Simon Penny (2017)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Robot creature & mobile robot, Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Artists who build behaving machines have long practised a theory of embodied cognition that AI ignored.
- What it is: Penny critiques the computational theory of mind and draws on enactive and distributed cognition, cybernetics and his own robotic works such as Petit Mal to argue for a performative aesthetics of interactive art.
- How it works: Book-length theory from four decades of practice, published in the Leonardo series.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262036757/ (MIT Press / Leonardo, 2017)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PU_WDouhkw8

#### A Sea of Data: Apophenia and Pattern (Mis-)Recognition — Hito Steyerl (2016)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Surveillance & biometrics, Dataset & training data
- Idea: Pattern recognition is also pattern projection; machines hallucinate the order their owners want to see.
- What it is: Steyerl writes about intelligence agencies and neural networks drowning in data and finding patterns that are not there, using Google's DeepDream images as an example of apophenia.
- How it works: Essay combining media theory, surveillance history and image analysis.
- Lens: Opacity & latent space, Classification, bias & surveillance
- Paper: https://www.e-flux.com/journal/72/60480/a-sea-of-data-apophenia-and-pattern-mis-recognition/ (e-flux journal 72, 2016)
- Images: https://images.e-flux.com/test/cad7b8d2-d37e-4c14-825a-431c296346ff?width=1200&height=630

#### Invisible Images (Your Pictures Are Looking at You) — Trevor Paglen (2016)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Computer vision, Dataset & training data
- Idea: The most consequential images are ones no human looks at.
- What it is: Paglen argues that most images are now made by machines for other machines, such as licence-plate readers and face recognisers, and that this invisible visual culture escapes the tools of art history.
- How it works: Essay drawing on his research with computer-vision systems for the works It Began as a Military Experiment and Sight Machine.
- Lens: Machine seeing, Opacity & latent space
- Paper: https://thenewinquiry.com/invisible-images-your-pictures-are-looking-at-you/ (The New Inquiry, 8 December 2016)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JZjGsaJ1OcU
- Images: https://thenewinquiry.com/app/uploads/2016/12/57paglen01.jpg

#### The Multiple Bodies of a Machine Performer — Louis-Philippe Demers (2016)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Robot creature & mobile robot, Industrial robot arm
- Idea: A machine performer's presence comes from how its movement is read, not from how humanlike it looks.
- What it is: Demers analyses how audiences perceive agency in robots on stage, drawing on his own works such as The Tiller Girls, and separates a machine performer's physical, perceived and narrative bodies.
- How it works: Practice-based analysis in the volume Robots and Art: Exploring an Unlikely Symbiosis, edited by Herath, Kroos and Stelarc.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Alterity & the uncanny, Failure, glitch & error
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-981-10-0321-9_14 (Robots and Art, Springer, 2016)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bf-r34FzLhs

#### Phantom Images — Harun Farocki (2004)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Computer vision, Autonomous vehicle & drone
- Idea: When images become steps in a process, seeing turns into doing, and the human viewer drops out.
- What it is: Farocki's essay on "operational images", images from missile cameras and industrial vision systems that neither entertain nor inform but are part of an operation, written alongside his installation cycle Eye/Machine (2001–03).
- How it works: Essay based on archival footage of guided weapons and machine-vision systems gathered for Eye/Machine.
- Lens: Machine seeing
- Paper: https://www.harunfarocki.de/installations/2000s/2003/eye-machine-iii.html (Public 29, 2004)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tERIscWmpSo
- Project page: https://www.harunfarocki.de/installations/2000s/2003/eye-machine-iii.html

#### Foundation and Development of Robotic Art — Eduardo Kac (1997)
- Type: Paper · Machines: Robot creature & mobile robot, Humanoid & android, Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Robotic art split early into three lines: anthropomorphic, cybernetic-responsive and bio-hybrid.
- What it is: Kac traces robotic art from three 1960s works, Nam June Paik and Shuya Abe's Robot K-456, Tom Shannon's Squat and Edward Ihnatowicz's SAM and Senster, to telepresence and web-controlled robots of the 1990s.
- How it works: Art-historical survey in the Art Journal issue on art and technology.
- Lens: Embodiment & kinesthesia, Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://doi.org/10.1080/00043249.1997.10791834 (Art Journal 56(3), 1997)
- Project page: https://www.ekac.org

#### The Vision Machine — Paul Virilio (1988)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Computer vision, Autonomous vehicle & drone, Surveillance & biometrics
- Idea: When machines see for us, perception becomes logistics and the human eye is optional.
- What it is: Virilio describes the rise of automated perception, cameras and computers that see and interpret without a human viewer, as a "sightless vision" rooted in military logistics.
- How it works: Essay in media archaeology, from perspective painting to smart weapons; French original La Machine de vision (Galilée, 1988).
- Lens: Machine seeing
- Paper: https://iupress.org/9780253209016/the-vision-machine/ (Galilée, 1988; English: BFI / Indiana University Press, 1994)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/148033-L.jpg

#### Beyond Modern Sculpture: The Effects of Science and Technology on the Sculpture of This Century — Jack Burnham (1968)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system, Robot creature & mobile robot
- Idea: Sculpture's long wish to make the object alive ends in the machine that behaves.
- What it is: Burnham surveys twentieth-century sculpture from vitalism to kinetic, light and cybernetic art, and predicts a move from static objects to responsive systems and artificial life.
- How it works: Art-historical and systems-theoretical survey.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation, Embodiment & kinesthesia
- Paper: https://archive.org/details/beyondmodernscul0000burn (George Braziller, 1968)
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/14444956-L.jpg

#### Cybernetic Serendipity: The Computer and the Arts — Jasia Reichardt (1968)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system, Robot creature & mobile robot
- Idea: The first large art show of computers presented machines as collaborators and characters, not just tools.
- What it is: The catalogue of Reichardt's ICA exhibition, published as a special issue of Studio International, documenting computer graphics, music, poetry and cybernetic machines by Gordon Pask, Nam June Paik, Edward Ihnatowicz and many others.
- How it works: Exhibition catalogue with artists' statements, diagrams and essays by scientists and engineers.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://cyberneticserendipity.net (Studio International special issue, 1968)
- Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5mH9DysESqo
- Images: https://covers.openlibrary.org/b/id/8992379-L.jpg
- Project page: https://cyberneticserendipity.net

#### Systems Esthetics — Jack Burnham (1968)
- Type: Book & essay · Machines: Cybernetic & artificial-life system
- Idea: Once art is understood as a system rather than an object, a machine or program in the gallery is no longer a tool but the work itself.
- What it is: Burnham's essay argues that art is moving from finished objects towards 'unobjects' and systems: works that organise relations between people, materials, information and machines, in which invisible parts matter as much as visible ones. Two years later he tested the idea in the exhibition Software at the Jewish Museum in New York.
- How it works: Critical essay drawing on general systems theory and cybernetics, with examples including Hans Haacke's systems works; published in Artforum, September 1968.
- Lens: Agency, autonomy & co-creation
- Paper: https://www.artforum.com/features/systems-esthetics-201372/ (Artforum, September 1968)
- Images: https://www.artforum.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/featured00_large-24.jpg
- Project page: https://www.artforum.com/features/systems-esthetics-201372/

## Resources & links: people, institutions and websites

### Artists & designers

- **!Mediengruppe Bitnik** (Zurich, CH / London, UK) — Swiss artist duo (Carmen Weisskopf and Domagoj Smoljo) whose Random Darknet Shopper, a bot with a weekly bitcoin budget, bought goods on the darknet and was then 'arrested' by Swiss police. Known for: Delivery for Mr. Assange (2013); Random Darknet Shopper (2014); Alexiety (2019–). https://www.bitnik.org/
- **aaajiao (Xu Wenkai) / 徐文恺** (Berlin, DE / Shanghai, CN) — Chinese artist who works with the internet, bots and data as the material of everyday life under networked control; his avatar aaajiao reflects on identity inside platforms. Known for: GFWlist (2010); Remnants of an Electronic Past (2016); Deep Sleep (2020). http://www.aaajiao.com/
- **Adam Harvey** (Berlin, DE, 1981–) — American artist-researcher of counter-surveillance whose CV Dazzle makeup defeats face detection, and whose Exposing.ai traced millions of photos scraped into face-recognition datasets. Known for: CV Dazzle (2010); Stealth Wear (2013); HyperFace (2017); Exposing.ai / MegaPixels (2019–, with Jules LaPlace). https://ahprojects.com/
- **Addie Wagenknecht** (Austria / US, 1981–) — American artist whose Optimization of Parenthood uses a robot arm that rocks her baby's cradle when it cries, questioning what care becomes when it is automated. Known for: Optimization of Parenthood (2011–); Asymmetric Love (2013); Data and Dragons (2015). https://www.placesiveneverbeen.com/
- **Agnieszka Kurant** (New York, US, 1978–) — Polish artist of collective and non-human intelligence; A.A.I. consists of termite mounds built from coloured sand, 'artificial artificial intelligence' that echoes the crowdworkers behind AI. Known for: A.A.I. (2014); Crowd Crystal (2019). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnieszka_Kurant
- **Agnieszka Pilat** (San Francisco, US) — Polish-born painter who treats Boston Dynamics' Spot robots as studio companions and co-painters, staging machines as a new species learning to make marks. Known for: Heterobota (NGV Triennial, 2023); Paintings with Boston Dynamics' Spot (2021–). https://www.agnieszkapilat.com/
- **Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg** (London, UK, 1982–) — British artist whose The Substitute brings back the last male northern white rhino as an AI-driven digital animal, asking why we prefer artificial life to the life we let die. Known for: The Substitute (2019); Resurrecting the Sublime (2019); Pollinator Pathmaker (2021). https://www.daisyginsberg.com/
- **American Artist** (Los Angeles, US, 1989–) — American artist whose My Blue Window renders the city through a predictive-policing dashboard, confronting the racial logic of computational risk. Known for: Black Gooey Universe (2018); My Blue Window (2019); Shady Grove (2021). https://americanartist.us/
- **Andrew Norman Wilson** (Los Angeles, US, 1983–) — American artist who, while a contractor at Google, filmed the separately badged book-scanning workers, and then collected Google Books pages showing the scanners' fingers. Known for: Workers Leaving the Googleplex (2011); ScanOps (2012–). https://www.andrewnormanwilson.com/
- **Anicka Yi** (New York, US, 1971–) — Korean-American artist who 'biologises the machine': in In Love With the World, floating 'aerobes' drifted through Tate's Turbine Hall as a new machine species with their own sensing and behaviour. Known for: Biologizing the Machine (tentacular trouble) (2019); In Love With the World (Tate Turbine Hall, 2021). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anicka_Yi
- **Anna Ridler** (London, UK, 1985–) — British artist who hand-builds her own datasets; Myriad (Tulips) displays 10,000 tulip photos she took and labelled, making visible the human labour and choices inside a training set. Known for: Myriad (Tulips) (2018); Mosaic Virus (2018); Traces of Things (2021). https://annaridler.com/
- **Annie Dorsen** (New York, US, 1973–) — American theatre maker of 'algorithmic theatre'; in Hello Hi There two chatbots restage the Chomsky–Foucault debate on human nature, live and different each night. Known for: Hello Hi There (2010); A Piece of Work (2013); Prometheus Firebringer (2023). https://www.anniedorsen.com/
- **Arthur Ganson** (Cambridge, US, 1955–) — American kinetic sculptor of gentle, philosophical machines; in Machine with Concrete a motor drives a chain of gears whose last one is set in concrete and would turn once in two trillion years. Known for: Machine with Concrete (1992); Machine with Oil (1990); Cory's Yellow Chair (1995). https://www.arthurganson.com/
- **Auger & Loizeau (James Auger & Jimmy Loizeau)** (London, UK) — British speculative designers whose Carnivorous Domestic Entertainment Robots feed on flies and mice to power themselves, re-imagining domestic robots as living things. Known for: Audio Tooth Implant (2001); Carnivorous Domestic Entertainment Robots (2009); Afterlife (2001–09). https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q55217959
- **Automato.farm** (Shanghai, CN / London, UK) — Design studio of Simone Rebaudengo, Matteo Loglio and Saurabh Datta; in Ethical Things a fan asks online crowdworkers to resolve its moral dilemmas. Known for: Objects of Research (2016); Politics of Power (2016); Ethical Things (2015); BIY.world (2019). http://automato.farm/
- **Ayoung Kim / 金雅瑛** (Seoul, KR, 1979–) — South Korean artist whose Delivery Dancer's Sphere follows a female delivery rider in a Seoul run by an algorithmic platform that bends time and space. Known for: Delivery Dancer's Sphere (2022); Delivery Dancer's Arc: 0° Receiver (2024); PH Express (2018). https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayoung_Kim
- **Ben Grosser** (Urbana, US) — American artist of software culture; Computers Watching Movies shows what a computer vision system 'looks at' in famous films, as sketched traces of machine attention. Known for: Computers Watching Movies (2013); Facebook Demetricator (2012–); Go Rando (2017); Minus (2021). https://bengrosser.com/
- **Bill Vorn** (Montreal, CA, 1959–) — Canadian robotic artist whose machines act out misery and hysteria: the octopus-like Hysterical Machines flail when visitors approach, provoking empathy for crude mechanisms. Known for: La Cour des Miracles (1997, with Louis-Philippe Demers); Hysterical Machines (2006); Inferno (2015). https://billvorn.concordia.ca/
