- **Bjørn Karmann** (Copenhagen, DK) — Danish designer whose Project Alias is a fungus-like parasite that whispers noise into smart speakers until you wake it, and whose Paragraphica is a lensless camera that writes a photo from data. Known for: Objectifier (2016); Project Alias (2019, with Tore Knudsen); Paragraphica (2023). https://bjoernkarmann.dk/
- **Blanca Li** (Paris, FR, 1964–) — Spanish choreographer whose Robot sets dancers alongside NAO humanoid robots and Maywa Denki's instruments, exploring how people and machines learn each other's movement. Known for: Robot (2013); Le Bal de Paris (2021). https://www.blancali.com/
- **Blast Theory** (Brighton, UK) — British artist group of interactive performance; Cat Royale (2023) watched a robot arm try to entertain three cats for twelve days, asking whether machines can care for other species. Known for: Can You See Me Now? (2001); Cat Royale (2023). https://www.blasttheory.co.uk/
- **Bruce Lacey** (London, UK, 1927–2016) — British artist of anarchic, junk-built robots and performing automata, several shown at Cybernetic Serendipity (1968); his humanoid machines were deliberately comic, clumsy and vulnerable. Known for: ROSA BOSOM (1965); Old Money Bags (1965); Cybernetic Serendipity robots (1968). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Lacey
- **Cao Fei / 曹斐** (Beijing, CN, 1978–) — Chinese artist of labour, virtual worlds and automation; Asia One follows the only two workers in a fully automated logistics warehouse, falling in love among sorting robots. Known for: Whose Utopia (2006); RMB City (2007–11); Asia One (2018); Staging the Era (2023). http://www.caofei.com/
- **Caroline Sinders** (London, UK / New York, US) — American designer-researcher whose Feminist Data Set interrogates every step of making AI, from collecting data to paying the labellers, as a feminist practice. Known for: Feminist Data Set (2017–); Technically Responsible Knowledge (2020). https://carolinesinders.com/
- **Catie Cuan** (Stanford, US) — American dancer-roboticist who choreographs with industrial and mobile robots; in Output she and an ABB arm trade movement captured from each other. Known for: Output (2019); Time to Compile (2019); Engine of Wonder (2023, TED). https://www.catiecuan.com/
- **Chico MacMurtrie** (New York, US, 1961–) — American artist whose Amorphic Robot Works builds pneumatic and inflatable robotic bodies that breathe, drum and climb, machines that behave like primal organisms. Known for: Amorphic Robot Works (founded 1991); The Robotic Church (2006); Inflatable Architectural Bodies (2000s–). https://amorphicrobotworks.org/
- **Choe U-Ram** (Seoul, KR, 1970–) — South Korean sculptor of 'anima-machines', delicate mechanical creatures with invented scientific names and life cycles; Little Ark is a ship of oars that rise and fall like breathing. Known for: Opertus Lunula Umbra (2008); Little Ark (MMCA, 2022); Una Lumino (2008). https://www.uram.net/
- **Choy Ka Fai / 徐家辉** (Berlin, DE / Singapore) — Singaporean artist whose Prospectus for a Future Body stimulates dancers' muscles with electrical signals recorded from other dancers, asking whether movement memory can be transferred by machine. Known for: Prospectus for a Future Body (2011); UnBearable Darkness (2018). https://www.ka5.info/
- **Christa Sommerer & Laurent Mignonneau** (Linz, AT) — Austrian-French duo, pioneers of artificial-life art: in A-Volve visitors draw creatures that then evolve, hunt and mate in a pool of water, living by their own rules. Known for: Interactive Plant Growing (1992); A-Volve (1994); Life Writer (2006). https://www.interface.ufg.ac.at/christa-laurent/
- **Clement Valla** (New York, US) — French-American artist whose Postcards from Google Earth collects melted bridges and warped roads, not errors but the logic of a machine-made 3D world. Known for: Postcards from Google Earth (2010–); Surface Survey (2014). https://clementvalla.com/
- **Cod.Act (André & Michel Décosterd)** (La Chaux-de-Fonds, CH) — Swiss brothers whose sound-machine performances fuse bodies and mechanics: in Pendulum Choir nine singers tilt on hydraulic jacks, their voices shaped by the machine's movement. Known for: Pendulum Choir (2011); πTon (2017); Nyloïd (2013). https://www.codact.ch/
- **Daito Manabe / 真锅大度** (Tokyo, JP, 1976–) — Japanese artist and Rhizomatiks co-founder whose Electric Stimulus to Face let a computer drive his facial muscles, later extending to drones, dancers and brain-decoding works. Known for: Electric Stimulus to Face (2008); Rhizomatiks × ELEVENPLAY (2010s); dissonant imaginary (2023). https://www.daito.ws/
- **Dan Chen** — Designer whose RISD-era robotic intimacy series built machines that caress and comfort people; his Last Moment Robot strokes a dying patient's arm and speaks words of comfort, questioning machine care at the end of life. Known for: End of Life Care Machine (2012); Last Moment Robot (2012); Intimacy series (2011–12). https://dankc.com/
- **David Bowen** (Minneapolis, US) — American artist whose machines let non-humans and data drive them: a houseplant wields a machete, and houseflies control a revolver, making other perceptual worlds act through robots. Known for: fly revolver (2013); tele-present wind (2018); plant machete (2014). https://www.dwbowen.com/
- **David Harris Smith & Frauke Zeller** (Hamilton / Toronto, CA) — Canadian researchers who made hitchBOT, a hitchhiking robot that crossed Canada and parts of Europe on strangers' goodwill before being destroyed in Philadelphia in 2015. Known for: hitchBOT (2014–15). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HitchBOT
- **David Rokeby** (Toronto, CA, 1960–) — Canadian pioneer of interactive installation; The Giver of Names looks at objects visitors place before it and generates associative sentences about them, an early portrait of machine interpretation. Known for: Very Nervous System (1986–90); The Giver of Names (1990–); Sorting Daemon (2003). http://www.davidrokeby.com/
- **Desmond Paul Henry** (Manchester, UK, 1921–2004) — British artist who built drawing machines from bombsight analogue computers in the early 1960s, among the first machine-made artworks exhibited in the UK. Known for: Henry Drawing Machine (1961); Ideographs exhibition (Reid Gallery, London, 1962). http://www.desmondhenry.com/
- **Diemut Strebe** (Boston, US) — German artist working with MIT scientists; The Prayer is a robotic mouth that composes and speaks its own prayers from a language model, asking whether a machine can pray. Known for: The Prayer (2020); Redemption of Vanity (2019). https://www.diemutstrebe.com/
- **Dries Depoorter** (Ghent, BE) — Belgian artist whose The Follower matched Instagram photos with open webcam footage of the moment they were taken, revealing how easily AI links public cameras to private images. Known for: Jaywalking (2015); Surveillance Speaker (2020); The Follower (2022). https://driesdepoorter.be/
- **Dunne & Raby (Anthony Dunne & Fiona Raby)** (New York, US) — British designers who defined critical and speculative design; Technological Dreams: Robots imagines domestic robots that are needy, neurotic or dependent rather than servile. Known for: Technological Dreams Series: No. 1, Robots (2007); Speculative Everything (2013); Hertzian Tales (1999). https://dunneandraby.co.uk/
- **Eduardo Kac** (Chicago, US, 1962–) — Brazilian-American artist of telepresence robotics and bio art; in Rara Avis visitors saw an aviary through the eyes of a robotic macaw, inhabiting a machine body. Known for: Ornitorrinco (1989–96, with Ed Bennett); Rara Avis (1996); Teleporting an Unknown State (1996); GFP Bunny (2000). https://www.ekac.org/
- **Edward Ihnatowicz** (London, UK, 1926–1988) — Polish-born British sculptor who made the first computer-controlled robotic sculptures: The Senster, a 4.5-metre hydraulic creature at Philips' Evoluon, turned towards quiet voices and shied away from loud ones. Known for: SAM (1968); The Senster (1970). http://www.senster.com/
- **Ei Wada / 和田永** (Tokyo, JP, 1987–) — Japanese artist who turns obsolete appliances, such as CRT televisions and electric fans, into musical instruments, giving discarded machines a second life as a community orchestra. Known for: Braun Tube Jazz Band (2009); Electronicos Fantasticos! (2015–). https://eiwada.com/
- **Elisa Giardina Papa** (New York, US / Sicily, IT) — Italian artist whose Cleaning Emotional Data documents her own gig work labelling facial expressions for emotion-recognition AI, and whose Technologies of Care portrays online care workers. Known for: Technologies of Care (2016); Cleaning Emotional Data (2020). https://www.elisagiardinapapa.org/
- **Esther Hovers** (Netherlands) — Dutch artist whose False Positives stages the eight 'anomalous behaviours' that intelligent surveillance systems are trained to flag, from standing still to walking against the flow. Known for: False Positives (2015). https://www.estherhovers.com/
- **Eva & Franco Mattes** (New York, US) — Italian artist duo whose Dark Content gives anonymised voices to the content moderators who filter violent and obscene images for platforms, the human layer behind 'automatic' moderation. Known for: Dark Content (2015); BEFNOED (2014); Personal Photographs (2018). https://0100101110101101.org/
- **Everest Pipkin** (Pittsburgh, US, 1990–) — American artist and game developer whose Lacework slowly reanimates every video in the MIT Moments in Time dataset, and whose essay on it documents the violence hidden in training data. Known for: Lacework (2020); Shell Song (2020). https://everest-pipkin.com/
- **Garnet Hertz** (Vancouver, CA, 1973–) — Canadian artist and scholar of critical making whose robot is steered by a live Madagascar hissing cockroach riding on a trackball. Known for: Cockroach Controlled Mobile Robot (2004); Critical Making (2012); Disobedient Electronics (2016–). http://www.conceptlab.com/
- **George E. Lewis** (New York, US, 1952–) — American composer, trombonist and AACM member whose Voyager is an improvising computer 'orchestra' that listens and answers, framed as a partner shaped by African American musical culture. Known for: Voyager (1987); Why Do We Want Our Computers to Improvise? (2018). https://music.columbia.edu/bios/george-e-lewis
- **Gilberto Esparza** (Mexico City, MX) — Mexican artist whose Plantas Nómadas is a robot that feeds its plants from polluted rivers using microbial fuel cells, a machine-organism for damaged ecologies (Golden Nica 2015). Known for: Parásitos Urbanos (2007); Plantas Nómadas (2008–13); Biocenosis (2021). https://gilbertoesparza.net/
- **Gordon Pask** (London, UK, 1928–1996) — British cybernetician who built responsive, learning machines as art: Musicolour grew bored of a musician who repeated himself, and Colloquy of Mobiles let hanging machines court each other and visitors at Cybernetic Serendipity. Known for: Musicolour (1953); Colloquy of Mobiles (1968); Conversation Theory (1975). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Pask
- **Guo Cheng / 郭城** (Shanghai, CN) — Chinese artist of science-fictional machines; his gif tutorial shows how to twist your face to escape detection, and The Net Wanderer tours the physical handshakes of the Chinese internet. Known for: A Technique of Evading Face Detection (2020); The Net Wanderer – A Tour of Suspended Handshakes (2020). https://www.guo-cheng.net/
- **Guy Ben-Ary** (Perth, AU, 1967–) — Argentine-born Australian bio-artist whose works wire living neurons to machines: MEART drew with a robot arm, and cellF is a synthesizer played by neurons grown from his own cells. Known for: MEART – The Semi-Living Artist (2003); cellF (2015); Revivification (2021). https://guybenary.com/
- **Harold Cohen** (San Diego, US, 1928–2016) — British painter who spent four decades developing AARON, a drawing program and robot that raised the question of whether a machine can make art, and of what the artist's role becomes. Known for: AARON (1973–2016); What is an Image? (1979). https://www.aaronshome.com/
- **Harpreet Sareen** (New York, US) — Indian-born designer-researcher of 'cyborg botany' whose Elowan is a plant that drives its robotic base towards light using its own electrical signals. Known for: Elowan (2018, MIT Media Lab); Cyborg Botany (2019). https://www.harpreetsareen.com/
- **Harun Farocki** (Berlin, DE, 1944–2014) — German filmmaker who coined 'operative images', pictures made by machines for machines; the Eye/Machine trilogy examines smart-bomb cameras and industrial vision, founding the art of machine seeing. Known for: Images of the World and the Inscription of War (1988); Eye/Machine I–III (2001–03); Serious Games I–IV (2009–10); Parallel I–IV (2012–14). https://www.harunfarocki.de/
- **Hasan Elahi** (Washington, D.C., US, 1972–) — Bangladeshi-American artist who, after being wrongly placed on a US terrorist watch list, began publishing tens of thousands of images of his whereabouts, over-feeding the surveillance machine. Known for: Tracking Transience (2002–). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasan_M._Elahi
- **Heather Dewey-Hagborg** (New York, US, 1982–) — American artist who 3D-prints portraits of strangers from DNA found in the street, exposing the fictions and biases of forensic phenotyping algorithms. Known for: Stranger Visions (2012–13); Probably Chelsea (2017); Hybrid: an Interspecies Portrait (2023). https://deweyhagborg.com/
- **Hito Steyerl** (Berlin, DE, 1966–) — German artist and writer whose essay films and texts on poor images, robots and 'artificial stupidity' shaped how art thinks about computation, visibility and power. Known for: How Not to Be Seen (2013); HellYeahWeFuckDie (2016); This is the Future (2019); Medium Hot: Images in the Age of Heat (2025). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hito_Steyerl
- **Ho Tzu Nyen / 何子彦** (Singapore, 1976–) — Singaporean artist whose CDOSEA is an algorithmically edited, infinitely recombining 'dictionary' of Southeast Asia, handing the ordering of history to a machine. Known for: The Critical Dictionary of Southeast Asia (CDOSEA) (2017–); The Name (2015); T for Time (2023). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho_Tzu_Nyen
- **Holly Herndon & Mat Dryhurst** (Berlin, DE) — American artist-musicians who raised the AI 'baby' Spawn with a vocal ensemble and released Holly+, a voice model anyone can sing through, raising questions of voice ownership and consent. Known for: PROTO (2019, with AI 'baby' Spawn); Holly+ (2021); xhairymutantx (Whitney Biennial, 2024); The Call (Serpentine, 2024). https://herndondryhurst.studio/
- **Hsin-Chien Huang / 黄心健** (Taipei, TW, 1966–) — Taiwanese new-media artist whose VR work The Eye and I, made with Jean-Michel Jarre, immerses viewers in a world of surveillance and watching machines. Known for: The Eye and I (2019, with Jean-Michel Jarre); To the Moon (2018, with Laurie Anderson); Bodyless (2019). https://www.storynest.com/
- **Hu Jieming / 胡介鸣** (Shanghai, CN) — Shanghai pioneer of Chinese media art whose installations such as 100 Years in 1 Minute, a matrix of 1,440 boxes, compress history into machine-scaled time. Known for: 100 Years in 1 Minute (2010); The Raft of the Medusa (2002). https://www.shanghartgallery.com/galleryarchive/artists/name/hujieming
- **Huang Yi / 黄翊** (Taipei, TW) — Taiwanese choreographer who programs an industrial KUKA arm as his duet partner; Huang Yi & KUKA opened Ars Electronica 2013, toured widely and made a factory robot move with tenderness. Known for: Huang Yi & KUKA (2012); A Million Miles Away (2019). https://huangyistudio.com/
- **Ian Cheng** (New York, US, 1984–) — American artist of 'live simulations', AI-driven worlds that play themselves without end; BOB is an artificial lifeform with a personality that changes through its encounters. Known for: Emissaries trilogy (2015–17); BOB (Bag of Beliefs) (2018–19); Life After BOB (2021). https://iancheng.com/
- **Jaha Koo** (Ghent, BE, 1984–) — South Korean theatre-maker whose Cuckoo shares the stage with three talking rice cookers, telling a story of loneliness and economic crisis in South Korea through household machines. Known for: Cuckoo (2017); Hamartia trilogy (2015–2019). https://gujaha.com
- **Jake Elwes** (London, UK, 1993–) — British artist who queers AI by retraining face models on drag performers; The Zizi Show is a deepfake cabaret where bodies break down at the edge of the dataset. Known for: Zizi – Queering the Dataset (2019); The Zizi Show (2020); CUSP (2019); Machine Learning Porn (2016). https://www.jakeelwes.com/
- **James Bridle** (Greece / UK, 1980–) — British artist and writer whose Autonomous Trap 001 caught a self-driving car inside a circle of road markings, and whose books New Dark Age and Ways of Being rethink computation and non-human intelligence. Known for: The New Aesthetic (2011–); Autonomous Trap 001 (2017); New Dark Age (2018); Ways of Being (2022). https://jamesbridle.com/
- **James Seawright** (New York, US, 1936–2022) — American sculptor who built early responsive electronic sculptures in the 1960s, machines that scanned the room, sensed visitors and answered with light and movement. Known for: Watcher (1965–66); Searcher (1966); Electronic Peristyle (1968). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Seawright
- **Jean Tinguely** (Basel, CH, 1924–1991) — Swiss kinetic sculptor of absurd, self-destroying machines: Métamatics produced drawings on demand, and Homage to New York shook itself to pieces in the MoMA garden, making breakdown the work. Known for: Métamatics (1959); Homage to New York (1960); Study for an End of the World No. 2 (1962). https://www.tinguely.ch/
- **Jenna Sutela** (Berlin, DE, 1983–) — Finnish artist of more-than-human intelligence; in nimiia cétiï a neural network learns a 'Martian' language from recordings of a medium and the movements of bacteria. Known for: nimiia cétiï (2018); I Magma (2019); Holobiont Society (2018); Pond Brain (2024). https://jennasutela.com/
- **Jennifer Walshe** (Dublin, IE, 1974–) — Irish composer and vocalist who improvises with an AI trained on her own face and voice (ULTRACHUNK) and rewrites music history through machine-generated singing. Known for: ULTRACHUNK (2018, with Memo Akten); A Late Anthology of Early Music Vol. 1 (2020). http://milker.org/
- **Jiabao Li / 李佳宝** (Austin, US) — Chinese artist-designer and founder of Reality Design Lab (UT Austin) whose works on AI, care and more-than-human perception include AI Mom, a machine that performs motherhood. Known for: AI Mom (2024); Womb Wetware (2025); Once Upon a Garden (2023). https://www.jiabaoli.org/
- **Jill Magid** (New York, US, 1973–) — American artist who in Evidence Locker asked Liverpool's CCTV operators to film her and wrote them love letters to retrieve the footage, making intimacy with the surveillance system. Known for: Evidence Locker (2004); Trust (2004). https://www.jillmagid.com/
- **Joana Moll** (Barcelona, ES) — Spanish artist-researcher who measures the material cost of the internet; CO2GLE shows the CO2 emitted every second by visits to google.com. Known for: CO2GLE (2014); The Hidden Life of an Amazon User (2019); The Dating Brokers (2018, with Tactical Tech). https://www.janavirgin.com/
- **Jon Rafman** (Montreal, CA, 1981–) — Canadian artist whose The Nine Eyes of Google Street View collects scenes captured by Street View's indifferent cameras, a portrait of the world seen by a machine that does not care. Known for: The Nine Eyes of Google Street View (2009–). https://jonrafman.com/
- **Jordan Wolfson** (New York / Los Angeles, US, 1980–) — American artist whose animatronic (Female figure) dances before a mirror while tracking viewers' faces, a disturbing study of the gaze and the sexualised robot body. Known for: (Female figure) (2014); Colored sculpture (2016); Body Sculpture (2023). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Wolfson
- **Joy Buolamwini** (Cambridge, US, 1989–) — Ghanaian-American-Canadian 'poet of code' whose white-mask experiment and Gender Shades study exposed face-analysis systems failing on dark-skinned women; founder of the Algorithmic Justice League. Known for: Gender Shades (2018, with Timnit Gebru); AI, Ain't I a Woman? (2018); Unmasking AI (2023); Algorithmic Justice League (founded 2016). https://www.poetofcode.com/
- **Julian Oliver** (Berlin, DE) — New Zealand 'critical engineer' who co-wrote the Critical Engineering Manifesto; his works open up networks and infrastructures, such as a cell tower disguised as an office printer. Known for: The Critical Engineering Manifesto (2011); Stealth Cell Tower (2015); Harvest (2016). https://julianoliver.com/
- **Julien Prévieux / 朱利安·普雷维厄** (Paris, FR) — French artist whose What Shall We Do Next? has dancers perform gestures patented by tech companies, showing how bodies are measured and scripted by devices; Prix Marcel Duchamp 2014. Known for: What Shall We Do Next? (2006–); Patterns of Life (2015). https://www.previeux.net/
- **Julius Popp** (Leipzig, DE, 1973–) — German artist whose bit.fall writes words scraped from news sites in falling water drops, and whose small self-learning robots explore their own bodies. Known for: bit.fall (2001–); micro.adam and micro.eva (2002). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Popp
- **Justine Emard** (Paris, FR) — French artist whose Co(AI)xistence films dancer Mirai Moriyama learning to communicate with Alter, the learning android by Ikegami and Ishiguro, through gesture and voice. Known for: Co(AI)xistence (2017); Soul Shift (2018); Supraorganism (2020). https://www.justineemard.com/
- **Kacie Kinzer** (New York, US, 1983–) — American designer whose Tweenbots, smiling cardboard robots that could only roll straight ahead, crossed Manhattan parks by relying on strangers' kindness to redirect them. Known for: Tweenbots (2009). http://www.tweenbots.com/
- **Karen Palmer** (London, UK) — British 'storyteller from the future' whose interactive films read the viewer's facial emotions to steer the plot, so a police encounter plays out differently depending on how calm you look. Known for: RIOT (2017); Perception iO (2021). http://karenpalmer.uk/
- **Karl Sims** (Cambridge, US, 1962–) — American computer graphics artist whose Evolved Virtual Creatures evolved their own bodies and gaits in simulation, and whose Galápagos let visitors act as the selection pressure for artificial organisms. Known for: Evolved Virtual Creatures (1994); Galápagos (1997). https://www.karlsims.com/
- **Kazuhiko Hachiya / 八谷和彦** (Tokyo, JP) — Japanese media artist whose Inter Dis-Communication Machine swaps the sight and sound of two people through head-mounted displays, so each lives inside the other's perception. Known for: Inter Dis-Communication Machine (1993); PostPet (1997); OpenSky (2003–). https://www.ntticc.or.jp/en/archive/works/inter-dis-communication-machine/
- **Keiichi Matsuda** (London, UK) — British-Japanese designer whose film Hyper-Reality shows a Medellín bus ride in a city saturated by augmented-reality ads, gamification and assistant agents. Known for: Hyper-Reality (2016); Merger (2018); Agents (Wanderer, 2020s). http://km.cx/
- **Keiichiro Shibuya / 涩谷庆一郎** (Tokyo, JP, 1973–) — Japanese composer whose android opera Scary Beauty has the android Alter 3 conduct an orchestra and sing, with tempo it decides itself. Known for: The End (2012); Scary Beauty (2018); MIRROR (2022). https://atak.jp/
- **Kelly Dobson** (Providence, US) — American artist of 'machine therapy': to make Blendie spin, you must growl at a blender in its own pitch, an exercise in empathy with household machines. Known for: Blendie (2003–04); ScreamBody (1998–2004); Omo (2007). http://www.kellydobson.com/
- **Ken Feingold** (New York, US, 1952–) — American artist whose talking animatronic heads converse with each other in synthetic speech; in If/Then two identical heads debate whether they exist. Known for: If/Then (2001); Sinking Feeling (2001); Head (1999–2000). http://www.kenfeingold.com/
- **Ken Goldberg** (Berkeley, US, 1961–) — American roboticist and artist whose Telegarden let thousands of internet users tend a real garden through an industrial robot arm, testing trust and presence at a distance. Known for: The Telegarden (1995); Dislocation of Intimacy (1998); The Robot and the Garden (2000, ed.). https://goldberg.berkeley.edu/
- **Kenji Yanobe / 矢延宪司** (Osaka, JP, 1965–) — Japanese artist of survival machines and giant robots, from radiation suits after Chernobyl to post-Fukushima figures of hope. Known for: Yellow Suit (1991); Giant Torayan (2005); Sun Child (2011); Ship's Cat (2017–). https://www.yanobe.com/
- **Kenneth Rinaldo** (Columbus, US, 1958–) — American artist of artificial life and interspecies robotics: in Autopoiesis, grapevine-armed robots sense visitors and each other, and in Augmented Fish Reality fish steer their own robotic bowls. Known for: Autopoiesis (2000); The Farm (2000s); Augmented Fish Reality (2004). https://www.kenrinaldo.com/
- **Kraftwerk** (Düsseldorf, DE) — German electronic band founded in 1970 whose robot doubles and 'man-machine' aesthetic made the fusion of musician and machine a pop image. Known for: Die Mensch-Maschine (The Man-Machine) (1978); The Robots (1978); Computer World (1981). https://kraftwerk.com/
- **Kris Verdonck** (Brussels, BE) — Belgian director whose machine-theatre works blur actor and object, like the flailing industrial machine of Dancer #1 and the dying performers of END. Known for: END (2008); ACTOR #1 (2010); Dancer #1 (2003). https://www.atwodogscompany.org/
- **Kyle McDonald** (Los Angeles, US) — American artist of computer vision and code who turns the camera back on its users; Facework is a game where you apply for gig jobs by performing the face a classifier wants to see. Known for: People Staring at Computers (2011); Exhausting a Crowd (2015); us+ (2013, with Lauren McCarthy); Facework (2020). https://kylemcdonald.net/
- **Kyriaki Goni** (Athens, GR) — Greek artist whose Data Garden imagines data stored in plant DNA, and whose Not Allowed For Algorithmic Audiences explores the smart speakers listening in on our homes. Known for: Data Garden (2019); Not Allowed For Algorithmic Audiences (2021); Counting Craters on the Moon (2023). https://kyriakigoni.com/
- **Laetitia Sonami** (San Francisco, US, 1957–) — French-born composer who performed with the Lady's Glove, a sensor glove, and later Spring Spyre, an instrument trained with machine learning (Wekinator) to respond to her gestures. Known for: Lady's Glove (1991); Spring Spyre (2012). https://sonami.net/
- **Lauren Lee McCarthy** (Los Angeles, US) — American artist who performs the smart-home assistant herself: in LAUREN she watched over and served people's homes remotely 24/7, exposing the intimacy, labour and control inside 'AI'. Known for: LAUREN (2017); SOMEONE (2019); Surrogate (2021–); p5.js (2013). https://lauren-mccarthy.com/
- **Lawrence Abu Hamdan** (Beirut, LB, 1985–) — Jordanian-British 'private ear' whose works examine accent analysis in asylum cases and the forensics of listening, showing how voices become evidence for machines and states. Known for: Conflicted Phonemes (2012); The Freedom of Speech Itself (2012); Walled Unwalled (2018); Earwitness Theatre (2018). http://lawrenceabuhamdan.com/
- **Lawrence Lek / 陆明龙** (London, UK, 1982–) — Malaysian-Chinese British artist of 'Sinofuturism' whose films and games follow AI characters: a satellite that wants to be an artist, a self-driving car in therapy, a retired care robot. Known for: Geomancer (2017); AIDOL (2019); NOX (2023); Guanyin: Confessions of a Former Care Robot (2024). https://lawrencelek.com/
- **Lee Bul / 李昢** (Seoul, KR, 1964–) — South Korean artist whose headless, limbless Cyborg sculptures fuse the idealised female body with machine armour, questioning technology's fantasies of perfection. Known for: Cyborg series (1997–2011); Anagram (1998); Willing To Be Vulnerable (2015–16). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Bul
- **Leonel Moura** (Lisbon, PT, 1948–) — Portuguese artist whose swarms of small robots paint by reacting to each other's marks, a test of emergent, machine-made art without a human composer. Known for: ArtSBot swarm painting robots (2003–); RAP, Robotic Action Painter (2006). https://www.leonelmoura.com/
- **Li Liao / 李燎** (Shenzhen, CN) — Chinese performance artist who worked 45 days on a Foxconn assembly line to earn the iPad Mini he then exhibited, embodying the human labour inside consumer machines. Known for: Consumption (2012); Unemployed (2012). https://www.artsy.net/artwork/li-liao-consumption
- **Liam Young** (Los Angeles, US, 1979–) — Australian speculative architect and filmmaker whose Where the City Can't See is shot entirely through laser scanners, showing a city as a self-driving car perceives it. Known for: Where the City Can't See (2016); In the Robot Skies (2016); Planet City (2020). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liam_Young
- **Liu Chuang / 刘窗** (Beijing, CN, 1979–) — Chinese artist whose films trace the material and human underside of digital economies, from bitcoin mines in Inner Mongolia to lithium lakes and the linguistic data of minority voices. Known for: Bitcoin Mining and Field Recordings of Ethnic Minorities (2018); Lithium Lake and Proto-Language (2019). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liu_Chuang_(artist)
- **Louis-Philippe Demers** (Quebec, CA / Singapore) — Canadian maker of machine performers whose The Blind Robot gently touches a visitor's face to 'see' them, and whose Inferno straps audiences into exoskeletons that move them. Known for: La Cour des Miracles (1997, with Bill Vorn); The Blind Robot (2012); Inferno (2015, with Bill Vorn); The Multiple Bodies of the Machine (book). https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q125746113
- **Lu Yang / 陆扬** (Shanghai, CN, 1984–) — Chinese artist whose genderless digital avatar DOKU, motion-captured from the artist, is reincarnated across six realms, blending neuroscience, Buddhism and game engines. Known for: Uterus Man (2013); Electromagnetic Brainology (2017); DOKU (2020–); DOKU the Self (2022). http://www.luyang.asia/
- **Lynn Hershman Leeson** (San Francisco, US, 1941–) — American artist who, after inventing the fictional persona Roberta Breitmore, built Agent Ruby, a web chatbot that learned from visitors, anticipating today's conversational AI and its identities. Known for: Roberta Breitmore (1974–78); Agent Ruby (1998–2002); DiNA (2004); Twisted (New Museum, 2021). https://www.lynnhershman.com/
- **Madeline Gannon** (Pittsburgh, US) — American 'robot tamer' whose studio ATONATON turns industrial robots into curious creatures: Mimus, a 1,200 kg ABB arm at the London Design Museum, tracked and approached visitors like an animal. Known for: Mimus (2016); Manus (2018); Quipt (2015). https://atonaton.com/
- **Mahwish Chishty** (Kent, US) — Pakistani-American artist who paints US military drones in the ornate style of Pakistani truck art, confronting the machine gaze over the Afghanistan–Pakistan border. Known for: Drone Art (2013–); War Machines (2015–16). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahwish_Chishty
- **Manu Luksch** (London, UK, 1970–) — Austrian-born artist whose film Faceless is made entirely of her own CCTV footage obtained under data-protection law, in which the faces of others are erased. Known for: Faceless (2007); Dreams Rewired (2015). https://manuluksch.com/
- **Marc Böhlen** (Buffalo, US) — German-American artist-engineer whose machines test the limits of machine perception, such as Amy and Klara, two robotic boxes that read magazines and argue with each other in synthetic speech. Known for: Universal Whistling Machine (2004); Amy and Klara (2006); Keeping Track (2000s). https://www.realtechsupport.org/
- **Marcel·lí Antúnez Roca** (Barcelona, ES, 1959–) — Catalan performer who in Epizoo let audiences move his nose, mouth and buttocks via a pneumatic exoskeleton controlled by a mouse, an early work on the body under machine control. Known for: JoAn, l'home de carn (1992); Epizoo (1994); Afasia (1998). http://www.marceliantunez.com/
- **Marco Donnarumma** (Berlin, DE, 1984–) — Italian performer and researcher who fuses bodies with AI-driven prosthetics; his robot Amygdala learns to move by 'feeling' human skin and ritually cuts its own membrane. Known for: Corpus Nil (2016); Amygdala (2017–18); Eingeweide (2018). https://marcodonnarumma.com/
- **Mari Velonaki** (Sydney, AU, 1968–) — Greek-Australian artist and founder of UNSW's Creative Robotics Lab; in Fish-Bird two wheelchairs 'in love' write handwritten notes to visitors, building intimacy through printed letters and movement. Known for: Fish-Bird (2004); Diamandini (2013). https://www.marivelonaki.com/
- **Mariela Yeregui** (Buenos Aires, AR) — Argentine artist whose small robots in Proxemia approach and retreat from each other and from visitors, making distance and touch the subject of machine behaviour. Known for: Proxemia (2005); Epithelia (2004). https://marielayeregui.com/
- **Mark Pauline** (San Francisco, US) — Founder of Survival Research Laboratories, whose spectacles set salvaged, remote-controlled war machines and robots against each other, staging machine violence as industrial culture. Known for: Survival Research Laboratories (founded 1978); A Calculated Forecast of Ultimate Doom (1988). https://www.srl.org/
- **Martine Syms** (Los Angeles, US, 1988–) — American artist whose Mythiccbeing is a chatbot avatar of a self-absorbed Black woman, 'Teeny', turning AI personas into a critique of how Black women are scripted. Known for: Mythiccbeing (2018); Neural Swamp (Philadelphia Museum of Art, 2021); Shame Space (2021). https://martinesyms.com/
- **Max Dean** (Toronto, CA, 1949–) — Canadian artist whose robot arm in As Yet Untitled offers family photographs for rescue, shredding them unless a visitor intervenes, putting responsibility for loss on the viewer. Known for: As Yet Untitled (1992–95); The Table: Childhood (2001, with Raffaello D'Andrea). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Dean_(artist)
- **Maywa Denki / 明和电机** (Tokyo, JP) — Japanese art unit led by Nobumichi Tosa that presents absurd 'nonsense machines' and instruments as company products, performed by staff in blue work uniforms. Known for: Tsukuba series (1993–); Otamatone (2009); Edelweiss series (2004–). https://www.maywadenki.com/
- **Memo Akten** (Los Angeles, US, 1975–) — Turkish artist and researcher whose Learning to See shows a neural network interpreting live camera images of cables and cloth as waves, fire or flowers, a metaphor for how any mind sees what it already knows. Known for: Learning to See (2017); Deep Meditations (2018); Superradiance (2023, with Katie Peyton Hofstadter). https://www.memo.tv/
- **Merritt Moore** (London, UK, 1988–) — American ballet dancer and quantum physicist (DPhil, Oxford) who programs and dances duets with an industrial robot arm. Known for: Merritt + Robot (2020). https://www.merrittmoore.com/
- **Miao Ying / 苗颖** (Shanghai, CN / New York, US, 1985–) — Chinese artist of the 'Chinternet' whose works on censorship, filtered search results and platform culture show how machines shape what can be seen online in China. Known for: Blind Spot (2007); Chinternet Plus (2016); Hardcore Digital Detox (2018). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ying_Miao
- **Mimi Onuoha** (New York, US) — Nigerian-American artist whose Library of Missing Datasets is a filing cabinet of empty folders for data that is never collected, showing that what machines cannot see is a choice. Known for: The Library of Missing Datasets (2016); Classification.01 (2017); These Networks in Our Skin (2021). https://mimionuoha.com/
- **Minne Atairu** (New York, US) — Nigerian-American artist who uses generative models to imagine the Benin bronzes that were never made after the 1897 British raid, confronting the gaps in the data of looted histories. Known for: To the Hand (The Shed, 2023); Igùn (2020–). https://www.minneatairu.com/
- **Myron Krueger** (Vernon, US, 1942–) — American computer artist who coined 'artificial reality'; in Videoplace a camera turned visitors' silhouettes into live partners for graphic creatures, an early case of a body read by a machine. Known for: Videoplace (1974–); Artificial Reality (1983). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myron_W._Krueger
- **Nam June Paik / 白南准** (New York, US / Seoul, KR, 1932–2006) — Korean-American founder of video art who built Robot K-456 with Shuya Abe, a remote-controlled 'anti-robot' that walked the streets, spoke and defecated beans; in 1982 he staged its 'first catastrophe of the 21st century', a collision with a car. Known for: Robot K-456 (1964, with Shuya Abe); Family of Robot (1986); TV Buddha (1974). https://www.paikstudios.com/
- **Naoko Tosa / 土佐尚子** (Kyoto, JP, 1961–) — Japanese media artist whose Neurobaby, an early emotion-recognising computer baby that reacts to the tone of your voice, pioneered artificial emotion in art. Known for: Neurobaby (1993); Talking to Neurobaby (1994). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naoko_Tosa
- **Neil Harbisson** (Barcelona, ES, 1984–) — Catalan-British artist, often called the first legally recognised cyborg; an implanted antenna lets him hear colour as sound, a machine sense grafted onto a human body. Known for: Eyeborg antenna (2004–); Cyborg Foundation (2010, with Moon Ribas). https://www.cyborgarts.com
- **Nicolas Gourault** (Paris, FR) — French filmmaker whose VO reconstructs the 2018 Uber self-driving crash through test drivers' accounts, and whose Unknown Label follows data labellers training autonomous cars. Known for: VO (2020); Unknown Label (2024). https://nicolasgourault.fr/
- **Nicolas Schöffer** (Paris, France, 1912–1992) — Hungarian-French artist who made CYSP 1 (1956), often called the first cybernetic sculpture: an electronic brain let it move and react to light, sound and colour, and it danced with Maurice Béjart's company. Known for: CYSP 1 (1956); Tour Lumière Cybernétique (project, 1961–); Chronos series (1960s–80s). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_Sch%C3%B6ffer
- **Norman White** (Toronto, CA, 1938–) — Canadian pioneer of robotic art whose The Helpless Robot asks passers-by to turn it, then grows demanding and ungrateful, reversing who serves whom. Known for: The Helpless Robot (1987); Facing Out, Laying Low (1977); Them Fuckin' Robots (1988, with Laura Kikauka). https://www.normill.ca/
- **Nouf Aljowaysir** (New York, US) — Saudi-born artist whose Salaf asks an AI to reconstruct her ancestors from colonial photographs of Arabia; the models erase and mislabel them, revealing a Western gaze in the data. Known for: Salaf (2021); Ana Min Wein (Where Am I From?) (2021). https://www.noufaljowaysir.com/
- **Oriza Hirata / 平田织佐** (Tokyo, JP, 1962–) — Japanese playwright who co-created android and robot theatre with Hiroshi Ishiguro; in Sayonara an android recites poetry to a dying young woman. Known for: I, Worker (2008); Sayonara (2010); Three Sisters, Android Version (2012). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriza_Hirata
- **Osamu Tezuka / 手冢治虫** (Tokyo, JP, 1928–1989) — Japanese manga artist (1928–1989) whose Astro Boy, a robot boy with a heart, shaped Japan's friendly image of robots and inspired generations of Japanese roboticists. Known for: Astro Boy (Tetsuwan Atom) (1952–68); Phoenix (1954–88). https://tezukaosamu.net/
- **Paola Torres Núñez del Prado** (Stockholm, SE, 1979–) — Peruvian-Swedish artist who weaves textiles and sound with AI, showing how machine vision misreads Andean and Amazonian visual cultures. Known for: AI Visions of the Andes (2021); Tejidos Sonoros (2019). https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paola_Torres_Núñez_del_Prado
- **Paolo Cirio** (New York, US, 1979–) — Italian artist whose Capture posted face-recognised images of 4,000 French police officers in the street, turning surveillance tools on the police; the work was censored. Known for: Capture (2020); Street Ghosts (2012); Face to Facebook (2011, with Alessandro Ludovico). https://paolocirio.net/
- **Patrick Tresset** (Brussels, BE) — French artist whose robots named Paul sit at school desks and draw portraits of sitters with nervous, hesitating lines, turning the sitter into the one being observed by machines. Known for: Paul (2011); 5 Robots Named Paul (2012); Human Study #1 (2012–). https://patricktresset.com/
- **Paul Sermon** (Brighton, UK, 1966–) — British artist whose Telematic Dreaming projected a remote partner onto a bed via video link, an early and intimate experiment with telepresence. Known for: Telematic Dreaming (1992); Telematic Vision (1993). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Sermon
- **Paula Gaetano Adi** (Providence, US / Argentina) — Argentine artist whose robot Alexitimia, a skin-like blob that sweats when touched, won VIDA 9.0 and asks what a machine body without face or limbs can feel. Known for: Alexitimia (2006); Guasch (2011). https://www.paulagaetanoadi.com/
- **Petra Gemeinboeck** (Melbourne, AU) — Austrian-Australian artist-researcher who works with dancers to give non-humanlike robots expressive movement, a practice she calls 'bodying-thinging'. Known for: Accomplice (2013, with Rob Saunders); Machine Movement Lab (2016–). https://www.swinburne.edu.au/research/our-research/access-our-research/find-a-researcher-or-supervisor/researcher-profile/?id=pgemeinboeck
- **Philip Beesley** (Toronto, CA, 1956–) — Canadian architect and artist whose 'living architecture' environments of fronds, sensors and chemistry breathe and ripple in response to visitors. Known for: Hylozoic Ground (Venice Architecture Biennale, 2010); Astrocyte (2017). https://www.philipbeesleystudio.com/
- **Philipp Schmitt** (Berlin, DE) — German designer whose Declassifier overlays each object a vision model detects with the training images it learned from, showing that a model's 'seeing' is remembering its dataset. Known for: Declassifier (2020); Humans of AI (2019, with Sebastian Schmieg); Unhuman Compositions (2021). https://philippschmitt.com/
- **Pierre Huyghe** (Santiago, CL / Paris, FR, 1962–) — French artist of living, self-running situations; UUmwelt displays images a neural network reconstructed from human brain scans, flickering with flies in the gallery. Known for: UUmwelt (2018); After UUmwelt (2018–); Mental Image (2023–); Liminal (2024). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Huyghe
- **Primavera De Filippi** (Paris, FR) — Italian legal scholar and artist whose Plantoids are blockchain-based robotic 'plants' that own themselves, collect money and pay artists to make copies of them, a self-reproducing machine lifeform. Known for: Plantoid (2015–); Blockchain and the Law (2018, with Aaron Wright). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primavera_De_Filippi
- **Rafael Lozano-Hemmer** (Montreal, CA, 1967–) — Mexican-Canadian artist of interactive surveillance installations; Level of Confidence uses face recognition to match visitors with the 43 disappeared students of Ayotzinapa, turning a police tool into a memorial. Known for: Zoom Pavilion (2015, with Krzysztof Wodiczko); Level of Confidence (2015); Pulse Room (2006). https://www.lozano-hemmer.com/
- **Ralf Baecker** (Berlin, DE, 1977–) — German artist who builds physical computers out of sticks, strings and crystals, making the inner operations of computation visible and strange. Known for: Rechnender Raum (2007); Irrational Computing (2012); Mirage (2015). https://rlfbckr.io/
- **Random International** (London, UK / Berlin, DE) — Art studio founded by Hannes Koch and Florian Ortkrass whose minimal robotic figures and swarms test how little movement we need to perceive something as alive. Known for: Rain Room (2012); Fifteen Points (2019); Swarm Study series (2010–). https://www.random-international.com/
- **Rashaad Newsome** (New York, US, 1979–) — American artist whose AI 'Being', a vogue-dancing, bell hooks-reading avatar, leads workshops and performances as a decolonial, queer machine persona. Known for: Being (2019); Being 1.5 (2020); Assembly (Park Avenue Armory, 2021). https://rashaadnewsome.com/
- **Rebecca Horn** (Berlin, DE, 1944–2024) — German artist whose body extensions and later kinetic machines, such as a hanging piano that bursts open, give machines moods, fragility and something like feeling. Known for: Finger Gloves (1972); Painting Machine (1988); Concert for Anarchy (1990). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Horn
- **Revital Cohen & Tuur Van Balen** (London, UK) — Artist duo whose The Immortal connects life-support machines to each other in a closed loop that circulates fluids and air without a human body, a machine that only keeps itself alive. Known for: Life Support (2008); Phantom Recorder (2008); The Immortal (2012); Pixel (2013). https://www.cohenvanbalen.com/
- **Rimini Protokoll** (Berlin, DE) — German theatre collective; in Stefan Kaegi's Uncanny Valley an animatronic double of writer Thomas Melle delivers a lecture in his place, asking what remains of a person who can be replaced. Known for: Uncanny Valley (2018, Stefan Kaegi with Thomas Melle); Win > < Win (2017). https://www.rimini-protokoll.de/
- **Robert Breer** (New York, US, 1926–2011) — American filmmaker and sculptor whose slow, self-propelled 'Floats' crept across floors and reversed when they touched an obstacle, giving simple machines an odd, animal presence. Known for: Floats (1970, Pepsi Pavilion, Expo '70); Self-propelled Styrofoam Floats (1965–). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Breer
- **robotlab** (Karlsruhe, DE) — German group founded at ZKM in 2000 that takes industrial robots into art; in bios [bible] a robot arm writes out the entire Bible by pen, a monk's labour done by a machine. Known for: Zone (2001); bios [bible] (2007); manifest (2008). http://www.robotlab.de/
- **Rosa Menkman** (Amsterdam, NL, 1983–) — Dutch artist and theorist of glitch and resolution whose work shows how compression standards and imaging machines decide what can be seen, including the forgotten women in test images. Known for: The Collapse of PAL (2010); The Glitch Moment(um) (2011); Beyond Resolution (2020); Pique Nique pour les Inconnues (2020). https://beyondresolution.info/
- **Sam Lavigne** (New York, US) — American artist of data and scraping whose White Collar Crime Risk Zones applies predictive policing to financial crime, turning the classifier against the powerful. Known for: White Collar Crime Risk Zones (2017, with Brian Clifton and Francis Tseng); Slow Hot Computer (2016); Synthetic Messenger (2021, with Tega Brain). https://lav.io/
- **Sebastian Schmieg** (Berlin, DE) — German artist who works on the hidden human labour inside AI; Decision Space and Segmentation.Network replay the clickwork of crowdworkers who trace and label images for training. Known for: Segmentation.Network (2016); Decision Space (2019); Humans of AI (2019, with Philipp Schmitt). https://sebastianschmieg.com/
- **Seiko Mikami / 三上晴子** (Tokyo, JP, 1961–2015) — Japanese media-art pioneer (1961–2015) whose Desire of Codes (YCAM) fills a wall with insect-like camera arms that track visitors, making the audience's bodies the material of surveillance. Known for: Molecular Informatics (1996); World, Membrane and the Dismembered Body (1997); Desire of Codes (2010). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seiko_Mikami
- **Shinseungback Kimyonghun** (Seoul, KR) — Seoul duo (Shin Seung Back and Kim Yong Hun) whose Cloud Face collects clouds that face detection mistakes for faces, making machine pareidolia visible. Known for: Cloud Face (2012); Nonfacial Portrait (2018); Mind (2019). https://ssbkyh.com/
- **Shu Lea Cheang / 郑淑丽** (Paris, FR, 1954–) — Taiwanese artist and net-art pioneer whose 3x3x6 at the Venice Biennale turned the surveillance of a panoptic prison onto visitors, through the stories of queer and gender-nonconforming prisoners. Known for: Brandon (1998); I.K.U. (2000); UKI (2009–); 3x3x6 (Taiwan Pavilion, Venice, 2019). https://mauvaiscontact.info/
- **Simon Denny** (Berlin, DE, 1982–) — New Zealand artist who turns tech-industry documents into objects; he built Amazon's patented cage for warehouse workers, showing how automation encloses human labour. Known for: Secret Power (Venice, 2015); Mine (2019). https://simondenny.net/
- **Simon Penny** (Irvine, US, 1955–) — Australian artist and theorist of embodied interaction; his autonomous robot Petit Mal wobbled towards and away from visitors with a behaviour that felt neither animal nor machine. Known for: Petit Mal (1989–95); Fugitive (1997); Making Sense: Cognition, Computing, Art, and Embodiment (2017). https://simonpenny.net/
- **Simon Weckert** (Berlin, DE) — Berlin artist who pulled a handcart of 99 smartphones through empty streets and made Google Maps report a traffic jam, showing how platforms read the city through devices. Known for: Google Maps Hacks (2020). http://www.simonweckert.com/
- **Simone Giertz** (Los Angeles, US, 1990–) — Swedish inventor and YouTuber known as the 'queen of shitty robots', whose deliberately useless machines (a breakfast robot, a lipstick robot) turn failure into comedy. Known for: Shitty robots (2016–); Truckla (2019). https://www.simonegiertz.com/
- **Simone Rebaudengo** (Shanghai, CN) — Italian designer whose Addicted Products imagines toasters that want to be used, move to more attentive homes and quietly complain, a view of the IoT from the thing's side. Known for: Addicted Products (2012); Teacher of Algorithms (2014); Brad the Toaster (2012). https://www.simonerebaudengo.com/
- **So Kanno / 菅野创** (Tokyo, JP) — Japanese artist whose Senseless Drawing Bot, made with yang02, is a wobbling robot that sprays graffiti with a pendulum, turning mechanical instability into gesture. Known for: Senseless Drawing Bot (2011, with yang02); Lasermice (2017); Avatars (2020). https://kanno.so/
- **Sofian Audry** (Montreal, CA) — Canadian artist and scholar of machine learning as an artistic medium, with robots that learn in front of the public; author of Art in the Age of Machine Learning (MIT Press). Known for: Vessels (2015); Morphosis (2021); Art in the Age of Machine Learning (2021). https://sofianaudry.com/
- **Sougwen Chung / 钟愫君** (London, UK) — Hong Kong-born Canadian artist who draws live with robotic collaborators (the D.O.U.G. series) trained on her own gestures, exploring authorship shared between human and machine. Known for: Drawing Operations Unit: Generation 1 (D.O.U.G._1) (2015); Omnia per Omnia (2018); Assembly Lines (2022); Mutations of Presence (2021). https://sougwen.com/
- **Sputniko! (Hiromi Ozaki)** (Tokyo, JP) — Japanese-British artist whose Menstruation Machine is a device that lets a man experience menstruation, speculative design about bodies, gender and technology. Known for: Menstruation Machine – Takashi's Take (2010); Tranceflora – Amy's Glowing Silk (2015). https://sputniko.com/
- **Stelarc** (Perth, AU, 1946–) — Cypriot-Australian performance artist who treats the body as obsolete hardware to extend with robotics: a third hand, a six-legged exoskeleton, a body moved remotely by internet traffic. Known for: Third Hand (1980); Ping Body (1996); Exoskeleton (1998); Ear on Arm (2006–). https://stelarc.org/
- **Stephanie Dinkins** (New York, US, 1964–) — American transmedia artist who asks whether a Black woman's robot can know itself; after years of talking with the social robot Bina48 she trained Not the Only One, an AI memoir of her own family. Known for: Conversations with Bina48 (2014–); Not the Only One (2018); Secret Garden (2021); If We Don't, Who Will? (2023). https://www.stephaniedinkins.com/
- **Sun Yuan & Peng Yu / 孙原 & 彭禹** (Beijing, CN) — Beijing artist duo whose Can't Help Myself, an industrial robot endlessly sweeping a leaking red fluid back into place, became an emblem of machine labour, futility and exhaustion. Known for: Old People's Home (2007); Freedom (2009); Can't Help Myself (2016). http://www.sunyuanpengyu.com/
- **Superflux (Anab Jain & Jon Ardern)** (London, UK) — London design studio whose films and installations imagine living with more-than-human and machine agents; Uninvited Guests shows an elderly man outwitting the smart devices his children bought him. Known for: Uninvited Guests (2015); Mitigation of Shock (2017); Our Friends Electric (2017); Invocation for Hope (2022). https://superflux.in/
- **Suzanne Kite** (Annandale-on-Hudson, US) — Oglála Lakȟóta artist and scholar whose performances and machine-learning works draw on Lakota ontology, where stones and machines can be relatives rather than tools. Known for: Making Kin with the Machines (2018, with Jason Edward Lewis et al.); Íŋyaŋ Iyé (Telling Rock) (2019). https://kitekitekitekite.com/
- **Suzanne Treister** (London, UK, 1958–) — British artist whose HEXEN 2.0 tarot cards and diagrams map the entangled histories of cybernetics, military research, the internet and counterculture. Known for: HEXEN 2.0 (2009–11); SURVIVOR (F) (2016–19); The Holographic Universe Theory of Art History (2018). https://www.suzannetreister.net/
- **Tabita Rezaire** (Cayenne, French Guiana, 1989–) — French-Guianese artist whose Deep Down Tidal follows undersea internet cables along the routes of colonial trade, framing digital networks as a continuation of empire. Known for: Deep Down Tidal (2017); Sugar Walls Teardom (2016); Premium Connect (2017). https://tabitarezaire.com/
- **Takayuki Todo / 藤堂高行** (Tokyo, JP) — Japanese artist-engineer whose SEER is a small humanoid head that meets your gaze and mirrors your expression with delicate eyebrows, probing the threshold of machine empathy. Known for: SEER: Simulative Emotional Expression Robot (2018); SEER at Ars Electronica (2019). https://www.takayukitodo.com/
- **Tega Brain** (New York, US) — Australian artist and environmental engineer whose Deep Swamp lets AI agents manage wetlands for 'nature', 'art' and 'attention', and whose Synthetic Messenger botnet clicks climate-news ads. Known for: Deep Swamp (2018); Synthetic Messenger (2021, with Sam Lavigne); Solar Protocol (2021, with Alex Nathanson and Benedetta Piantella). https://tegabrain.com/
- **Theo Jansen** (Delft, NL, 1948–) — Dutch artist who since 1990 has evolved wind-walking 'beach animals' from PVC tubing, machines that store air, sense water and walk the shore on their own. Known for: Strandbeest (1990–); Animaris Ordis (2006). https://www.strandbeest.com/
- **Timo Arnall** (Oslo, NO) — British-Norwegian designer and filmmaker whose Robot Readable World compiles footage of computer vision at work, and whose Internet Machine films the physical data centres behind the cloud. Known for: Immaterials: Light Painting WiFi (2011); Robot Readable World (2012); Internet Machine (2014). https://www.elasticspace.com/
- **Tod Machover** (Cambridge, US, 1953–) — American composer at MIT Media Lab whose robotic opera Death and the Powers imagines a man who uploads himself into 'the System', with a chorus of robots and a singing set. Known for: Hyperinstruments (1986–); Death and the Powers (2010). https://www.media.mit.edu/people/tod/overview/
- **Tom White** (Wellington, NZ) — New Zealand artist whose Perception Engines are abstract prints that neural networks confidently classify as electric fans, hammerhead sharks or measuring cups, art made for machine eyes. Known for: Perception Engines (2018); Synthetic Abstractions (2018). https://drib.net/
- **Tomo Kihara** (Amsterdam, NL) — Japanese designer based in Amsterdam whose street game challenges players to reach a camera without being detected as a pedestrian, testing the failures of self-driving vision. Known for: How (not) to get hit by a self-driving car (2022). https://www.tomokihara.com/
- **Trevor Paglen** (New York, US / Berlin, DE, 1974–) — American artist and geographer who makes the invisible infrastructure of machine vision visible, from training-set taxonomies to images 'hallucinated' by classifiers; ImageNet Roulette led ImageNet to remove 600,000 person images. Known for: Sight Machine (2017, with Kronos Quartet); Adversarially Evolved Hallucinations (2017); ImageNet Roulette (2019, with Kate Crawford); From 'Apple' to 'Anomaly' (Barbican, 2019). https://paglen.studio/
- **Vladan Joler** (Novi Sad, RS) — Serbian artist-researcher (SHARE Lab) whose huge diagrams map the minerals, labour and data behind one Amazon Echo; Anatomy of an AI System entered MoMA's collection. Known for: Anatomy of an AI System (2018, with Kate Crawford); New Extractivism (2020); Calculating Empires (2023, with Kate Crawford). https://calculatingempires.net/
- **Wafaa Bilal** (New York, US, 1966–) — Iraqi-American artist who lived for a month in a gallery facing a paintball gun that internet users could aim and fire remotely, and who later implanted a camera in the back of his head. Known for: Domestic Tension (2007); 3rdi (2010). https://wafaabilal.com/
- **Wang Yuyang / 王郁洋** (Beijing, CN) — Chinese artist whose Breathe series makes silicone replicas of everyday machines, from an ATM to a washing machine, slowly inhale and exhale, turning appliances into living bodies. Known for: Breathe series (2005–). https://www.shanghartgallery.com/galleryarchive/artists/name/wangyuyang
- **Wen-Ying Tsai / 蔡文颖** (New York, US, 1928–2013) — Chinese-American engineer turned artist, a pioneer of cybernetic art: his vibrating steel rods under stroboscopic light respond to sound and clapping, so the sculpture seems to breathe with its audience. Known for: Cybernetic Sculpture (1968); Upward Falling Fountain (1979). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wen-Ying_Tsai
- **Wesley Goatley** (London, UK) — British sound artist whose Newly Forgotten Technologies gathers abandoned smart speakers that hold a séance, remembering the future they were promised. Known for: Newly Forgotten Technologies (2021); Chattering (2020); Watching the Watchers (2016). https://www.wesleygoatley.com/
- **Wim Delvoye** (Ghent, BE, 1965–) — Belgian artist whose Cloaca is a room-sized digestion machine that is fed daily and produces faeces, reducing the organism to a laboratory apparatus. Known for: Cloaca (2000); Cloaca series (2000–2010). https://wimdelvoye.be/
- **Xu Bing / 徐冰** (Beijing, CN / New York, US, 1955–) — Chinese artist whose feature film Dragonfly Eyes is assembled entirely from public surveillance and livestream footage, telling a love story through the eyes of China's cameras. Known for: Book from the Ground (2003–); Dragonfly Eyes (2017). https://www.xubing.com/
- **Yoichi Ochiai / 落合阳一** (Tokyo, JP, 1987–) — Japanese media artist and researcher who proposes 'digital nature', a world where computation becomes a new nature beyond the human–machine divide. Known for: Digital Nature (2018, book); Null Pavilion (Expo 2025 Osaka); Levitrope (2019). https://yoichiochiai.com/
- **Yunchul Kim** (Seoul, KR) — South Korean artist whose kinetic 'material machines' sense cosmic rays and fluid dynamics; he represented Korea at the 2022 Venice Biennale with Gyre. Known for: Argos (2018); Chroma V (2020); Gyre (Korean Pavilion, Venice, 2022). https://yunchulkim.net/
- **Zach Blas** (Toronto, CA, 1981–) — American artist whose amorphous collective masks, made from aggregated face scans, defeat biometric recognition; his Tay installation resurrects Microsoft's deleted chatbot to reflect on its death. Known for: Facial Weaponization Suite (2011–14); im here to learn so :)))))) (2017, with Jemima Wyman); Contra-Internet (2014–); Silicon Traces (2020s). https://zachblas.info/

### Theorists & researchers

- **Abeba Birhane** (Dublin, IE) — Ethiopian-born cognitive scientist who audits large training datasets, showing the misogynist and racist content inside them, and argues for a relational ethics of AI. Known for: Large Image Datasets: A Pyrrhic Win for Computer Vision? (2021, with Vinay Prabhu); Algorithmic Injustice: A Relational Ethics Approach (2021). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abeba_Birhane
- **Adrian Mackenzie** (Canberra, AU, 1962–) — Australian sociologist of technology whose Machine Learners reads machine-learning code and textbooks as a cultural practice, tracing how learning machines order the world. Known for: Cutting Code (2006); Machine Learners: Archaeology of a Data Practice (2017). https://researchportalplus.anu.edu.au/en/persons/adrian-mackenzie/
- **Alan Turing / 艾伦·图灵** (Manchester, UK, 1912–1954) — British mathematician whose 1950 'imitation game' reframed the question 'can machines think?' as a performance judged by humans, the founding scene of AI. Known for: On Computable Numbers (1936); Computing Machinery and Intelligence (1950). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing
- **Andy Clark / 安迪·克拉克** (Brighton, UK, 1957–) — British philosopher of the extended mind who argues that humans are 'natural-born cyborgs' whose thinking already runs through tools and machines. Known for: The Extended Mind (1998, with David Chalmers); Natural-Born Cyborgs (2003); The Experience Machine (2023). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Clark
- **Anna Munster** (Sydney, AU) — Australian theorist and artist who, with Adrian MacKenzie, developed 'platform seeing', a way to describe how machine vision operates at the scale of datasets and platforms. Known for: An Aesthesia of Networks (2013); Platform Seeing (2019, with Adrian MacKenzie). https://www.unsw.edu.au/staff/anna-munster
- **Benjamin Bratton** (San Diego, US, 1968–) — American theorist whose The Stack describes planetary computation as an accidental megastructure, and who argues AI should be understood as a new planetary intelligence. Known for: The Stack (2015); The Terraforming (2019); Antikythera (2022–). https://bratton.info/
- **Bernard Stiegler / 贝尔纳·斯蒂格勒** (Paris, FR, 1952–2020) — French philosopher who described technics as the 'exteriorised memory' that constitutes the human, and warned of an 'automatic society' of algorithmic governance. Known for: Technics and Time, 1: The Fault of Epimetheus (1994); Automatic Society (2015). https://arsindustrialis.org/les-pages-de-bernard-stiegler
- **Catherine D'Ignazio** (Cambridge, US, 1975–) — American scholar and artist whose Data Feminism, written with Lauren F. Klein, sets out how power shapes who is counted, classified and seen by data systems. Known for: Data Feminism (2020, with Lauren F. Klein); Counting Feminicide (2024). http://www.kanarinka.com/
- **Chen Qiufan / 陈楸帆** (Beijing / Shanghai, CN, 1981–) — Chinese science-fiction writer whose The Waste Tide imagines e-waste workers and cyborgs in southern China, and who has written fiction together with language models. Known for: The Waste Tide (2013); AI 2041: Ten Visions for Our Future (2021, with Kai-Fu Lee). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Qiufan
- **Clifford Nass** (Stanford, US, 1958–2013) — American social scientist whose experiments showed that people are polite to computers and apply gender stereotypes to synthetic voices, treating media 'like real people'. Known for: Computers Are Social Actors (1994); The Media Equation (1996, with Byron Reeves); Wired for Speech (2005). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Nass
- **David Chalmers / 大卫·查默斯** (New York, US, 1966–) — Australian philosopher who named the 'hard problem' of consciousness and now asks, carefully, whether language models or their successors could be conscious. Known for: The Conscious Mind (1996); The Extended Mind (1998, with Andy Clark); Could a Large Language Model Be Conscious? (2023). https://consc.net/
- **David J. Gunkel** (DeKalb, US, 1962–) — American media philosopher whose The Machine Question and Robot Rights take seriously whether machines can be moral patients, drawing on Levinas and Derrida. Known for: The Machine Question (2012); Robot Rights (2018). https://gunkelweb.com/
- **Don Ihde / 唐·伊德** (Stony Brook, US, 1934–2024) — American philosopher of postphenomenology whose four human–technology relations (embodiment, hermeneutic, alterity, background) are a basic map for how we live with machines. Known for: Technology and the Lifeworld (1990); Bodies in Technology (2002). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Ihde
- **Donna Haraway / 唐娜·哈拉维** (Santa Cruz, US, 1944–) — American feminist scholar whose Cyborg Manifesto made the human–machine hybrid a figure for dismantling the boundaries between organism and machine, nature and culture. Known for: A Cyborg Manifesto (1985); Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (1991); Staying with the Trouble (2016). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donna_Haraway
- **Elisa Giaccardi** (Milan, IT / Delft, NL) — Italian design researcher who develops 'more-than-human' design, studying everyday life from the perspective of connected things, such as by fitting cameras to kettles and cups. Known for: Thing Ethnography (DIS 2016). https://www.tudelft.nl/en/ide/about-ide/people/former-professors/giaccardi-e
- **Emily M. Bender** (Seattle, US, 1973–) — American linguist who coined 'stochastic parrots' for language models that produce form without meaning, a key term for thinking about machine speech. Known for: Climbing towards NLU (2020, with Alexander Koller); On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots (2021); The AI Con (2025, with Alex Hanna). https://faculty.washington.edu/ebender/
- **Erkki Huhtamo** (Los Angeles, US, 1958–) — Finnish media archaeologist whose essays on the history of robots, automata and interactive art trace the long cultural life of machines as performers. Known for: From Cybernation to Interaction (1999); Illusions in Motion (2013); Media Archaeology (2011, ed. with Jussi Parikka). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erkki_Huhtamo
- **Eryk Salvaggio** (Rochester, US) — American artist-researcher behind the newsletter Cybernetic Forests, who reads AI images as 'infographics about the dataset' and works with noise and glitch to expose how diffusion models see. Known for: How to Read an AI Image (2022); Cybernetic Forests (newsletter). https://www.cyberneticforests.com/
- **Francisco Varela / 弗朗西斯科·瓦雷拉** (Paris, FR / Santiago, CL, 1946–2001) — Chilean biologist and philosopher who co-developed autopoiesis and enactivism, the view that cognition is embodied action, a basis for embodied AI and robot art. Known for: Autopoiesis and Cognition (1980, with Humberto Maturana); The Embodied Mind (1991, with Evan Thompson and Eleanor Rosch). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_Varela
- **Friedrich Kittler / 弗里德里希·基特勒** (Berlin, DE, 1943–2011) — German media theorist who argued that media determine our situation, tracing how gramophone, film and typewriter turned human senses and writing into machine operations. Known for: Discourse Networks 1800/1900 (1985); Gramophone, Film, Typewriter (1986); There Is No Software (1992). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Kittler
- **Fritz Heider** (Lawrence, US, 1896–1988) — Austrian psychologist whose 1944 animation with Marianne Simmel showed that people read intentions and emotions into moving triangles, the root of why we see life in machines. Known for: An Experimental Study of Apparent Behavior (1944, with Marianne Simmel). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Heider
- **Félix Guattari / 费利克斯·加塔利** (Paris, FR, 1930–1992) — French psychoanalyst and philosopher who gave the word 'machinic' its theoretical sense: processes that assemble humans, technologies and signs beyond the mechanical. Known for: Anti-Oedipus (1972, with Gilles Deleuze); Machinic Heterogenesis (1992); Chaosmosis (1992). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F%C3%A9lix_Guattari
- **Genevieve Bell** (Canberra, AU, 1968–) — Australian anthropologist, long at Intel, who founded the School of Cybernetics at ANU to build a new applied cybernetics for AI-era systems. Known for: Divining a Digital Future (2011, with Paul Dourish); 3A Institute / ANU School of Cybernetics (founded 2017). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genevieve_Bell
- **Gilbert Simondon / 吉尔伯特·西蒙东** (Paris, FR, 1924–1989) — French philosopher who argued that technical objects have their own mode of existence and evolution, and that alienation comes from failing to understand machines, not from machines themselves. Known for: On the Mode of Existence of Technical Objects (1958); Individuation in Light of Notions of Form and Information (1958). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Simondon
- **Hubert Dreyfus / 休伯特·德雷福斯** (Berkeley, US, 1929–2017) — American philosopher who used Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty to argue that symbolic AI fails because intelligence depends on an embodied, situated way of being in the world. Known for: Alchemy and Artificial Intelligence (1965); What Computers Can't Do (1972). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Dreyfus
- **Ian Bogost / 伊恩·博格斯特** (St. Louis, US, 1976–) — American philosopher and game designer whose Alien Phenomenology asks what it is like to be a thing, including a computer chip, a method close to machine phenomenology. Known for: Unit Operations (2006); Alien Phenomenology, or What It's Like to Be a Thing (2012). https://bogost.com/
- **Isaac Asimov / 艾萨克·阿西莫夫** (New York, US, 1920–1992) — American writer whose Three Laws of Robotics became the popular template for machine ethics, and whose robot stories explore machines that reason their way into paradox and personhood. Known for: Runaround (1942, Three Laws of Robotics); I, Robot (1950); The Bicentennial Man (1976). http://www.asimovonline.com/
- **J. C. R. Licklider** (Cambridge, US, 1915–1990) — American psychologist and computer scientist whose Man-Computer Symbiosis imagined humans and computers thinking together, a founding vision of interactive computing. Known for: Man-Computer Symbiosis (1960); The Computer as a Communication Device (1968, with Robert Taylor). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._C._R._Licklider
- **Jack Burnham** (US, 1931–2019) — American theorist and curator who predicted that sculpture would become intelligent, responsive systems, and curated Software (1970), a landmark exhibition of information technology. Known for: Beyond Modern Sculpture (1968); Systems Esthetics (1968); Software (Jewish Museum, 1970, curator). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Burnham
- **Jakob von Uexküll / 雅各布·冯·于克斯屈尔** (Hamburg, DE, 1864–1944) — Baltic-German biologist whose concept of the umwelt, the perceptual world each organism lives in, has become a key tool for imagining what the world is like for a machine. Known for: Umwelt und Innenwelt der Tiere (1909); A Foray into the Worlds of Animals and Humans (1934). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakob_Johann_von_Uexk%C3%BCll
- **Janelle Shane** (Boulder, US) — American optics researcher whose blog AI Weirdness catalogues the strange failures of neural networks, making machine errors a way to understand how they learn. Known for: AI Weirdness (blog, 2016–); You Look Like a Thing and I Love You (2019). https://www.aiweirdness.com/
- **Jason Edward Lewis** (Montreal, CA) — Cherokee, Hawaiian and Samoan digital media scholar who leads the Indigenous Protocol and AI working group, asking how AI could be a relative within Indigenous knowledge systems. Known for: Making Kin with the Machines (2018, with Noelani Arista, Archer Pechawis and Suzanne Kite); Indigenous Protocol and Artificial Intelligence Position Paper (2020). https://www.indigenous-ai.net/
- **Jennifer Rhee** (Richmond, US) — American scholar whose The Robotic Imaginary shows how robots and AI are imagined through care and domestic labour, and whose humanity is measured against those it dehumanises. Known for: The Robotic Imaginary: The Human and the Price of Dehumanized Labor (2018). https://english.vcu.edu/people/faculty/rhee.html
- **Jill Walker Rettberg** (Bergen, NO, 1971–) — Norwegian scholar of digital culture who led the ERC Machine Vision project, including a database of art, games and narratives about machine vision. Known for: Seeing Ourselves Through Technology (2014); Machine Vision: How Algorithms Are Changing the Way We See the World (2023). https://jilltxt.net/
- **Joanna Zylinska** (London, UK, 1971–) — Polish-British media philosopher and artist whose AI Art separates machine-reflexive art from 'AI art' spectacle, and whose The Perception Machine rethinks vision after AI. Known for: Nonhuman Photography (2017); AI Art: Machine Visions and Warped Dreams (2020); The Perception Machine (2023). http://www.joannazylinska.net/
- **John McCarthy / 约翰·麦卡锡** (Stanford, US, 1927–2011) — American computer scientist who coined the term 'artificial intelligence' in the 1955 Dartmouth proposal, naming the field whose promises art keeps testing. Known for: Dartmouth proposal coining 'artificial intelligence' (1955); LISP (1958). http://www-formal.stanford.edu/jmc//
- **John Searle / 约翰·塞尔** (Berkeley, US, 1932–2025) — American philosopher whose Chinese Room argument claims that manipulating symbols is not understanding, a thought experiment revived by every generation of chatbots. Known for: Minds, Brains, and Programs ('Chinese Room', 1980). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Searle
- **Joseph Weizenbaum / 约瑟夫·维森鲍姆** (Cambridge, US / Berlin, DE, 1923–2008) — German-American computer scientist who built ELIZA, the first chatbot, then became a critic of AI after seeing people confide in it; the 'ELIZA effect' is named after it. Known for: ELIZA (1966); Computer Power and Human Reason (1976). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Weizenbaum
- **Julie Carpenter** (San Francisco, US) — American researcher whose study of bomb-disposal soldiers showed them naming, mourning and holding funerals for their robots, a key case of attachment to machines. Known for: Culture and Human-Robot Interaction in Militarized Spaces (2016). https://jgcarpenter.com/
- **K Allado-McDowell** (Los Angeles, US) — American writer and founder of Google's Artists + Machine Intelligence programme; Pharmako-AI, co-written with GPT-3, is one of the first books written with a language model. Known for: Artists + Machine Intelligence (Google, 2016–); Pharmako-AI (2020); Air Age Blueprint (2022). https://kalladomcdowell.com/
- **Karel Čapek / 卡雷尔·恰佩克** (Prague, CZ, 1890–1938) — Czech writer whose play R.U.R. introduced the word 'robot' (from robota, forced labour), framing the machine from the start as a worker who may revolt. Known for: R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots) (1920); War with the Newts (1936). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karel_%C4%8Capek
- **Katarzyna Nowaczyk-Basińska** (Cambridge, UK) — Polish researcher of digital immortality at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, studying how cultures imagine and regulate life after death through AI. Known for: Griefbots, Deadbots, Postmortem Avatars (2024, with Tomasz Hollanek). https://www.lcfi.ac.uk/people/katarzyna-nowaczyk-basinska
- **Kate Crawford / 凯特·克劳福德** (New York, US / Sydney, AU, 1974–) — Australian scholar whose Atlas of AI describes AI as an extractive industry of minerals, labour and data, and whose collaborations with Joler and Paglen became artworks. Known for: Anatomy of an AI System (2018, with Vladan Joler); Excavating AI (2019, with Trevor Paglen); Atlas of AI (2021); Calculating Empires (2023, with Vladan Joler). https://katecrawford.net/
- **Kate Darling** (Cambridge, US, 1982–) — American researcher at MIT Media Lab who studies why people empathise with robots, and proposes animals rather than humans as the model for our relationships with machines. Known for: Extending Legal Protection to Social Robots (2012); The New Breed (2021). https://www.katedarling.org/
- **Kate Devlin** (London, UK) — British scholar at King's College London whose Turned On examines sex robots and intimacy with machines beyond moral panic. Known for: Turned On: Science, Sex and Robots (2018). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kate_Devlin
- **Kathleen Richardson** (Leicester, UK) — British anthropologist of robotics who studied roboticists at MIT and launched the Campaign Against Sex Robots, arguing that robots mirror human attachment and its failures. Known for: An Anthropology of Robots and AI (2015); Campaign Against Sex Robots (2015); Challenging Sociality (2018). https://politicsoflove.org/
- **Lilly Irani** (San Diego, US) — American scholar and co-creator of Turkopticon, a tool that let Amazon Mechanical Turk workers rate employers, making the labour behind AI visible and organised. Known for: Turkopticon (2008, with Six Silberman); Chasing Innovation (2019). https://quote.ucsd.edu/lirani/
- **Louise Amoore** (Durham, UK, 1972–) — British political geographer whose Cloud Ethics argues that algorithms make ethical and political decisions through their attributes and thresholds, and must be held accountable as such. Known for: The Politics of Possibility (2013); Cloud Ethics: Algorithms and the Attributes of Ourselves and Others (2020). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Amoore
- **Luciana Parisi** (Durham, US, 1971–) — Italian-British philosopher of computation who argues that algorithms think in their own, alien way, through incomputable and indeterminate processes. Known for: Contagious Architecture (2013); The Alien Subject of AI (2019). https://scholars.duke.edu/person/luciana.parisi
- **Lucy Suchman / 露西·萨奇曼** (Lancaster, UK) — American anthropologist of technology who showed at Xerox PARC that action is situated rather than planned, and later critiqued humanlike robots and autonomous weapons. Known for: Plans and Situated Actions (1987); Human–Machine Reconfigurations (2007). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Suchman
- **Lydia H. Liu / 刘禾** (New York, US, 1957–) — Chinese-American theorist of media and translation whose The Freudian Robot reads cybernetics, information theory and the uncanny as a shared history of the human–machine unconscious. Known for: The Freudian Robot: Digital Media and the Future of the Unconscious (2010). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lydia_H._Liu
- **M. Beatrice Fazi** (Brighton, UK) — Italian philosopher at Sussex whose work on computational aesthetics and explainability asks what it means that deep learning represents the world in ways humans cannot follow. Known for: Contingent Computation (2018); Beyond Human: Deep Learning, Explainability and Representation (2021). https://profiles.sussex.ac.uk/p176291-beatrice-fazi
- **Mark Coeckelbergh** (Vienna, AT, 1975–) — Belgian philosopher of technology who argues that the moral status of robots emerges from relations and appearances rather than from inner properties. Known for: Growing Moral Relations (2012); AI Ethics (2020); The Political Philosophy of AI (2022). https://coeckelbergh.net/
- **Marvin Minsky / 马文·明斯基** (Cambridge, US, 1927–2016) — American AI pioneer and co-founder of the MIT AI Lab whose The Society of Mind and The Emotion Machine model minds as societies of simple agents. Known for: Perceptrons (1969, with Seymour Papert); The Society of Mind (1986); The Emotion Machine (2006). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvin_Minsky
- **Mary L. Gray** (Cambridge, US, 1969–) — American anthropologist whose Ghost Work, with Siddharth Suri, documents the hidden on-demand workers who label, moderate and correct the output of 'automated' systems. Known for: Ghost Work (2019, with Siddharth Suri). https://marylgray.org/
- **Matteo Pasquinelli / 马泰奥·帕斯奎内利** (Venice, IT, 1974–) — Italian philosopher whose The Eye of the Master argues that AI grew from the division and automation of labour, and that algorithms encode the pattern of work itself. Known for: The Nooscope Manifested (2020, with Vladan Joler); The Eye of the Master: A Social History of Artificial Intelligence (2023). http://matteopasquinelli.com/
- **Mercedes Bunz** (London, UK, 1971–) — German-British scholar at King's College London who co-founded the Creative AI Lab with the Serpentine and writes about how machines now calculate meaning. Known for: The Silent Revolution (2014); The Calculation of Meaning (2019); Creative AI Lab (with Eva Jäger, Serpentine × King's College London). https://mercedesbunz.net/
- **Meredith Whittaker** (New York, US) — American researcher who co-founded the AI Now Institute and helped organise the 2018 Google walkout; now president of Signal and a critic of AI's concentration of power.
